lessons.title: How the Pieces Move
lessons.summary: Meet every piece on the board

steps.title: Welcome
steps.text:
Sixty-four squares, thirty-two pieces, infinite stories. That's chess.

The board you see in front of you is the starting position of every game ever played by Capablanca, Fischer, Kasparov, and Carlsen. White always moves first, then Black, alternating until one king is checkmated, the players agree to a draw, or time runs out.

## What you'll learn here

- How each of the **six piece types** moves and captures
- Why some pieces are stronger than others
- The vocabulary you'll use for the rest of your chess life

Don't try to memorize everything. Each piece has one or two simple rules — once you've moved them a few times, the patterns become muscle memory.

> The pieces are characters in a story. Learn how each one walks before you ask them to dance.

steps.title: The Pawn
steps.text:
The humble pawn — the soul of chess, said the master Philidor.

A pawn is the only piece that **moves and captures differently**. It marches forward one square at a time, never sideways and never backward. On its very first move, it has the option to leap two squares — a single jolt of energy before its long, slow career.

## Three things every pawn can do

- **Step forward** one square, only if that square is empty
- **Leap two squares** from its starting rank — handy for the opening
- **Capture diagonally** one square forward, taking an enemy piece

And one magical reward awaits: a pawn that reaches the far side **promotes** into any piece you choose (queens are the popular pick). A foot soldier becomes a queen. That's the dream.

For example, from the starting square, the e-pawn can play {{e3}} or {{e4}}.

> Pawns can never go back — choose their path with care.

steps.prompt: Push the e-pawn two squares to claim the center with **{{e4}}**.
steps.hint: On a pawn's very first move, it can leap two squares. The center is a great place to land.

steps.title: The Knight
steps.text:
The knight is the trickster of the chessboard.

Unlike every other piece, the knight does **not** travel in straight lines. It hops in an **L-shape**: two squares one direction (rank or file), then one square perpendicular. From a central square, a knight reaches up to eight different squares — like petals around a flower.

## What makes knights special

- **They jump.** No other piece can leap over friendly or enemy pieces — knights soar over them.
- **They love the center.** A knight on the rim attacks just two or three squares; a knight in the center attacks eight.
- **They're slow but devastating.** A knight can take four moves to cross the board, but in the right outpost it's a monster.

From h1, the knight can hop to {{Nf2}} or {{Ng3}}. Notice how the L-shape works — count two squares one way, one square the other.

> A knight on the rim is dim. A knight in the middle is a riddle.

steps.prompt: Develop the knight toward the action. Try **{{Nf2}}** or **{{Ng3}}** — both are L-shaped jumps from h1.
steps.hint: Two squares one direction, then one square perpendicular. From h1, what squares does that reach?

steps.title: The Bishop
steps.text:
Bishops are the diagonal aristocrats. They glide as far as they like along the slanted lines of the board — but only on **one color forever**.

The bishop you see here lives on dark squares; its partner (when she joins) will live on light squares. Together they cover the whole board. Apart, each one has half the world hidden from her.

## Bishop fundamentals

- **Range is long, but blocked by pieces.** A bishop's beam stops at the first piece in its path.
- **Open positions are paradise.** Few pawns means the bishop can stretch.
- **The two bishops together** are called the *bishop pair* and are slightly stronger than a pair of knights.

From c1, this bishop can swing to {{Bd2}}, {{Be3}}, {{Bf4}}, all the way to {{Bh6}} if nothing is in the way.

> A bishop is a long-range sniper. Give her open lines and she'll dominate.

steps.title: The Rook
steps.text:
Rooks are the heavy infantry — straight lines and brute force.

A rook moves any number of squares along **ranks** (rows) or **files** (columns). Like a bishop, its beam stops at the first piece. Unlike a bishop, it can change colors and reach every square on the board, eventually.

## What rooks love

- **Open files.** A file with no pawns is a rook's highway.
- **The 7th rank** (or 2nd from your opponent's side). Rooks here harvest pawns and harass the king.
- **Endgames.** With the board emptied, rooks become unstoppable.

A rook's other special trick is **castling** — the only time a king and rook move together, on the same turn. We'll cover that in its own lesson.

> Bring rooks out late. They're slow to develop, but in the endgame they rule.

steps.title: The Queen
steps.text:
The queen is the most powerful piece on the board — by a long way.

She moves like a **rook and bishop combined**: any number of squares along ranks, files, OR diagonals. From a central square, she can attack 27 squares at once. No other piece comes close.

## A note of caution

- **Don't bring her out too early.** Each time she's attacked, she has to retreat — and you waste a tempo.
- **Trade carefully.** Losing a queen for less is usually losing the game.
- **In attacks, she's the conductor.** Pair her with a knight or bishop and devastating combinations appear.

A queen on d1 can flow to {{Qd5}}, swing to {{Qa4}}, or strike along {{Qh5}} — only blocked when she meets a piece.

> Power is patient. Develop your minor pieces first; the queen joins the dance later.

steps.title: The King
steps.text:
The king is the heart of every position. Lose him, and the game is over.

The king plods just **one square in any direction**: forward, backward, sideways, or diagonally. Modest range, but he carries the whole game on his shoulders. He can never step into a square attacked by an enemy piece — that would be illegal, since walking into check ends the game.

## Two phases, two roles

- **Opening and middlegame:** *hide him.* Castle as soon as you can. The king belongs in a corner, behind a wall of pawns.
- **Endgame:** *activate him.* With queens off and danger reduced, the king becomes a fighting piece worth roughly three pawns.

This switch — from cowering to charging — is one of chess's deepest ideas.

> Protect your king as if your life depends on it. Because in chess, it does.

lessons.title: Check & Checkmate
lessons.summary: Understand the goal of every game

steps.title: The Goal
steps.text:
Chess has exactly **one** way to win: deliver **checkmate**. That means attacking the enemy king in a way he cannot escape — no square to run to, no piece to block with, no way to capture the attacker.

## Three terms to lock in

- **Check** — the king is attacked, but has at least one legal way out.
- **Checkmate** — the king is attacked, and there's no legal move at all. Game over.
- **Stalemate** — the king is *not* in check, but the side to move has no legal move. Draw.

In the position you see, your queen and king are working together. The king cuts off the e7, d6, and f6 escape squares; the queen will deliver the final blow. This pattern — king + queen vs lone king — should always be a win.

> The king never actually dies in chess. He simply runs out of moves.

steps.prompt: Slide the queen to the back rank for **{{Qb8#}}** (or **{{Qh8#}}**) — the king has nowhere to run.
steps.hint: Your king on e6 already controls d7, e7, and f7. Hit the 8th rank with the queen and the king is trapped.

steps.title: Different Angle, Same Idea
steps.text:
Same ingredients, different layout. The king-and-queen pattern is incredibly common, so you want it in your bones.

Notice the recipe:

- **Your king** stands one square away from the enemy king, taking three of his escape squares.
- **Your queen** delivers check — and because the kings are face-to-face, the enemy king has no flight square.

When the kings stand on the same file or rank with one square between them, that's called *opposition*. It's a magical formation: it lets the queen step in for the kill without being captured.

> King and queen working together is the gold standard mating duo.

steps.prompt: Cut off the 8th rank with **{{Qa8#}}** — the king has no escape.
steps.hint: Your king already covers c7, d7, and e7. You need a queen move that attacks d8 from a square the king can't capture.

steps.title: Back-Rank Mate
steps.text:
The most-played mating pattern in club chess: the **back-rank mate**.

A castled king is safe — until those same loyal pawns become his prison. When the f, g, and h pawns haven't moved, the king has no escape route. A rook or queen sliding onto the back rank delivers mate without a single sacrifice.

## What to look for

- The enemy king on the **back rank** with **no escape squares**.
- An **open file** to that back rank for your rook or queen.
- No defender on the back rank to capture you or block.

For example, after {{Ra8+}}, if Black has no piece to interpose and the king can't run, it's mate. That's exactly what's about to happen here.

> Always make a *luft* — push a pawn, free your king. Forget, and back-rank mate finds you sooner or later.

steps.prompt: Slide the rook to the back rank with **{{Ra8#}}** — the king's own pawns trap him.
steps.hint: The king on g8 can only flee to f7 or h7 — but his pawns block both. So a rook on the 8th rank ends it.

lessons.title: Castling
lessons.summary: Move king and rook in a single step

steps.title: What Is Castling?
steps.text:
Castling is the **only move in chess** where two pieces move at once — your king and one of your rooks, on the same turn.

It does two priceless things in a single tempo:

- **Hides the king** in a corner, tucked behind a wall of pawns
- **Activates a rook**, dropping it onto a central or semi-open file

## Two flavors

- **Kingside castle (short)**: written {{O-O}}. King hops two squares toward the h-rook; the rook lands next to him.
- **Queenside castle (long)**: written {{O-O-O}}. King hops two squares toward the a-rook; the rook flies over him to the other side.

In the position above, both sides have set up perfectly to castle either way. Imagine playing {{O-O}} — your king is suddenly safe, your rook on f1 eyes the e-file.

> Castling is two great moves wrapped into one. Don't waste it.

steps.title: The Four Rules
steps.text:
Castling looks magical, but it has strict requirements. Forget any of them and the move is illegal.

## The four conditions

1. **Neither piece has moved.** The king and the chosen rook must both be on their original squares, untouched.
2. **The squares between them are empty.** No bishop or knight blocking the path.
3. **The king is not in check.** You can't castle to escape a check.
4. **The king doesn't pass through or land on an attacked square.** The transit squares must be safe too.

A classic mnemonic: *can't castle into, out of, or through check*.

Notice that the **rook** is allowed to be attacked or to pass through an attacked square — only the king's path matters. That's a subtle but useful detail in queenside castling.

> If you're not sure you can castle, double-check those four rules. The engine never forgives an illegal move.

steps.prompt: Castle kingside with **{{O-O}}** — king to g1, rook to f1, both safe in one move.
steps.hint: In most chess interfaces you simply move the king two squares toward the h-file rook — the rook follows automatically.

steps.prompt: Now Black castles long with **{{O-O-O}}** — king to c8, rook to d8, attacking down the d-file.
steps.hint: Move the king two squares toward the a-file rook. The rook hops over to d8 in the same motion.

steps.title: Both Kings Tucked In
steps.text:
Both sides have castled — White short, Black long — and the position now has its full character.

Notice what changed:

- **Both kings are off the e-file.** No more accidental pins or pokes from a queen.
- **All four rooks are connected** along their back ranks. They can swing to any open file.
- **Both armies are battle-ready.** The fight for the center can begin.

When you castle on **opposite sides** (one player short, one long), watch out — pawn storms become deadly because each side can hurl pawns at the other king without exposing his own. A racing attack often decides the game.

> Aim to castle by move 10. Late castles get caught in the middle of the board.

lessons.title: En Passant
lessons.summary: The pawn capture most players never learn

steps.title: A Sneaky Rule
steps.text:
En passant — French for *in passing* — is the strangest, most-forgotten rule in chess. And yet, it's perfectly logical once you see why it exists.

When pawns were first allowed to leap two squares from their starting rank (a medieval rule change to speed up openings), the change had a side-effect: a pawn could *skip past* an enemy pawn that should have been able to capture it. To restore fairness, the rules added an exception — that pawn can still be captured, but **only on the very next move**.

## The conditions, all at once

- An enemy pawn moves **two squares** from its starting rank
- Your pawn sits **right next to it** on the same rank (the 5th for White, the 4th for Black)
- You capture **diagonally**, landing on the square the pawn *would* have been on if it had moved one square
- You must do it **immediately** — wait one move, lose the right forever

> En passant is the rule that proves chess is older than you think.

steps.title: The Opportunity
steps.text:
Here's a real chance to use it. Black just played **...f7-f5**, racing two squares past your pawn on e5.

If Black had only stepped one square (...f7-f6), your e5 pawn could have captured normally with {{exf6}}. Black's two-square jump tries to skip past that capture.

En passant says: *not so fast.* You can still play {{exf6}} — your pawn moves diagonally to f6, and the Black pawn on f5 is removed from the board. It's almost as if you caught the runner mid-stride.

The little notation `f6` after the side-to-move letter in the FEN tells you that **f6 is the en-passant target square** for one move.

> The capturing pawn lands BEHIND the captured pawn — the one square it tried to skip.

steps.prompt: Capture en passant with **{{exf6}}** — your pawn lands on f6 and the f5 pawn vanishes.
steps.hint: Treat the f5 pawn as if it were on f6, and capture diagonally. The pawn disappears even though you didn't land on it.

steps.title: One-Shot Rule
steps.text:
And just like that, the f5 pawn is gone and yours is on f6 — deep in Black's territory, two squares from promotion.

## Two final reminders

- **Use it or lose it.** The right to capture en passant lasts exactly one move. If you don't take immediately, the option vanishes.
- **Only pawns can do it.** Knights, bishops, rooks, queens, and kings cannot capture en passant.

Most beginners go years without ever playing this move. Now you'll spot it instantly — and even better, you'll *anticipate* it. Knowing en passant exists changes how you push pawns next to enemy pawns.

> The rule everyone forgets becomes the move you'll never miss.

lessons.title: Piece Values
lessons.summary: Learn what every piece is worth

steps.title: The Approximate Values
steps.text:
Before you can trade pieces wisely, you need a rough sense of what each one is *worth*.

Chess pieces don't have an official price tag, but generations of analysis have settled on a useful approximation — measured in pawn units.

## The standard scale

- **Pawn = 1**
- **Knight = 3**
- **Bishop = 3** *(slightly more in open positions; about 3.25)*
- **Rook = 5**
- **Queen = 9**
- **King = priceless** *(but worth about 4 in fighting strength once the queens come off)*

A few useful ratios pop out:

- A rook beats a minor piece (knight or bishop) by 2 — that's called *winning the exchange*.
- Two minor pieces (3 + 3 = 6) usually beat a rook (5).
- Three minor pieces (9) roughly equal a queen — but the pieces are usually more flexible.

> These numbers are a compass, not a calculator. Position trumps points.

steps.title: Trading Principles
steps.text:
Knowing values is half the story. Knowing *when* to trade is the other half.

## Three rules of thumb

- **When you're ahead in material, trade pieces.** Each trade brings you closer to a winning endgame, and reduces your opponent's chances of finding swindles.
- **When you're behind, keep pieces on the board.** Pieces are puzzle-makers — keep the puzzle alive and you keep your chances.
- **A sacrifice is intentional.** Giving up a knight for a pawn looks like a blunder; if it leads to mate, it's brilliance. Always count moves, not pieces.

## Position can flip the values

- A *bad bishop* (locked behind its own pawns) might be worth a pawn or two.
- A *strong knight* on a protected outpost can outshine a rook.
- *Two bishops* on an open board are stronger than two knights — that's the famous **bishop pair**.

> Trade like a banker: only when you profit, in points or in position.

steps.prompt: Reinforce your center by pushing **{{d4}}** or **{{c4}}** — both stake more space and open lines.
steps.hint: The center is where pieces unfold. Two friendly pawns abreast in the middle is a foundation worth fighting for.

lessons.title: Stalemate & Draws
lessons.summary: Half a point is sometimes a win

steps.title: Stalemate
steps.text:
Stalemate is the cruelest rule in chess — and the most beautiful, depending on which side you're on.

It happens when **the side to move has zero legal moves but is NOT in check**. The result? An immediate **draw**, no matter how lopsided the material count.

Look at the diagram: the Black king on h8 has nowhere to go. He can't step to g8 (attacked by your king on g6), can't go to h7 (also attacked), and he isn't in check on h8. If it's Black's turn here, it's stalemate.

## Why stalemate exists

- It rewards careful technique and punishes carelessness.
- It gives the losing side a fighting chance even in dire positions.
- It teaches you that *attacking the king isn't enough — you must leave him a legal move until you can mate*.

> Even with king and queen vs lone king, a sloppy move can stalemate. Always give the enemy king at least one legal square — until you can finish him.

steps.title: Other Ways to Draw
steps.text:
Stalemate is just one of several paths to a half-point. Knowing them all saves games — and earns them.

## The five main draw types

- **Stalemate** — no legal moves, not in check.
- **Threefold repetition** — the same position (with the same side to move and the same castling/en-passant rights) appears three times. Either player can claim the draw.
- **Fifty-move rule** — fifty consecutive moves by both sides without a pawn move or a capture. Either player may claim.
- **Insufficient material** — neither side has the firepower to mate. King vs king, K + N vs K, or K + B vs K are the classic dead draws.
- **Agreement** — both players simply agree to halve the point.

Two more, less common: **dead position** (mate is mathematically impossible for either side) and **timeout vs insufficient material** in online play.

> A draw is half a win. Sometimes it's a victory.

steps.title: Avoiding Accidents
steps.text:
Stalemate is **the** technique you must master before claiming you can checkmate.

In this position you're losing on material — Black's queen is going to dominate — but if Black plays carelessly, *you* might escape with a stalemate.

## The two-second checklist before every move

1. *Will my opponent have at least one legal move after this?*
2. *Are any of my opponent's pieces stuck (no legal squares for the king, all pawns blocked, all pieces pinned)?*
3. *Am I about to take their last mobile piece?*

If the answer to question 1 is **no** and the king is **not** in check — you've just stalemated. Many a winning position has been thrown away by an overconfident queen move.

## Famous lesson

In the simplest endgame — King + Queen vs King — the most common stalemate trap is putting the queen one square in front of the cornered king with no escape. Always leave the enemy king a flight square until your king is close enough to deliver mate.

> When you're winning, your job is to stay calm. The win is already there — don't gift it back.

lessons.title: Reading Chess Notation
lessons.summary: Decode any chess move in algebraic notation

steps.title: The Coordinate System
steps.text:
Chess has its own language — **algebraic notation** — and once you know it, you can read any game from history, follow any commentary, and study any book.

Every square on the board has a unique name made of a **letter** and a **number**.

## How squares are named

- **Files** (the columns going up the board) are letters **a–h**, left to right from White's point of view.
- **Ranks** (the rows) are numbers **1–8**, starting from White's first row.
- Combine the two and every square is uniquely named — *file first, then rank*.

So White's king starts on **e1**, his queen on **d1**, and the most famous square in chess — the one White's pawn often grabs first — is **e4**.

Quick orienteer: a1 is the bottom-left corner from White's side; h8 is the top-right.

> If you can name every square without thinking, you're already ahead of most casual players.

steps.title: Piece Letters
steps.text:
Each piece (except the pawn) gets a single capital letter.

## The piece alphabet

- **K** — King
- **Q** — Queen
- **R** — Rook
- **B** — Bishop
- **N** — Knight (`N` because `K` is already King)
- *(pawn — no letter at all)*

A move is just **piece letter + destination square**. So {{Nf3}} means *knight to f3*. Pawn moves skip the letter — {{e4}} simply means *the pawn that can legally reach e4*.

## Captures

- An **x** between piece and square marks a capture: {{Nxe5}} = *knight captures on e5*.
- A **pawn capture** uses the pawn's starting file: {{exd5}} = *the e-pawn captures on d5*.

> Pawns are humble: no letter, but they get to use their file when they capture.

steps.title: Special Symbols
steps.text:
A handful of extra marks let notation describe everything that can happen on the board.

## The full toolkit

- **+** — check. Example: {{Bb5+}}.
- **#** — checkmate. Example: {{Qh7#}}.
- **O-O** — kingside (short) castling.
- **O-O-O** — queenside (long) castling.
- **=Q** — promotion (any piece). Example: {{e8=Q}} promotes the e-pawn to a queen on e8.
- **!** and **?** — annotator's marks for *good* and *dubious* moves; **!!** brilliant, **??** blunder.

## Disambiguation

When two same-color pieces could move to the same square, you add either the file or rank of the moving piece:

- {{Nbd2}} — the *b-file* knight moves to d2 (when the other knight could too).
- {{R1e1}} — the rook on the *1st rank* moves to e1 (when both rooks share the e-file).

> Once you can read notation, you can read every chess book in history.

steps.hint: No piece letter means it's a pawn. Push the e-pawn two squares to e4.

steps.prompt: Now bring out a knight with **{{Nf3}}** — attacking e5 and developing toward the center.
steps.hint: Capital N means knight. From g1, it lands on f3 in an L-shape.

lessons.title: How to Think
lessons.summary: A simple 3-step process for every move

steps.title: The Three Questions
steps.text:
Strong players don't just react — they follow a tiny mental routine on **every** move. The earlier you build the habit, the faster you'll improve.

## The three questions

1. **What is my opponent threatening?** Look at their last move. Did it attack a piece? Open a line? Prepare a tactic?
2. **What are MY checks, captures, and threats?** Scan the whole board. Tactics live in *forcing* moves. List them before you choose.
3. **What's the best reply if I play my candidate?** Imagine your move on the board, then ask: how would *I* respond as Black?

Three little questions. Asked honestly, they cut your blunder rate in half.

A quick example: imagine White just played {{Bg5}}, pinning a knight. Question 1: *what's threatened?* The knight can't move without exposing the queen. Question 2: *what are my forcing replies?* Maybe {{h6}} chases the bishop. Question 3: *what happens after h6?* The bishop retreats or trades.

> Three questions, one minute. The cheapest rating points you'll ever earn.

steps.title: The Blunder Check
steps.text:
Almost every lost game contains a moment where you played fast and missed something obvious. That moment is preventable.

## The 5-second blunder check

Before your hand leaves the piece, freeze and run a tiny scan:

- Is any of **my pieces** suddenly hanging (undefended, attacked)?
- Can my opponent give a **check** that wins something?
- Is there a **simple capture** for free that I just allowed?
- Did I just walk into a **fork, pin, or skewer**?

If the answer to all four is *no*, play the move. If *yes*, find another move.

This simple ritual costs nothing in classical games and only seconds in blitz. It catches most one-move blunders — the kind that haunt every chess player.

> Sit on your hands. Then look again. Then play.

steps.title: Candidate Moves
steps.text:
Chess is not picking *the* move — it's choosing *between* moves.

Grandmasters look at the board, identify **2–3 candidate moves**, calculate each briefly, and compare. Beginners often calculate one move deeply and play it without ever asking *was there something better?*

## How to generate good candidates

- Start with **forcing moves**: checks, captures, and direct threats.
- Add **developing moves**: bring an idle piece into the game.
- Add **prophylaxis**: stop your opponent's plan before it starts.
- Reject quickly: if a move loses material or violates a principle for no reason, drop it from your shortlist.

Then compare your finalists head-to-head: *which leaves my position the strongest after my opponent's best reply?*

## Why this matters

- It prevents tunnel vision (locking in on the first move you saw).
- It surfaces tactics — sometimes Move B is great precisely because Move A is good.
- It makes you a calmer player, because you've ruled out alternatives instead of guessing.

> Pick three, choose one. Repeat for thirty moves. That's chess.

lessons.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
lessons.summary: Avoid the traps every beginner falls into

steps.title: The Big Five
steps.text:
Every player loses the same handful of games as a beginner. Skip these mistakes and you'll skip a thousand losses.

## The five classic blunders

1. **Moving the same piece twice in the opening.** Every tempo wasted is a piece your opponent develops for free.
2. **Forgetting to castle.** A king in the center invites tactics — even strong middlegames collapse without a tucked-away king.
3. **Bringing the queen out too early.** She gets chased by minor pieces, and every retreat is a move you didn't develop.
4. **Playing automatic moves.** Recapturing without thinking, defending a pawn that wasn't attacked, copying the opponent — autopilot is fatal.
5. **Playing without a plan.** A move with no purpose is a wasted move. Every move should improve a piece, threaten something, or prepare a break.

A classic example: after **{{e4}} {{e5}} {{Qh5}}?!**, White hopes for a quick attack. Black just plays **{{Nc6}}** and **{{Nf6}}** — and the queen has to retreat while Black develops with tempo.

> The opening is a race. Develop, don't dance.

steps.title: Don't Grab Every Pawn
steps.text:
Pawn-grabbing is the most seductive trap in chess. *It's free material!* — except, often, it isn't.

In the position above, White has just played the Center Game with **{{e4}} {{e5}} {{d4}}**. If Black greedily grabs with {{exd4}}, White recaptures, develops with tempo, and gets a big lead in piece activity.

## Three questions before any pawn snatch

- **Will I have to move the same piece again?** If yes, you're losing tempo.
- **Will my opponent develop a piece with check or threat while recapturing?** Every check costs you another move.
- **Will my king or king's pawn cover get exposed?** A weak king is rarely worth a single pawn.

A pawn is one point. **Three tempos** of development is also worth roughly one point. So *every* pawn grab that costs three tempos is a losing trade.

> Take pawns when they're free, not when they're bait.

steps.title: Watch Your Opponent's Threats
steps.text:
Half of all losing positions come from a single source: ignoring what the opponent just did.

When your opponent moves, they have a **reason**. Maybe they're attacking a piece. Maybe they're opening a file. Maybe they're vacating a square for a knight. Find the reason — *before* you choose your own move.

## The opponent's-move scan

- *What did this move attack?* (Anything new under fire?)
- *What did this move defend?* (Are they preparing a follow-up?)
- *What did this move open?* (A new diagonal, file, or rank?)
- *What did this move threaten?* (A check next move? A fork?)

If you can't answer, look longer. The threat is usually there.

## A real-world example

If your opponent plays **{{Bg5}}**, the obvious threat is the pin on your knight. The subtle threat is doubling your pawns after **{{Bxf6}}**, or — if you've castled — opening lines toward your king.

> Your move begins by understanding theirs.

lessons.title: The Three Principles
lessons.summary: Center, development, king safety

steps.title: The Three Laws
steps.text:
Every great opening — from the Italian to the Sicilian — rests on the same three pillars. Master them and you'll never have a *bad* opening, even if you've never seen the position before.

## The three laws of the opening

1. **Control the center.** The four squares **d4, e4, d5, e5** are the most valuable real estate on the board. Pieces that control them reach more squares; pieces that don't are spectators.
2. **Develop your pieces quickly.** Get every minor piece (knights, bishops) off the back rank in the first 8–10 moves. *Don't* move the same piece twice unless you must.
3. **Get your king safe.** Castle by move 10. A king in the middle is a king in danger.

A model opening sequence: {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{Nc6}} {{Bc4}} {{Bc5}} {{O-O}}. White has already done all three things — pawn in the center, two pieces developed, king tucked away.

> Develop with purpose. Castle without delay. The middlegame begins where the opening principles end.

steps.prompt: Stake your claim with a central pawn — play **{{e4}}** or **{{d4}}**.
steps.hint: Both moves grab a center square and open lines for two pieces at once (queen and a bishop). That's the cheapest first-move principle.

steps.title: Now Develop
steps.text:
The pawns lay the foundation; now the pieces move in.

## Order of development

- **Pawns first** — but only the central ones, just enough to open lines.
- **Knights before bishops.** Knights have fewer good squares (usually f3, c3 or f6, c6), so develop them first to commit fewer choices.
- **Bishops to active squares.** They want diagonals that hit the enemy camp.
- **Queen last among the minor pieces.** She's too valuable to expose early.
- **Rooks last of all** — they finish the development by occupying open files.

Why knights first? Because **{{Nf3}}** does triple duty: develops a piece, attacks the e5 pawn, and prepares castling. Few moves accomplish so much at once.

> Move every piece once before you move any piece twice.

steps.prompt: Develop a knight toward the center — **{{Nf3}}** is the classical choice (attacks e5), or **{{Nc3}}** also works.
steps.hint: Both moves bring a knight into the action. Which one also attacks Black's e5 pawn?

steps.title: Bishops Next
steps.text:
Both knights belong on f3 and c3 (or c4 in some openings). Now the bishops want to be unleashed.

## Choosing a bishop's home

- **{{Bc4}}** — the *Italian Game* setup. The bishop eyes f7, the most vulnerable square in Black's camp because only the king defends it.
- **{{Bb5}}** — the *Ruy Lopez* setup. Pressures the c6 knight (which defends e5) — chess's oldest serious opening.
- **{{Bd3}}** — solid but blocks the d-pawn. Common in 1.d4 systems.
- **{{Be2}}** — modest but flexible. The bishop supports a kingside attack later.

Notice that Black has mirrored you with {{Nc6}}. Symmetry is fine for a few moves — the player who breaks symmetry usefully often gets the advantage.

> A bishop with a target is worth two without one.

steps.prompt: Develop your light-squared bishop. **{{Bc4}}** is the classical Italian — it stares at f7.
steps.hint: Where does Black's f7 pawn need defending? A bishop on c4 strikes that exact square.

steps.title: King Safety
steps.text:
Two minor pieces out, center claimed, lines open — this is the ideal moment to **castle**.

Castling does three things in one move:

- Tucks the king into a corner, behind a wall of pawns
- Connects the rooks (they can now defend each other along the back rank)
- Brings a rook to the center — usually f1 or d1, where it controls a half-open file

## A useful checklist before castling

- Is the **f-pawn** still on its starting square? (Moving it weakens the castled king.)
- Are there any **immediate threats** I should meet first?
- Will I castle into the **same side** as my opponent (positional game) or the **opposite side** (sharp pawn-storm fight)?

From the position above, the natural follow-up is {{O-O}}. After that, you'll think about the d-file, the c-pawn break, and active rook moves.

> Castle early, castle on time, and the middlegame opens with you in shape.

lessons.title: The Italian Game
lessons.summary: Classical, principled, still played at the top

steps.title: The Italian
steps.text:
The Italian Game is one of the **oldest** openings in chess and still — incredibly — one of the most popular at every level, including the top of the world rankings.

## The defining moves

The canonical sequence is {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{Nc6}} {{Bc4}}. Three principled moves, three pieces developed, and a bishop pointed at f7 — the weakest square in Black's camp.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** finish development with {{Nc3}} (or {{c3}} preparing d4), castle short, and slowly build a kingside attack or push d4 to claim the center.
- **Black's plan:** mirror with **...Nf6** and **...Bc5** (the Giuoco Piano) or **...Be7** (the quieter Hungarian), castle short, and contest the center with **...d6** or **...d5**.
- **Pawn structure:** symmetric early, often becoming a closed center after **c3 / d3 / d6**.

## Why it works

The Italian respects every opening principle: a central pawn, two minor pieces out, the king ready to castle. There's no need for hyper-specific theory — just good moves.

> Classical chess at its purest: pieces out, king safe, fight in the center.

steps.prompt: Open with the king's pawn — play **{{e4}}**.
steps.hint: The most popular first move in chess history opens lines for both the queen and the f1 bishop.

steps.prompt: Develop with **{{Nf3}}** — a knight that attacks **e5** and prepares castling.
steps.hint: Two birds with one stone: this move develops a piece AND attacks Black's central pawn.

steps.prompt: Plant the bishop with **{{Bc4}}** — pointing straight at the f7 square.
steps.hint: The most vulnerable square in Black's camp is f7, defended only by the king. A bishop on c4 stares right at it.

lessons.title: The Sicilian Defense
lessons.summary: Black's sharpest response to 1.e4

steps.title: The Sharpest Reply
steps.text:
The **Sicilian Defense** is Black's most-played, most-feared, and most-analyzed answer to **{{e4}}**. It says, in effect: *I'm not interested in symmetry — I want to fight.*

## The opening move

After {{e4}} {{c5}}, Black has done something subtle but powerful. Instead of mirroring with ...e5, the c-pawn challenges White's center from the side. It does **not** block the c-file (which is exactly the file Black wants for counterplay).

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** play {{Nf3}} and {{d4}} to open the position (the *Open Sicilian*), develop pieces aggressively, and build a kingside attack.
- **Black's plan:** trade the c-pawn for the d-pawn (after **...cxd4**), seize the *half-open c-file*, develop with **...Nc6**, **...d6**, **...Nf6**, **...e6** or **...g6**, and counter-attack on the queenside.
- **Pawn structure:** wildly asymmetric — Black often has a *backward d-pawn* and pawns at e6+d6, while White has a powerful e4 pawn and aims for f2-f4-f5 storms.

## Why grandmasters love it

The Sicilian creates **imbalance from move one**. White attacks one wing, Black the other. Decisive games are far more common than draws — and that's why every world champion has had to learn it cold.

> Symmetry is for friendly games. The Sicilian wants a fight.

steps.prompt: Open with the most principled first move — play **{{e4}}**.
steps.hint: 1.e4 is White's classical opening choice — it claims a center square and frees the queen and the f1 bishop.

steps.prompt: Black plays the Sicilian — push **{{c5}}**, fighting for d4 from the flank.
steps.hint: Don't mirror with ...e5. Instead push the c-pawn — it attacks d4 without blocking the c-file Black wants.

steps.prompt: White's classical reply: **{{Nf3}}**, preparing **d4** for the Open Sicilian.
steps.hint: The knight develops, attacks ...e5 ideas, and clears the way for d2-d4 — the move that defines the Open Sicilian.

steps.title: Why the Sicilian?
steps.text:
Now you can see the genius of {{c5}}. Black is poised to play **...d6** or **...e6** and then jump into the half-open c-file with a rook later.

## The four main flavors of Black's setup

- **Najdorf** — {{c5}} {{Nf3}} {{d6}} {{d4}} {{cxd4}} {{Nxd4}} {{Nf6}} {{Nc3}} **a6** — the sharpest, most theoretical of all.
- **Dragon** — Black fianchettoes with **...g6** and **...Bg7**. Wild attacks on opposite sides.
- **Sveshnikov** — Black plays ...Nf6 and ...e5, accepting a backward d-pawn for piece activity.
- **Taimanov / Kan** — flexible setups with ...e6 and ...a6, slower but tough as nails.

Which flavor you choose says a lot about your style: tactical Najdorf players love calculation; Sveshnikov players love active pieces; Kan players love quiet, strategic squeezes.

> Pick a Sicilian flavor and learn it deeply. The reward is a lifetime of double-edged games.

lessons.title: The Queen's Gambit
lessons.summary: Offer a pawn to control the center

steps.title: The Classical Queen's Pawn
steps.text:
The **Queen's Gambit** is one of the most respected openings in chess history — a positional masterpiece that was *the* opening of choice in the 1920s and surged back into popular culture with the Netflix series of the same name.

## The defining sequence

The canonical line is {{d4}} {{d5}} {{c4}}. White offers the c-pawn, betting that if Black accepts, White will recover the pawn while controlling the center.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** apply long-term central pressure with {{Nf3}}, {{Nc3}}, {{Bf4}} or {{Bg5}}, and {{e3}}; castle short; eventually exploit a queenside or central majority.
- **Black's plan:** decline the gambit (the *Queen's Gambit Declined*) with **...e6**, **...Nf6**, **...Be7**; or play the *Slav* with **...c6**; or accept (rare at top level) and try to hold the extra pawn.
- **Pawn structure:** classical *Carlsbad* or *Tarrasch* structures — pawn chains running along c-d-e where small breaks like *minority attacks* decide the game.

## Why it's not a real gambit

The Queen's Gambit is not a true gambit because Black usually can't *keep* the c4 pawn safely. After {{dxc4}}, White recovers it with **{{e4}}** or **{{Nc3}}** plus **{{e3}}** while gaining tempo.

> The Queen's Gambit isn't about winning a pawn. It's about winning the center.

steps.prompt: Open with the queen's pawn — play **{{d4}}**.
steps.hint: 1.d4 stakes a center claim and prepares the trademark c4 break next.

steps.prompt: Now offer the gambit with **{{c4}}** — challenge Black's d5 pawn on the flank.
steps.hint: If Black takes with ...dxc4 you'll recover the pawn easily and own the center. Either way you win.

steps.title: Decline or Accept?
steps.text:
Black now has three main reactions, each defining a different opening *family*.

## Black's three main responses

- **Queen's Gambit Declined (QGD)** — **2...e6**. Solid as granite. Black accepts a slightly passive light-squared bishop in exchange for a rock-solid pawn structure.
- **Slav Defense** — **2...c6**. Black supports d5 with the c-pawn instead of locking in the bishop. Modern, popular, and theoretically rich.
- **Queen's Gambit Accepted (QGA)** — **2...dxc4**. Black grabs the pawn but plans to give it back. White recovers with {{e3}} or {{e4}} and develops with a small but real central edge.

A fourth, less popular option is the **Tarrasch** — **2...e6 3.Nc3 c5** — Black takes the offered pawn back later but plays for activity over solidity.

At grandmaster level, the QGD and Slav are dominant. At club level, the QGA appears often because it looks tempting to grab the pawn.

> The Queen's Gambit teaches patience. Pieces emerge slowly, the center is fought for square by square, and the player who understands long-term plans wins.

lessons.title: The Caro-Kann
lessons.summary: A rock-solid defense to 1.e4

steps.title: Solid and Sound
steps.text:
The **Caro-Kann Defense** is the choice of players who want to *survive the opening* and reach a healthy middlegame without memorizing reams of theory. It's been a workhorse for world champions like Capablanca, Karpov, and Anand.

## The defining sequence

The opening goes {{e4}} {{c6}}. With **...c6**, Black prepares **...d5** the next move — but unlike the French (1...e6), the c-pawn move *doesn't* block the light-squared bishop. After ...d5 and an eventual exchange, Black's bishop emerges actively to f5 or g4.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** challenge the center with **{{d4}}** and choose a setup — *Advance* ({{e5}}), *Exchange* ({{exd5}}), *Classical* ({{Nc3}} or {{Nd2}} dxe4 Nxe4), or *Two Knights* ({{Nc3}}, {{Nf3}}). Each leads to a distinct middlegame.
- **Black's plan:** play **...d5**, develop the c8 bishop *outside* the pawn chain (usually to f5), then **...e6**, **...Nd7**, **...Ngf6**, castle short, and look for a solid endgame edge.
- **Pawn structure:** often produces a *Caro-Kann pawn chain* (e6, d5) or, after exchanges, a clean symmetric structure where Black is happy to grind.

## Why play it

The Caro-Kann gives Black **a good light-squared bishop** (its most common complaint about the French is fixed) and a tough nut for White to crack. It rewards patience and excellent endgame technique.

> The Caro-Kann is the chess equivalent of a granite wall. Slow, steady, almost impossible to break.

steps.prompt: Black plays the Caro-Kann with **{{c6}}** — preparing **...d5** with full pawn support.
steps.hint: Unlike the French (1...e6), this move keeps Black's light-squared bishop free. Solid AND active.

steps.prompt: White's main reply: stake the full center with **{{d4}}**.
steps.hint: By playing d4, White builds the classical big center. If Black challenges with ...d5, the position becomes critical.

steps.title: The Break
steps.text:
Now Black plays the planned **...d5**, hitting White's e4 pawn directly. White must choose how to react — and the choice defines the rest of the game.

## Four main variations

- **Advance Variation** — **3.e5**. White pushes past, gaining space. Black gets the bishop out via **...Bf5** before locking it in.
- **Exchange Variation** — **3.exd5 cxd5**. Symmetric, calm, gives White a small space edge.
- **Classical (Capablanca) Variation** — **3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5**. Famous for the active Black bishop on f5.
- **Panov-Botvinnik Attack** — **3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4!** White transposes into IQP-style play with attacking chances.

A model game runs {{e4}} {{c6}} {{d4}} {{d5}} {{Nc3}} **dxe4** {{Nxe4}} **Bf5**. Black emerges with the bishop pair already broken in your favor and a flexible setup.

> The Caro-Kann teaches you that *flexibility wins more games than aggression*.

lessons.title: The English Opening
lessons.summary: Flexible flank play

steps.title: Control the Center From the Flanks
steps.text:
The **English Opening** ({{c4}}) is the connoisseur's choice — a flexible, hypermodern system favored by world champions like Botvinnik, Kasparov, Carlsen, and Caruana.

Instead of marching pawns to the center, White prepares **gradual control** with the c-pawn, develops pieces first, and decides on a structure based on what Black does.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** play {{c4}} first, then {{Nc3}} and {{Nf3}}, fianchetto the king's bishop with {{g3}} and {{Bg2}}, and castle. The center is fought over with d3 or d4 *later*.
- **Black's plan:** treat the English like a Queen's Gambit Declined or fight back symmetrically with **...c5**. The most fearless reply is **1...e5** (a *reversed Sicilian*), which can lead to wild play.
- **Pawn structure:** often *English / Hedgehog* shapes — Black's pawns on a6, b6, d6, e6, while White expands with c4-d4-e4 over the long term.

## A model line

{{c4}} {{e5}} {{Nc3}} {{Nf6}} {{g3}} **d5** {{cxd5}} **Nxd5** {{Bg2}}. White is set for a long, positional grind with the long-diagonal bishop pointing at Black's queenside.

## Why it's grandmaster-friendly

The English transposes into other openings *only when White wants it to*. If you play **1.c4**, you can choose later whether to head into a Queen's Gambit, an Indian Defense, or a pure English structure — the flexibility is enormous.

> Control without commitment. The English wins by patience.

steps.prompt: Open with the English — play **{{c4}}**.
steps.hint: 1.c4 challenges Black's d5 square from the flank and keeps the e- and d-pawns flexible for later.

steps.title: Flexible Follow-ups
steps.text:
What's powerful about 1.c4 is the menu of plans White keeps open.

## Four main White setups

- **Symmetric English** — White plays {{Nc3}}, {{g3}}, {{Bg2}}, {{Nf3}}, **0-0**, then chooses between {{d4}} (transposing to Queen's Gambit) or quiet manoeuvring.
- **Botvinnik System** — pawns at c4-d3-e4, knights to c3 and e2, bishop to g2. Bulletproof and flexible.
- **Reversed Sicilian** — if Black plays 1...e5, White essentially gets a Sicilian *with an extra tempo*. Sharp and rewarding.
- **Mikenas Attack** — 1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4!? — direct and aggressive, like a delayed 1.e4.

## Common transpositions

- After **1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6** — a *reversed Sicilian* tabiya.
- After **1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3** — a *Symmetrical English* heading toward Hedgehog.
- After **1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5** — White can play d4 and reach a *Queen's Gambit Declined* on his terms.

> If you dislike memorizing forced theory, the English gives you a system. If you love deep strategy, it gives you a lifetime of study.

lessons.title: Common Opening Traps
lessons.summary: Recognize (and avoid) classic blunders

steps.title: The Scholar's Mate
steps.text:
Every chess player learns the **Scholar's Mate** sooner or later — usually because someone has just unleashed it on them.

The basic recipe goes: {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Bc4}} {{Nc6}} {{Qh5}}. White has rushed the queen into the attack with one goal: target the **f7 square**, defended only by Black's king. If Black plays a careless move like **3...Nf6??**, White crashes through with **4.Qxf7#** — checkmate in four moves.

## Why does it work?

- **f7** is a uniquely weak square — only the king defends it.
- The queen on h5 attacks f7; the bishop on c4 attacks f7. Two attackers, one defender.
- A natural-looking knight move (like ...Nf6) blocks Black's queen from reaching f7's defense without solving the threat.

## How to refute it

- **3...g6** chases the queen and defends — most direct.
- **3...Qe7** defends f7 with the queen, perfectly safe.
- **3...Nf6??** is the move that loses — block the diagonal, but don't address the threat.

> Knowing a trap is a 100-rating-point gift. Falling for it once teaches you forever.

steps.title: The Punishment
steps.text:
Against an alert opponent, the Scholar's Mate is *not* a winning weapon — it's a **losing** one. The early queen sortie violates two opening principles at once:

- The queen is on h5 — exposed and easily chased.
- White hasn't developed a single other piece besides one bishop.

## Why Scholar's Mate fails at any decent level

- After **3...g6** the queen retreats to **4.Qf3** (still threatening f7) — and Black plays **4...Nf6** safely. Now Black has *two pieces developed* against White's *one*, and White's queen will be chased again.
- After **3...Qe7** Black is calm, has saved f7, and can play **...Nf6**, **...d6**, **...Bg7**, finishing development with a clear conscience.

## The lesson

If an opponent attacks your weakest square with one piece, you usually have a calm defensive move. **Don't panic** and don't grab the bait of attacking their queen *if* it costs you f7. Defend first, then chase.

> The Scholar's Mate punishes ignorance. Once you know it, you punish it instead.

steps.title: Develop, Don't Dash
steps.text:
Most opening traps share one feature: **the victim broke a basic principle**. They left their king in the center, walked into a fork, weakened f2/f7, or moved the same piece three times before developing the rest.

## The most common trap families

- **Légal's Mate** — White wins after a careless ...Bg4 pin: {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{d6}} {{Bc4}} **Bg4** {{Nc3}} **g6**?? {{Nxe5}}! and the bishop on g4 is undefended — Black loses material or worse.
- **Fishing Pole Trap** (Ruy Lopez) — Black plays **...h5** and **...Ng4** to bait the bishop on g5 into capturing, opening lines toward White's king after a sacrifice.
- **Noah's Ark Trap** (Ruy Lopez) — After White's bishop wanders to b3, Black traps it with **...c5-c4** if White isn't careful.
- **Fried Liver** — After {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{Nc6}} {{Bc4}} {{Nf6}} **{{Ng5}}** **d5** {{exd5}} **Nxd5**?! {{Nxf7}}!? — White sacs a knight for a furious king-hunt.

## The universal antidote

Apply the **three opening principles** every move:

1. Are my pieces developing toward the center?
2. Is my king on track to castle?
3. Did I just allow a check, capture, or fork?

Follow that checklist and you'll fall for far fewer traps than you set yourself.

> Most traps live in the *opponent's* mistakes. Play principled chess and watch them tumble in by themselves.

lessons.title: 1.e4 — The King's Pawn
lessons.summary: An overview of every major 1.e4 reply

steps.title: The Romantic Opening
steps.text:
**{{e4}}** is the most popular first move in the history of chess. Bobby Fischer called it *best by test*, and he had a point — the move does five things at once.

## What 1.e4 accomplishes

- **Claims a center square** — e4 is one of the four key squares.
- **Frees the queen** along the d1-h5 diagonal.
- **Frees the f1 bishop** along the a6-f1 diagonal.
- **Threatens nothing yet** — but creates instant possibilities.
- **Sets the tone** — open, tactical games are far more common after 1.e4 than 1.d4.

## What White generally wants

- Get pieces out fast (knights to f3 and c3).
- Pressure key squares like **f7** and **e5**.
- Castle short and use the e-file for rook activity.

## Why beginners should try it

Games after 1.e4 tend to be open, with clearer tactics and faster decisions. Practising 1.e4 sharpens your tactical eye in a way that slow d4 systems often don't.

> 1.e4 is the bright morning sun of chess — open lines, lively pieces, real fights.

steps.title: Black's Main Replies
steps.text:
Black has a rich menu of replies to 1.e4 — each defining a different chess universe.

## The big six

- **1...e5** — *Open Games*. Mirroring White's claim. Leads to the Italian, Ruy Lopez, Scotch, King's Gambit, Petroff, and more.
- **1...c5** — *Sicilian Defense*. The sharpest, most popular fighter's choice. Asymmetric, dynamic, full of theory.
- **1...e6** — *French Defense*. Solid and strategic. Black builds a pawn chain after **...d5**.
- **1...c6** — *Caro-Kann Defense*. Quiet and bulletproof. Prepares ...d5 with c-pawn support.
- **1...d5** — *Scandinavian Defense*. Direct: trade pawns immediately. Easy to learn.
- **1...Nf6** — *Alekhine's Defense*. Hypermodern provocation. Tempts White's pawns forward to attack them later.

## Less common but legitimate

- **1...d6** — *Pirc / Modern* — letting White build, then striking back.
- **1...g6** — *Modern Defense* — fianchetto first, decide later.
- **1...Nc6** — *Nimzowitsch Defense* — quirky but playable.

## How to choose what to play

- *Tactical, want to attack?* — Open Game with 1...e5 or Sicilian Najdorf.
- *Hate memorizing?* — Caro-Kann or Pirc.
- *Love positional play?* — French or Caro-Kann.

> Pick one defense and learn it deeply. Five strong systems beats fifty shallow ones.

steps.prompt: Meet 1.e4 with the classical reply — play **{{e5}}** and stake your own claim in the center.
steps.hint: 1...e5 is the time-honored answer. It mirrors White and opens the same diagonals for your bishop and queen.

lessons.title: 1.d4 — The Queen's Pawn
lessons.summary: Understanding 1.d4 systems

steps.title: The Positional Push
steps.text:
**{{d4}}** is the slow, strategic cousin of 1.e4. Instead of opening up immediately, it stakes a center claim with a pawn that's *defended by the queen* — a subtle but huge difference.

## What 1.d4 accomplishes

- Stakes the **d4 square**, which is naturally protected by the white queen on d1.
- Frees the **dark-squared bishop** to develop along the c1-h6 diagonal.
- Prepares the trademark **{{c4}}** push — the move that defines the Queen's Pawn family.
- Tends to lead to **closed**, *strategic* games where positional understanding beats raw calculation.

## Why grandmasters love it

- Black has fewer ways to seize the initiative.
- White can transpose between several systems (Catalan, Queen's Gambit, English, Trompowsky) based on Black's setup.
- Long-term squeezes are common — perfect for technical players.

> 1.d4 is the slow burn. The action takes longer to arrive — but lasts further into the game.

steps.title: Main Responses
steps.text:
Black's choice on move 1 against 1.d4 splits the chess world into two big camps: classical players who play **...d5**, and hypermodern players who prefer **...Nf6**.

## The major replies

- **1...d5** — *Classical*. Leads to the Queen's Gambit, Slav, and Semi-Slav. Solid, principled, and rich in theory.
- **1...Nf6** — *Indian Defenses*. The hypermodern family: King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian, Grünfeld, Bogo-Indian. Black lets White build the center and counterattacks later.
- **1...f5** — *Dutch Defense*. Sharp and risky. Black plays for kingside attacks at the cost of weakening the king's diagonal.
- **1...e6** — *flexible*. Often transposes into the Queen's Gambit Declined or French.
- **1...c5** — *Benoni* family. Black challenges immediately on the c-file.
- **1...d6** — *Old Indian* or *Modern* setups, where Black plays for ...e5 later.

## Choosing your response

- *Want a fortress?* — Slav or Queen's Gambit Declined.
- *Want to counter-attack?* — King's Indian or Grünfeld.
- *Want strategic depth?* — Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Indian.
- *Want imbalance?* — Benoni or Dutch.

## A model line for each side

A Queen's Gambit Declined goes {{d4}} {{d5}} {{c4}} {{e6}} {{Nc3}} **{{Nf6}}**. White builds slowly toward {{Nf3}}, {{Bg5}}, {{e3}}, and 0-0. Black builds with {{Be7}}, {{O-O}}, {{Nbd7}}, **...c6**, **...dxc4**.

> The 1.d4 family rewards patient students. Pick one Black system, learn its plans, and stand firm for years.

steps.prompt: Mirror White's center claim with the classical **{{d5}}** — solid, principled, time-tested.
steps.hint: 1...d5 stakes Black's own central pawn and prepares the Queen's Gambit Declined or Slav family.

lessons.title: The Ruy Lopez
lessons.summary: The oldest serious opening in chess

steps.title: The Spanish
steps.text:
Named after the 16th-century Spanish priest **Ruy López de Segura**, the Ruy Lopez (also called the *Spanish Game*) is the oldest serious opening still played at the highest levels of chess.

Every world champion has played it — Steinitz, Lasker, Capablanca, Alekhine, Botvinnik, Fischer, Karpov, Kasparov, Carlsen.

## The defining sequence

The canonical line is {{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{Nc6}} {{Bb5}}. The bishop pins the c6 knight to the e5 pawn — but the *real* threat is long-term, not immediate.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** maintain pressure on e5, develop with **{{c3}}**, **{{O-O}}**, **{{Re1}}**, **{{d4}}**, then expand on the kingside or center.
- **Black's plan:** challenge the bishop with **...a6** (the Morphy Defense), develop with **...Nf6**, **...Be7**, **0-0**, **...d6**, and either hold the e5 pawn (Closed Ruy) or release it for piece activity (Open Ruy).
- **Pawn structure:** characteristic Ruy Lopez chains — **e4-d3** for White vs **e5-d6** for Black, with manoeuvring on both wings.

## Why it's still relevant

The Ruy Lopez creates **strategic depth without forcing tactics**. It's a complete chess education in one opening — pawn structures, piece manoeuvres, attack and defense.

> Once you understand the Ruy Lopez, you understand classical chess.

steps.prompt: Open with the king's pawn — play **{{e4}}**.
steps.hint: 1.e4 stakes the center and is the gateway to the Ruy Lopez.

steps.prompt: Develop with **{{Nf3}}** — attacking e5 and preparing castling.
steps.hint: Nf3 is the knight move every classical opening starts with — it develops a piece AND attacks Black's central pawn.

steps.prompt: The defining move: play **{{Bb5}}** — the bishop steps out to pressure the c6 knight.
steps.hint: The Bb5 pin is *indirect*: it doesn't immediately win the e5 pawn (because of ...Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5 Qd4). It just slowly squeezes.

steps.title: Main Ideas
steps.text:
After **3.Bb5**, you'll often see beginners think *I can just take the knight!* — and discover that {{Bxc6}} **dxc6** {{Nxe5}} loses to **...Qd4!**, forking the knight and the e4 pawn. The Ruy Lopez is **not** about winning a pawn directly.

## What the Bb5 pin actually achieves

- It threatens to **damage Black's pawn structure** if and when {{Bxc6}} is played.
- It indirectly **undermines e5** — if Black ever lets White play {{Bxc6}} and then {{Nxe5}} without the **...Qd4** trick available, White wins a pawn.
- It limits Black's development — the c6 knight has to think before moving.

## Black's main responses

- **3...a6** (Morphy Defense, by far the most common) — kicks the bishop, asks it to commit. White retreats with **4.Ba4** or trades with **4.Bxc6**.
- **3...Nf6** (Berlin Defense) — Vladimir Kramnik used this to defeat Garry Kasparov for the world title in 2000.
- **3...d6** (Steinitz Defense) — solid but passive.
- **3...Bc5** (Classical) — bold, ignores the pin, prepares ...Nf6 and 0-0.

## A model main line

{{e4}} {{e5}} {{Nf3}} {{Nc6}} {{Bb5}} **a6** **{{Ba4}}** **Nf6** **{{O-O}}** **Be7** **{{Re1}}** **b5** **{{Bb3}}** **d6** **{{c3}}** **0-0** — the classical Closed Ruy.

> The Ruy Lopez is slow chess at its finest. Pieces shuffle, plans crystallize, and one tiny inaccuracy can decide the game ten moves later.

lessons.title: The London System
lessons.summary: The universal system — same setup, every time

steps.title: Why Play the London?
steps.text:
The **London System** is the chess equivalent of a bulletproof recipe — White plays *almost the same setup* against everything Black does. Less to memorize, more to play.

In recent years it's become hugely popular at the top level: Magnus Carlsen has used it in world championship matches, and grandmasters from Kramnik to Caruana have employed it as a surprise weapon.

## Why it's beginner-friendly

- **Almost no theory.** You play the same eight moves regardless of Black's setup.
- **Solid pawn structure.** The d4-c3-e3 setup is hard to crack.
- **Active dark-squared bishop.** Bf4 is one of the *best* squares for that piece — outside the pawn chain, eyeing the queenside.
- **Reliable plans.** The middlegame ideas repeat every time.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** {{d4}}, {{Bf4}}, {{Nf3}}, {{e3}}, {{c3}}, {{Nbd2}}, {{Bd3}}, **0-0**. Then expand with **h2-h3**, **Re1**, and aim for **e3-e4** or a queenside **a2-a4** push.
- **Black's plan:** play **...Nf6**, **...e6** or **...g6**, **...Be7** or **...Bd6**, **...c5** or **...c6**, and challenge the center. Modern Black setups attack the e3 pawn and the c3 weakness.
- **Pawn structure:** *Slav-Stonewall hybrid* — White's pawns at d4-c3-e3 form a triangle that limits Black's pieces.

> The London is chess on autopilot. Once you've played it ten times, you can play it in your sleep.

steps.prompt: Begin the London with **{{d4}}** — the foundation of the whole system.
steps.hint: Every London game starts with d4. The c1 bishop now has a clear path to f4.

steps.prompt: Develop the dark-squared bishop with **{{Bf4}}** *before* playing e3 — that's the key London move-order trick.
steps.hint: Always play Bf4 BEFORE e3, otherwise your own pawn locks in the bishop. This move-order trick is the heart of the system.

steps.title: The Full Setup
steps.text:
After {{d4}} and {{Bf4}}, the rest of the London System falls into place almost automatically.

## The full London recipe

1. **{{d4}}** — center pawn.
2. **{{Bf4}}** — bishop out before the e-pawn moves.
3. **{{Nf3}}** — second knight to its natural square.
4. **{{e3}}** — supports d4 and frees the f1 bishop.
5. **{{c3}}** — solidifies the center, prevents ...Nb4.
6. **{{Nbd2}}** — knight to a flexible square (not c3, where it would block the c-pawn).
7. **{{Bd3}}** — light bishop to its natural diagonal, eyeing h7.
8. **{{O-O}}** — castle short.

From there, White typically expands with **h2-h3** (preventing ...Bg4 pins), **Re1**, and an eventual **e3-e4** break or a kingside attack via **Ne5** and **Qf3**.

## Common Black setups against the London

- **Symmetric setup**: ...d5, ...Nf6, ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6, ...Bd6, ...0-0 — solid mirror.
- **King's Indian setup**: ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7 — fianchetto. Black plays ...c5 to challenge the center.
- **Modern challenge**: ...c5 immediately, ...Qb6 hitting the b2 pawn — a sharp test of the London move-order.

## A typical attacking pattern

A classic London attack runs **Ne5** + **Qf3** + **Bxh7+** — the *Greek Gift* sacrifice. The London structure is calm, but the kingside attack can be ferocious.

> Pick a system. Master it. The London teaches you how the same five squares can produce a thousand different middlegames.

lessons.title: The French Defense
lessons.summary: A solid pawn chain with counterattacking potential

steps.title: A Different Philosophy
steps.text:
The **French Defense** is the strategist's reply to 1.e4. With **1...e6**, Black announces: *I will not fight you symmetrically. I will build a wall, and behind it I will counter-attack.*

Named after a 19th-century correspondence match between London and Paris (Paris won), it's the choice of legends like **Botvinnik**, **Petrosian**, **Korchnoi**, and **Morozevich**.

## The defining sequence

The canonical line is {{e4}} {{e6}} {{d4}} {{d5}}. White has the bigger center for the moment, but Black is about to challenge it directly with **...d5**.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** advance with {{e5}} (Advance Variation), exchange with {{exd5}} (Exchange), or develop with {{Nc3}} or {{Nd2}} (Classical / Tarrasch). Each leads to a different battle.
- **Black's plan:** target White's d4 pawn with **...c5**, develop the queen's knight to **...Nc6**, fianchetto the b8 knight via **...Nd7-...Nb6** in some lines, and exchange the bad bishop. Counter-attack the center with **...f6** if White plays e5.
- **Pawn structure:** characteristic French chains — White's pawns at d4-e5 vs Black's at d5-e6, locked in a *closed pawn chain*. Each side attacks the *base* of the enemy chain.

## The French paradox

The one big problem: Black's **light-squared bishop on c8** gets hemmed in behind the e6 pawn. Solving (or accepting) the *bad French bishop* is the strategic theme of the entire opening.

> The French isn't passive. It's a coiled spring waiting to strike.

steps.prompt: Play the French setup with **{{e6}}** — preparing **...d5** with a granite pawn chain.
steps.hint: Don't push e5 (that would be 1...e5). Instead, prepare a Knight-supported ...d5 with a small but rugged pawn move.

steps.prompt: White claims the full center with **{{d4}}** — building the big pawn duo.
steps.hint: If you don't play d4, Black gets to challenge with ...d5 first. Stake your maximum center.

steps.title: The Blocked Center
steps.text:
After **2...d5**, the moment of truth arrives. White must commit to a setup, and each one creates a different game.

## The four major variations

- **Advance Variation** — **3.e5**. White locks the center, gains space, but the c8 bishop comes alive after **...Bd7-...Bb5** or via **...c5** breaks. Black plans **...c5**, **...Nc6**, **...Qb6**, **...Nge7**.
- **Exchange Variation** — **3.exd5 exd5**. Symmetrical and quiet — historically considered drawish, but White can play for a small edge with c4 breaks.
- **Classical Variation** — **3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7** (or **4.Bg5**). White keeps options open and Black accepts a cramped position with strong defensive resources.
- **Tarrasch Variation** — **3.Nd2**. White avoids the **...Bb4** pin and prepares c3 + Ngf3 + Bd3. Quiet but flexible.

## The French pawn-break dance

- **White plays {{f4}}-{{f5}}** to challenge the e6 pawn (base of Black's chain).
- **Black plays {{c5}}** — and later **...f6** — to challenge d4 and e5 (base of White's chain).

Whoever wins the pawn-chain race wins the middlegame.

> The French teaches you to think in *chains*, not in *pieces*. Master that, and your positional vision triples.

lessons.title: King's Indian Attack
lessons.summary: Reversed King's Indian — a White system

steps.title: A Flexible Weapon
steps.text:
The **King's Indian Attack** (KIA) is the King's Indian Defense — *played by White*. Same setup, same plans, just colors reversed: White fianchettoes the king's bishop, castles short, and then unleashes a slow, methodical kingside attack.

It was Bobby Fischer's secret weapon when he wanted to dodge mainstream theory. Even today, top players like **Hikaru Nakamura** and **Levon Aronian** trot it out as a surprise weapon.

## The defining sequence

A model order is {{Nf3}} **{{d5}}** {{g3}} **{{Nf6}}** {{Bg2}} **{{c5}}** **{{O-O}}** **{{Nc6}}** {{d3}} **{{e6}}** {{Nbd2}}. The key signature is the cluster: **Nf3, g3, Bg2, 0-0, d3, Nbd2, e4** — almost regardless of what Black does.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** complete the fianchetto setup, then push **{{e4}}** and eventually **{{e5}}**, opening lines toward the kingside. Pieces stack up: **Re1**, **Nf1-g3**, **h2-h4-h5**, and a kingside breakthrough.
- **Black's plan:** treat it like a French Defense or Sicilian — develop solidly, contest the queenside (**...b5, ...c5-c4, ...Rb8**), and exploit White's slow setup.
- **Pawn structure:** *KIA / French structure* — White pawns at d3-e4 vs Black at d5-e6, with attacks on opposite wings.

## Why it's grandmaster-friendly

The KIA is **one system against everything** — Sicilian, French, Caro-Kann all transpose into similar middlegames. You learn one set of plans and apply it for life.

> The KIA is chess's universal answer. Slow setup, sharp attack.

steps.prompt: Start with the most flexible first move: **{{Nf3}}**.
steps.hint: 1.Nf3 develops a piece and keeps every option open. It can transpose to Reti, English, Catalan, or — as here — the KIA.

steps.prompt: Begin the fianchetto with **{{g3}}** — preparing the bishop's long diagonal.
steps.hint: g3 prepares the fianchetto — the bishop will live on g2, eyeing the long h1-a8 diagonal.

steps.title: KIA Structure
steps.text:
After **{{Nf3}}** and **{{g3}}**, the rest of the King's Indian Attack falls into a familiar groove.

## The full setup

1. **{{Nf3}}** — flexible knight development.
2. **{{g3}}** — preparing the fianchetto.
3. **{{Bg2}}** — bishop to its long-diagonal home.
4. **{{O-O}}** — castle short, king tucked away.
5. **{{d3}}** — solid central support.
6. **{{Nbd2}}** — second knight (not on c3, where it would block c-pawn).
7. **{{e4}}** — *the* attacking move. The center awakens.

From there: **Re1**, **Nf1-h2** or **Nf1-g3**, **h2-h4-h5**, and a kingside avalanche.

## A model game plan

After Black's typical setup (**...d5, ...Nf6, ...e6, ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Be7**), White breaks with **e4-e5** kicking the f6 knight. Then **Nf1-g3** and **h4-h5** open lines. Combined with **Qe2** and **Bf4**, the attack on f7/h7 becomes deadly.

## The KIA's main appeal

- **One opening fits all.** Sicilian? French? Caro-Kann? You play the KIA against all three.
- **Strategically rich.** The middlegame plans repeat, but the tactics are fresh every game.
- **Hard to refute.** Even strong opponents have to be careful — Black's natural setups walk into White's plans.

> If you want one weapon for life, learn the KIA. You'll never be without an answer.

lessons.title: Najdorf Sicilian
lessons.summary: The sharpest opening in modern chess

steps.title: Fischer's Favorite
steps.text:
The **Najdorf Variation** of the Sicilian Defense is widely considered the **sharpest, most theoretical, most studied** opening in chess history. It was the favorite weapon of **Bobby Fischer** and **Garry Kasparov** — two of the most aggressive world champions ever — and remains a staple at the highest levels.

## How you reach the Najdorf

The defining sequence is {{e4}} **{{c5}}** {{Nf3}} **{{d6}}** {{d4}} **{{cxd4}}** {{Nxd4}} **{{Nf6}}** {{Nc3}} **a6** — and you're in. The little move **5...a6** is the soul of the variation.

## Why does **5...a6** matter?

- **Prevents Bb5+ pin/check ideas** that could disrupt Black's development.
- **Prepares ...e5** by removing the b5 square as a potential outpost for White's pieces.
- **Prepares ...b5** — Black's queenside pawn storm.
- **Stays flexible** — Black hasn't committed to a piece setup yet, leaving White to choose first.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** choose an attacking setup (English Attack, Bg5, Be2, Bc4) and aim for a kingside or central breakthrough. Castle long if possible (English Attack), then **g4-g5** to crash the kingside.
- **Black's plan:** develop with **...e5** or **...e6**, **...Be7** or **...Nbd7**, **...b5**, and counter-attack on the queenside. The Najdorf is famous for *opposite-side castling races*.
- **Pawn structure:** characteristic Najdorf chains — Black at d6/e6/a6/b5 vs White at e4/f3 (English Attack) or e4/f4 (Be2 lines).

> The Najdorf is chess at its most violent. Both kings under fire, every move a calculation, no quiet middlegames.

steps.title: Main Lines
steps.text:
On move 6, White faces an embarrassment of riches — *six* serious tries, each leading to a distinct middlegame.

## The big six White moves

- **6.Be3** — *English Attack*. White plays {{Be3}}, **f3**, **Qd2**, **0-0-0**, then **g2-g4-g5**. Mutual attacks on opposite sides. The most popular modern line.
- **6.Bg5** — *Classical Najdorf*. The bishop pins f6 and prepares to trade. Leads to wild theory in the **Poisoned Pawn** and **Goteborg** variations.
- **6.Bc4** — *Fischer-Sozin Attack*. Bobby Fischer's pet line. Bishop targets f7; White goes for direct kingside fireworks.
- **6.Be2** — *Classical / Opocensky*. Quiet, solid, modest goals. Often transposes into Scheveningen-style middlegames.
- **6.f3** — preparing the English Attack one move earlier.
- **6.h3** — modern fashion, popularized by **Magnus Carlsen** and **Wesley So**. Prepares **g4** without **f3** weaknesses.

## Choosing your weapon

- *Want maximum sharpness?* — English Attack with 6.Be3.
- *Want pure aggression?* — Bg5 Poisoned Pawn or Bc4 Fischer-Sozin.
- *Want positional play?* — 6.Be2 or 6.h3.

## The Najdorf cost

Learning the Najdorf is a **lifetime project**. Theory runs 20+ moves deep in many lines. Books on just one variation can run hundreds of pages.

> The Najdorf rewards study like no other opening. Investment goes in — wins come out.

steps.title: The Poisoned Pawn
steps.text:
After **6.Bg5 e6 7.f4**, Black faces a fork in the road. The famously poisoned reply is **7...Qb6!?** — daring White to defend the **b2** pawn.

## Why "poisoned"?

Because if Black greedily eats the pawn with **8...Qxb2**, White abandons the b-file in exchange for an enormous attack: **9.Rb1 Qa3** and now White has **Rb3** ideas, **e5 break**, **Bxf6 + Bd3**, and a roaring center.

## The Poisoned Pawn historic line

The critical line goes **6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 Qb6 8.Qd2 Qxb2 9.Rb1 Qa3 10.f5** — and now Black has to navigate a thicket of threats with the queen out of play. Spassky used this line against Fischer in the 1972 World Championship.

## What does each side gamble?

- **Black gambles:** the queen on a3 is exposed, and the queenside structure is shattered. But if White's attack fizzles, Black's extra pawn and bishop pair can decide the endgame.
- **White gambles:** the b2 pawn is gone, but White's pieces are screaming forward and Black's king is still in the center.

## Why study it

The Poisoned Pawn is *the* example of a modern computer-tested gambit — engines confirm Black is fine **with perfect play**, but the human margin for error is razor-thin. Both sides need 20+ moves of theory to survive.

> Greedy moves can win games — if you're prepared to walk a tightrope to defend them.

lessons.title: King's Indian Defense
lessons.summary: Hypermodern counterattack — the fighter's choice

steps.title: Let Them Build the Center
steps.text:
The **King's Indian Defense** (KID) is one of the most uncompromising openings ever invented. Black says: *take the center, build whatever you like — and then watch me tear it down*.

It was the lifelong weapon of **Garry Kasparov**, **Bobby Fischer**, **David Bronstein**, and many other fighters. When you play the King's Indian, you're not playing for a draw — you're playing to win, even if it's risky.

## How you reach it

The defining sequence is {{d4}} **{{Nf6}}** {{c4}} **{{g6}}** {{Nc3}} **{{Bg7}}**. Black fianchettoes the king's bishop and lets White build a massive center.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** complete the big center with {{e4}}, develop with {{Nf3}}, **{{Be2}}** (or Be3, h3 in the Sämisch), castle short, and either lock the center for a queenside attack or break with **c5/d5**.
- **Black's plan:** finish development with **...0-0**, **...d6**, **...Nbd7** or **...Nc6**, and play the central thrust **...e5**. After White locks with **d5**, Black launches **...f5-f4-f3** kingside pawn storms while White attacks the queenside with **c5**.
- **Pawn structure:** the *King's Indian Mar del Plata* — locked center with d5 vs e5, pieces redeployed to opposite wings, pawn races on both sides.

## The signature theme

In classical King's Indian middlegames, the question becomes: *whose attack arrives first?* If White breaks through on the queenside, the game ends. If Black's kingside avalanche reaches the white king, the game ends. There are very few quiet positions.

> The King's Indian: bring a chess set, leave with a war story.

steps.title: The Classical Main Line
steps.text:
After {{d4}} {{Nf6}} {{c4}} {{g6}} {{Nc3}} {{Bg7}} {{e4}} **d6** {{Nf3}} **0-0**, you've reached the **Classical King's Indian** — one of the most-analyzed positions in chess.

## The branching point

White chooses among several major systems on move 6:

- **6.Be2** — *Classical Main Line*. Quiet development. Black plays **...e5**, and after **7.0-0 Nc6 8.d5 Ne7**, Black is set up for the famous **kingside attack**.
- **6.h3** — *Mäkagonov System*. Prevents ...Bg4 pins, prepares Be3.
- **6.f3** — *Sämisch Variation*. Aggressive: White prepares Be3, Qd2, 0-0-0, and a queenside attack with sharp pawn pushes.
- **6.Bg5** — *Averbakh Variation*. Pin the f6 knight, discourage ...e5.
- **6.g3** — *Fianchetto Variation*. White also fianchettoes, leading to long, strategic battles.

## A classic Mar del Plata pattern

After **6.Be2 e5 7.0-0 Nc6 8.d5 Ne7 9.Ne1 Nd7 10.Be3 f5 11.f3 f4 12.Bf2 g5** — the famous pawn-storm formation. Black plans **...g4-g3** to crack White's king. White plans **c5-c6**, **Rb1**, **b4-b5** to crack Black's queenside. May the faster attacker win.

## Why grandmasters fear it

The King's Indian creates **mutual zugzwang on attack speed**. White is *objectively better* in many lines — but a single tempo loss leads to mate. That's why even Kasparov said he eventually stopped playing it.

> Both kings are in mortal danger from move 15. That's not a bug — that's the feature.

steps.title: Why It's Hard
steps.text:
The King's Indian is one of the most *demanding* openings to play well. The reasons are concrete.

## What makes it hard for Black

- **One bad pawn move can collapse the kingside.** Push **...f5** at the wrong moment and the e6 square becomes a hole forever.
- **The bishop pair** matters — losing the dark-squared bishop on g7 (the heart of the position) often dooms the attack.
- **Calculation depth.** Mar del Plata races demand 10-move-deep tactics on both wings simultaneously.
- **No second chances.** If White's queenside attack arrives one move first, the game is lost — no slow regrouping like in the French.

## What makes it rewarding

- **Imbalance from move 5.** No symmetric draws.
- **Attacks on the king.** Few openings produce as many beautiful checkmates as the King's Indian.
- **Strategic richness.** You learn pawn breaks, piece manoeuvring, attack-and-defense, all in one opening.

## Choosing the King's Indian for yourself

If you love **dynamic imbalance**, **mutual attacks**, and **calculated risk**, the King's Indian is the best opening on the planet. If you prefer slow, technical play, choose the Slav or Caro-Kann instead.

> The King's Indian is a black belt's opening. Train hard, fight harder.

lessons.title: Nimzo-Indian Defense
lessons.summary: Strategic masterpiece — pin and control

steps.title: The Bb4 Pin
steps.text:
The **Nimzo-Indian Defense** is one of the deepest, most respected openings in all of chess. Named after **Aron Nimzowitsch** — the father of *hypermodern chess* and author of *My System* — it's a strategic masterpiece based on one bold idea: **pin the c3 knight and threaten to ruin White's pawn structure**.

## How you reach it

The defining sequence is {{d4}} **{{Nf6}}** {{c4}} **{{e6}}** {{Nc3}} **{{Bb4}}**. Black's bishop on b4 pins the c3 knight to the king (well, *pins* it metaphorically — actually it's pinned to nothing, but **...Bxc3+** would double White's pawns).

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** avoid the doubled pawns (4.Qc2, 4.a3) or accept them in exchange for the bishop pair (4.e3, 4.f3). Then exploit the central majority and the long-diagonal bishop.
- **Black's plan:** trade the bishop on b4 for the c3 knight at the right moment, leaving White with **doubled c-pawns**. Then blockade those pawns and exploit the structural weakness.
- **Pawn structure:** the *Nimzo doubled c-pawns* (c4 and c3) — a long-term weakness Black plays against for 30+ moves.

## The eternal trade-off

White gets the **bishop pair**; Black gets a **damaged enemy structure**. Whose advantage is greater? It depends on whether the position opens (bishops shine) or stays closed (structure wins). That's the heart of every Nimzo-Indian middlegame.

> The Nimzo isn't about checkmate. It's about pawn structures, piece quality, and 50-move plans.

steps.title: Two Main Lines
steps.text:
On move 4, White has to choose how to handle the pin. Each choice creates a completely different middlegame.

## The four major White responses

- **4.Qc2** — *Capablanca Variation*. White avoids doubled pawns by recapturing with the queen. Modern, popular, slightly more flexible.
