- **4.e3** — *Rubinstein System*. The most flexible. White prepares **Nf3, Bd3, 0-0**, sometimes **a3** to chase the bishop. Allows ...Bxc3+ but compensates with the bishop pair.
- **4.f3** — *Kmoch / Sämisch*. Aggressive: White prepares **e4** and a kingside attack, accepting structural damage for activity.
- **4.a3** — *Sämisch / Hübner*. White challenges immediately: bishop must trade or retreat. Almost forces Bxc3+, and White gets the bishop pair plus the open b-file.

## Black's main responses to each line

- After **4.Qc2**: Black plays **...d5** or **...c5** with active piece play.
- After **4.e3**: Black has **...c5**, **...d5**, **...0-0**, **...d5+...c5** (Hübner Variation).
- After **4.f3**: Black plays **...d5** to challenge before White's e4 push lands.
- After **4.a3**: **...Bxc3+ 5.bxc3** is forced, and the strategic battle around White's doubled pawns begins.

## A model main line

{{d4}} {{Nf6}} {{c4}} {{e6}} {{Nc3}} {{Bb4}} **4.e3** **0-0** **5.Bd3** **d5** **6.Nf3** **c5** **7.0-0** **dxc4** **8.Bxc4** **Nbd7** — the *Karpov Variation*, balanced and strategic.

> Whichever line White picks, Black gets a position where understanding beats memorization.

steps.title: Strategic Depth
steps.text:
The Nimzo-Indian is famous for one thing above all: it's **the** opening where understanding pawn structures matters more than calculating tactics.

## The four classic Nimzo pawn structures

- **Doubled c-pawns** (after ...Bxc3+ bxc3) — White has c4-c3, Black plays against c3.
- **Hübner / Hanging Pawns** — Black's d-pawn and c-pawn stand isolated together, both attackable, both flexible.
- **Isolated Queen Pawn (IQP)** — sometimes White accepts an isolated d-pawn for piece activity.
- **Karlsbad-style** — symmetric pawn chains where small breaks decide the game.

## The Nimzo-Indian thinking process

- Is the position **opening up**? Then the bishop pair becomes valuable.
- Is the position **staying closed**? Then doubled pawns and weak squares decide.
- Where does Black **blockade**? Usually with a knight on c4 or e4 — squares the doubled pawns can't defend.
- Where does White **break**? With **e3-e4** or **c4-c5** to liberate the bishops.

## The legacy

World champions **Mikhail Botvinnik**, **Tigran Petrosian**, **Anatoly Karpov**, and **Vladimir Kramnik** all played the Nimzo as their main weapon. Karpov specifically used it to win the world championship — and to *keep* it for over a decade.

> The Nimzo-Indian is positional chess in its purest form. Once you understand it, every other opening becomes easier.

lessons.title: Grünfeld Defense
lessons.summary: A counter-punching hypermodern system

steps.title: Let Them Overextend
steps.text:
The **Grünfeld Defense** is the counter-puncher's masterpiece — a hypermodern opening where Black *invites* White to build a huge center, knowing it will be hard to defend.

Named after the Austrian master **Ernst Grünfeld**, who introduced it in the 1920s, it's been the favored weapon of **Bobby Fischer**, **Vladimir Kramnik**, **Garry Kasparov**, and **Magnus Carlsen** at various points in their careers.

## How you reach it

The defining sequence is {{d4}} **{{Nf6}}** {{c4}} **{{g6}}** {{Nc3}} **{{d5}}**. The fearless **3...d5** is the soul of the system: Black challenges White's c-pawn directly while preparing to fianchetto.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** capture in the center with **{{cxd5}} {{Nxd5}} {{e4}}** (the Exchange Variation), or develop quietly with {{Nf3}}, {{Bf4}}, {{e3}}, {{Be2}} (Russian System) or {{Bg5}} (Smyslov System). Aim to build and *keep* a big center.
- **Black's plan:** fianchetto the king's bishop on **g7**, attack the d4 pawn with **...c5**, sometimes break with **...e5**, develop **...Nc6**, **...Bg4**, and prove that White's center is *over-extended*.
- **Pawn structure:** characteristic Grünfeld imbalance — White has central pawns at d4 and e4 (Exchange Variation), Black has fewer pawns but enormous piece activity.

## Why it's daring

The Grünfeld concedes the **center** voluntarily. Black bets that White's pawns will become *targets* rather than weapons. If Black is right, White's big center collapses; if wrong, Black is squashed.

> The Grünfeld is jazz: improvisation over a complex theme. Beautiful when it works.

steps.title: The Exchange Variation
steps.text:
The most common reply for White is the **Exchange Variation** — **4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.e4**. Black's knight retreats and White's center now has *two* central pawns (d4 and e4).

## Why this is critical

- White's pawns look intimidating — they cut Black's pieces in half and seem to dominate the board.
- But the pawns are **pawns** — they can be attacked. Pieces are flexible.
- Black plans **...Bg7**, **...c5** (hitting d4), **...Nc6**, **...Qa5** or **...Bg4** — full assault on the center.

## The Modern Exchange line

A famous main line is **5.e4 Nxc3 6.bxc3 Bg7 7.Nf3 c5 8.Be3 Qa5 9.Qd2 Nc6** — by move 9, Black is developed, attacking the center, and ready to undermine White's structure with **...cxd4** breaks.

## What the structure tells us

- White's **isolated d-pawn or doubled c-pawns** become the long-term targets.
- Black's **fianchetto bishop on g7** dominates the long diagonal — eyeing **a1, b2, c3, d4** all at once.
- The **c5 break** is Black's defining move — without it, the Grünfeld does nothing.

## Other White tries

- **Russian System** (4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Qb3) — White pressures d5 with the queen.
- **Bg5 / Smyslov System** — White develops the bishop early to discourage ...c5.
- **Saemisch / Tartakower** — White plays {{f3}} preparing e4.

> The Exchange Grünfeld: White builds, Black sniper-shoots.

steps.title: Classical Grünfeld Themes
steps.text:
The Grünfeld has a small set of recurring strategic themes. Master them, and you'll feel right at home in nearly any Grünfeld middlegame.

## The Black playbook

- **Fianchetto on g7.** The bishop is the engine of the entire opening. *Never* trade it for less than a knight unless absolutely necessary.
- **Pressure d4 with ...c5.** This is the defining break. Without it, White's center is too strong.
- **Castle short** — usually move 6 or 7. The fianchettoed bishop and castled king form the defensive triangle.
- **...Nc6, ...Bg4, ...Qa5.** Pieces target the central pawns and the c3 knight (which is overworked defending d4 and e4).
- **...Rfd8, ...Rac8.** Once developed, rooks pile onto the c- and d-files where the structural battle lives.

## The d4-d5 race

The critical question in many Grünfeld games: *will Black force d4 to advance to d5?* If yes, Black gets to attack the now-isolated d5 pawn from c6 and e6. If no, White's center stays intact and the bishop pair plus space matter.

## Famous Grünfeld games

- **Botvinnik–Fischer 1962** — Fischer used the Grünfeld to demolish the world champion in stunning style.
- **Kasparov–Karpov 1990 World Championship** — Kasparov's repeated Grünfeld wins changed mainstream theory.
- **Carlsen–Anand 2014** — Anand's Grünfeld was the surprise opening choice that made Carlsen sweat.

> The Grünfeld: small pieces, big ideas. Counter-attack as a way of life.

lessons.title: The Catalan
lessons.summary: Positional squeeze from move one

steps.title: The Long-Diagonal Weapon
steps.text:
The **Catalan Opening** is the *technician's* dream — a slow, positional, soul-grinding system that combines the queenside structure of the Queen's Gambit with the long-diagonal pressure of a fianchetto. Named after the 1929 Barcelona tournament, it became famous as a Grandmaster weapon used by **Vladimir Kramnik**, **Levon Aronian**, **Anish Giri**, and **Magnus Carlsen** to torture opponents for 60+ moves.

## How you reach it

The defining sequence is {{d4}} **{{Nf6}}** {{c4}} **{{e6}}** {{g3}}. The little **3.g3** announces the Catalan — White is going to put the bishop on g2 and dominate the long h1-a8 diagonal.

## What each side wants

- **White's plan:** complete the fianchetto with {{Bg2}}, develop with **{{Nf3}}**, **{{O-O}}**, **{{Nbd2}}** or **{{Nc3}}**, **{{Qc2}}**, **{{Rd1}}** or **{{e4}}**. The g2 bishop pressures d5/c6/b7 forever.
- **Black's plan:** decide whether to take the c-pawn (Open Catalan with **...dxc4**), keep solid with **...Be7, ...0-0, ...c6** (Closed Catalan), or play sharply with **...c5**. Free the c8 bishop is always priority one.
- **Pawn structure:** *Catalan structure* — White's pawns at d4-c4 (or after exchange, just d4) with no central pawn on e2-e4, and a bishop on g2. Black's pawns at d5-e6 form a Slav-like wall.

## Why it's so hard to face

The Catalan has very few tactical traps. White just plays *good move after good move* — and slowly, the bishop on g2 starts dominating, the queenside pawns squeeze, and Black runs out of breathing room.

> The Catalan is the chess equivalent of a python: not a single bite, just a slow, inescapable squeeze.

steps.title: Why the Fianchetto?
steps.text:
The g3 + Bg2 setup looks calm, but the bishop on g2 is one of the most powerful pieces in chess. Here's why.

## The g2 bishop's range

- The **a8-h1 diagonal** runs through the most important squares on the board: b7, c6, d5, e4, f3, g2, h1. Combined with **c4**, the bishop creates lasting pressure on the queenside light squares.
- Even when **...dxc4** occurs, the bishop *extends its reach* further down the diagonal — that's why White is happy to *give up* the c4 pawn temporarily.
- The bishop is also a *defensive piece* — it covers White's king on g1 and the entire h1-a8 axis behind the king.

## The Catalan gambit theme

In the **Open Catalan** (after **3...d5 4.Nf3 dxc4**), White often *doesn't* try to recover the c4 pawn immediately. Instead, White plays **5.Bg2** and develops, betting the long-term pressure outweighs one pawn.

A famous example line: **5.Bg2 a6 6.0-0 Nc6 7.e3 Bd7 8.Qe2** — White's pieces flow into perfect squares, and the missing c-pawn becomes irrelevant.

## The Closed Catalan

If Black declines with **...Be7, ...0-0, ...c6, ...Nbd7**, the Catalan structure stays intact. White then plays **Bf4** or **Bg5**, **Rd1**, **Nc3-e2-f4**, and slowly probes for weaknesses.

> The Catalan bishop is a long-distance assassin. Give it time and it always finds a target.

steps.title: Catalan Dream Position
steps.text:
Every Catalan player has the same dream position in mind. Here it is.

## The Catalan dream setup

- **Bishop on g2** — fianchettoed and untouchable, dominating the long diagonal.
- **Knights on d2 and f3** — flexible, supporting central breaks.
- **Pawns on c4 and d4** — restricting Black's queenside.
- **Rooks connected on c1 and d1** — pressuring the c- and d-files.
- **Queen on c2 or e2** — supporting the central pawns and the bishop.
- **King on g1** — castled and safe.

From there, White probes: maybe a **c4-c5** push to gain space, maybe an **e2-e4** break to open the position, maybe a slow knight maneuver to **e5** to dominate the center.

## Black's defensive challenges

- The **c8 bishop** is the bad bishop of the Catalan. Black needs to find it a future — **...b6/Bb7** or **...Bd7-Bc6** are the main ideas.
- Black must **trade pieces** carefully. In the Catalan, exchanges usually favor White because his bishop on g2 outshines almost any Black piece.
- Black's queenside is **vulnerable**. The b7 square is a long-term weakness because of the g2 bishop's pressure.

## Why grandmasters love it

The Catalan produces one type of position — a **slight White edge** — over and over. It rewards endgame technique and patience. **Magnus Carlsen** has used it to grind opponents into dust in countless games, often converting a tiny edge over 80+ moves.

> The Catalan: nothing happens for thirty moves, then suddenly White is winning. That's mastery.

lessons.title: The Fork
lessons.summary: Attack two pieces at once

steps.title: Royal Fork
steps.text:
A **fork** is a single move that attacks two enemy pieces at the same time. Your opponent can only save one — you keep the other.

## Why the knight is the king of forks

The knight jumps over pieces, attacks eight squares from a strong central post, and **no piece can block its check**. Those traits make the knight the deadliest forker in chess.

## The geometry

A knight on a square *X* hits eight squares arranged like the corners of two interlocking rectangles. If two enemy targets sit on any of those eight squares, *X* is a fork square.

- King + queen on a knight pair of squares = **royal fork**
- King + rook = **family fork**
- Two unprotected pieces = a winning fork

## How to spot it

1. Find every undefended enemy piece.
2. List the squares each one *plus* the king sit on.
3. Look for a square that touches two of them with one knight jump.
4. Check that the fork square itself is safe (or that the gain is bigger than the loss).

Here the white knight is one hop from {{Nb4+}}, hitting both the king on c6 and the queen on d5.

> If you remember nothing else about tactics, remember this: *every undefended piece is a fork waiting to happen.*

steps.prompt: Play **{{Nb4+}}** — the knight forks king and queen on the same hop.
steps.hint: Look for the one knight square that touches both *c6* and *d5*.

steps.title: Queen Fork with Check
steps.text:
Knights are not the only forkers. The **queen** is a long-range fork machine — especially when the fork comes with check.

## Why check matters

A check is a *forced* response. While your opponent is busy moving the king (or blocking), the queen has already locked her eyes on the second target. The opponent does not get a tempo to defend it.

- Diagonal + file forks: the queen sits on a square that hits the king down one ray and a piece down another.
- Mate threats + material: a quiet-looking move that threatens both checkmate and a piece is a double attack in disguise.

## How to find it

1. Spot a check that is also a *capture* or that *aligns* the queen with another target.
2. Verify the fork square is defended or unreachable for the opponent.
3. Calculate the cleanup — *can the king step somewhere that defends the second piece?*

In this position, {{Qxe5+}} captures the knight **and** checks the king on e8 along the e-file. Black moves the king, White is up a knight.

> Forks with check are not optional for the defender. That is what makes them work.

steps.prompt: Capture the knight with **{{Qxe5+}}** — the check forks the king and pockets the piece.
steps.hint: What capture also lines the queen up with the enemy king?

lessons.title: The Pin
lessons.summary: Freeze a piece — it can't move away

steps.title: Absolute Pin
steps.text:
A **pin** is when an enemy piece sits between your attacker and a *more valuable* enemy piece behind it. The piece in front is glued to its square — moving would expose what's behind.

## The geometry

A pin needs three things on the same line — a file, a rank, or a diagonal:

1. Your **long-range attacker** ({{Rd2}}, queen, or bishop).
2. The **pinned piece** in the middle.
3. A **more valuable target** behind it.

Only rooks, bishops, and queens can pin — they move in straight lines. Knights, pawns, and kings cannot.

## Two flavors

- **Absolute pin** — the piece behind is the **king**. Moving the front piece would be illegal.
- **Relative pin** — the piece behind is just very valuable (e.g. a queen). The front piece *can* move, but it would lose material.

## How to spot pins in your games

1. Look at every long-range attacker you own.
2. Trace its lines through the position.
3. Mark any line that contains *two* enemy pieces with the more valuable one in the back.
4. If you see one, ask: *can I attack the pinned piece with another attacker?* A pinned piece cannot run — it's a target.

In this position the rook on d2 pins Black's queen on d6 against the king on d8. The queen is frozen — and we have a free shot.

> A pinned piece is not a piece. It is a target.

steps.prompt: Take the pinned queen with **{{Rxd6+}}** — she cannot move out of the way.
steps.hint: The queen is glued to the d-file. She is not defending herself; she is *being* the target.

lessons.title: Back-Rank Mate
lessons.summary: Exploit the king trapped behind his pawns

steps.title: The Classic Pattern
steps.text:
After castling, the king sits behind a wall of pawns. That wall is usually safety — but if the king has no escape squares on the back rank, the same wall becomes a **prison**.

## The visual trigger

Look for these three things on the enemy back rank:

- The **king** sits on a corner square (g8 or h8 for Black).
- The **pawns** in front of him are still on their starting squares (f7, g7, h7).
- The eighth rank is otherwise **empty** — no pieces in the way of an invading rook or queen.

When those three line up, a single move on the 8th rank can be checkmate.

## The geometry

Back-rank mate is just a **rook or queen check** on a rank where the enemy king has no flight squares. The king cannot capture (the attacker is defended or far away), cannot block (your piece is right next to him), and cannot move (his own pawns block him).

## How to find it

1. Count the enemy king's escape squares on the **back rank** and the **second rank**.
2. If there are zero or one, look for a way to attack the back rank with a heavy piece.
3. Count defenders — how many enemy pieces guard the back rank?
4. Either remove every defender or out-attack them.

Here the rook glides to {{Ra8#}} — checkmate, because the f7/g7/h7 pawn wall has become Black's coffin.

> The pawns that protect the king are the same pawns that trap him.

steps.prompt: Deliver checkmate on the back rank with **{{Ra8#}}**.
steps.hint: Where does the king run if you check on the back rank? Count his escape squares first.

steps.title: Trade & Mate
steps.text:
Often both sides have a back-rank weakness. Then it's a question of *who strikes first* — and the trick is to **eliminate the defender** before delivering mate.

## The pattern to recognize

- Both kings are stuck on their back rank with the pawn wall intact.
- Each side has a single rook (or queen) defending its back rank.
- One side gets to move first.

## Procedure

1. Identify the *defender* of the enemy back rank (almost always a single rook or queen).
2. Look for a way to **trade** that defender, **deflect** it, or **capture** it.
3. After the swap, walk in with mate.

Here both rooks face each other on the open d-file. Black's rook is the *only* thing defending d8. Trade it with {{Rxd8#}} — the recapture is impossible because the king has no escape square. The trade *is* mate.

> When two prisoners stand back-to-back, the one who shoots first walks free.

steps.prompt: Trade rooks **into** mate with **{{Rxd8#}}**. The exchange is the win.
steps.hint: Black's rook is the only defender of the back rank. What happens if you take it?

lessons.title: The Skewer
lessons.summary: Like a pin — but in reverse

steps.title: The Skewer
steps.text:
A **skewer** is the mirror image of a pin. You attack the *more valuable* piece in front; when it moves out of the way, you grab the *less valuable* piece behind it.

## The geometry

A skewer needs the same straight line as a pin — file, rank, or diagonal — but the order of targets is **reversed**:

1. Your **long-range attacker** ({{Ra1}}, queen, bishop).
2. The **valuable piece** out front (often the king).
3. A **less valuable piece** behind it on the same line.

When the front piece moves (and it must — especially under check), the back piece falls.

## Pin vs. skewer at a glance

- **Pin:** small piece in front, big piece behind. The small piece is *frozen*.
- **Skewer:** big piece in front, small piece behind. The big piece *flees* and the small piece is captured.

## How to spot it

1. Look for any line through the enemy king or queen.
2. Check what sits on that line *behind* the valuable target.
3. If a less valuable piece is back there, find a way to attack on that line — usually a check.
4. Calculate the recapture: is the skewer square defended?

Here the king is on d3 and the queen sits behind on d6. {{Rd1+}} hits the king on the d-file; the king must move and the queen drops.

> A skewer is what happens when the valuable piece is too brave to hide behind a smaller one.

steps.prompt: Skewer king and queen on the d-file with **{{Rd1+}}**.
steps.hint: What is on the d-file behind the king? A check forces him to step aside.

steps.title: Collect the Prize
steps.text:
After {{Rd1+}}, the king is in check and **must** step off the d-file — there is no piece to block and the rook cannot be captured.

## What follows

- The king walks to **e3**, **c3**, **e2**, or **c2** — any square not on the d-file.
- The queen on d6 is now exposed to {{Rxd5}} or, depending on the king's flight square, simply lost on the next move.
- White wins the queen for nothing.

## Why skewers are so deadly

- They almost always come **with check**, so the response is forced.
- Open files and long diagonals are the highways. Trade pieces to clear them.
- Even a humble rook can topple a queen if the alignment is right.

> The pin freezes; the skewer chases. Either way, somebody dies on the line.

lessons.title: Discovered Attack
lessons.summary: One piece moves — another attacks

steps.title: The Unmasking
steps.text:
A **discovered attack** is a two-for-one move. You move one of your pieces, *and the piece behind it* — which was blocked — suddenly attacks something. You get two threats from a single move.

## The setup

- A long-range piece of yours (rook, bishop, or queen) is aimed at an enemy target.
- One of your **own** pieces is sitting in the way, blocking the line.
- That blocking piece can move to make its own threat — and *uncover* the line at the same time.

## The geometry

You need three things on one line: your hidden attacker, your own blocker, and the enemy target. The blocker is the **firing pin** — when it leaves, the gun goes off.

## Two devastating variants

- **Discovered check** — the uncovered piece gives check while the moving piece grabs material elsewhere. The opponent *must* answer check, so the captured piece cannot be defended in time.
- **Double check** — both the moving piece *and* the uncovered piece attack the king at once. The king **must** move; you cannot block two checks with one piece, and capturing one leaves the other.

## How to find it

1. Identify any of your long-range pieces aimed at the enemy king or queen.
2. Check whether one of your own pieces stands in the way.
3. Ask: where can that blocker move to *attack something* of its own?
4. Choose the move that creates the largest second threat — ideally, also a check.

Here the rook on e1 already eyes e8. The knight on e4 is the firing pin. {{Nd6+}} attacks the king with the knight **and** uncovers the rook on e8 — a double check.

> A discovered attack is the one move that makes two threats. Look for the firing pin in your own army.

steps.prompt: Fire a **double check** with **{{Nd6+}}** — the knight checks, and the rook is unmasked.
steps.hint: Which knight square attacks the king *and* clears the e-file in one move?

steps.title: Why Double Check Is Lethal
steps.text:
Against a normal check the defender has three options: capture the checker, block it, or move the king. **Double check eliminates the first two.**

## Why blocking and capturing fail

- One piece cannot block two attacking lines simultaneously.
- Capturing one of the two attackers still leaves the other one giving check.
- That leaves only one legal reply: **the king must move.**

## Practical consequences

- Double checks are the foundation of many famous mating combinations.
- Even a queen sacrifice is fine if the resulting double check is forcing.
- A king with few flight squares and a double check is usually a *mated* king.

> Pin a king; he stays. Check a king; he dodges. *Double-check* a king; he runs — and you choose where.

lessons.title: Double Attack
lessons.summary: Threaten two things at once

steps.title: Two Threats, One Move
steps.text:
A **double attack** is the umbrella name for any move that creates two threats at once. The fork is a special case — the same piece hits two targets — but a double attack can be subtler than that.

## The flavors

- **Same-piece double attack** — a fork. One knight, two targets.
- **Different-piece double attack** — your move attacks one target, while *another* of your pieces was already attacking something else and now its threat becomes critical.
- **Threat + capture** — you capture a piece while simultaneously creating a mating threat the opponent must address.
- **Mate threat + material threat** — perhaps the most common in master games. The opponent has to defend mate; the material falls.

## The geometry

There is no single shape. The unifying idea is *forcing arithmetic*: the opponent has **one move** to answer **two problems**.

## How to find it

1. Count enemy weaknesses — undefended pieces, loose squares, mating ideas.
2. List moves that touch one weakness (captures, checks, threats).
3. For each, ask: *does it also create a second threat?*
4. The winning move is the one that makes the opponent choose which house to save while the other burns.

Here the queen on d5 is undefended. {{Nxd5}} simply wins her — a clean double attack: the knight takes a piece *and* there is no useful counter-threat for Black with the king sitting in the center.

> Every move you play has a *purpose*. The strongest moves have **two**.

steps.prompt: Snap up the unguarded queen with **{{Nxd5}}** — a textbook double attack.
steps.hint: Loose pieces drop off. Find the knight square that touches the queen.

steps.title: Train the Eye
steps.text:
Every strong tactical player walks through the position counting threats — both their own and their opponent's.

## A 30-second checklist

1. **Loose pieces:** which enemy pieces are undefended?
2. **Lined-up pieces:** any two enemy pieces on the same rank, file, or diagonal?
3. **King exposure:** is the king on a checkable square with limited escapes?
4. **Overworked defenders:** is one piece guarding two things?

If any answer is *yes*, look for the move that makes **two** of these problems erupt at the same time.

## A useful drill

- Set up a position from a tactic book.
- Before solving, list every undefended enemy piece and every check.
- The solution is almost always at the *intersection* of two threats.

> Single threats lose to a single defense. Double threats win games.

lessons.title: Remove the Defender
lessons.summary: Take out the piece that holds theirs together

steps.title: The Key Defender
steps.text:
Most positions are held together by **one** piece. Remove it, and the rest collapses. This tactic is called *removing the defender* (or sometimes *removing the guard*).

## What to look for

- A back-rank weakness defended by **one** rook.
- A pawn defending a knight, or a knight defending a key square.
- A queen pinned to defensive duty around the king.

If you can capture, trade, or chase that one piece away, the whole structure falls.

## The geometry

Map the **defenders** of every key enemy square. For a back-rank mate, the back rank is the key square; the defender is whichever piece controls it. For a hanging knight, the defender is whatever pawn or piece protects it.

## How to find it

1. Find the **threat** you wish you could play — usually a mate or a winning capture.
2. Identify the **single piece** that prevents that threat.
3. Find a way to **remove** that piece: capture it (even at material cost), trade it, or force it elsewhere.
4. Check that the *follow-up* still works after the recapture.

Here {{Rxf7}} demolishes Black's f7 defender. The black rook on f8 was guarding the back rank; if Black recaptures with {{Rxf7}}, the rook is *off* the back rank and White can come crashing through next move.

> A defender removed is a target unmasked.

steps.prompt: Smash the f7 pawn with **{{Rxf7}}** — and watch the back rank crumble.
steps.hint: Which piece guards Black's back rank? What happens if you force it to move?

steps.title: What Follows
steps.text:
After {{Rxf7}}, Black has to react. Whichever choice he makes, his structure has been pulled apart.

## Black's options

- **{{Rxf7}}** — pulls the rook off the back rank. White's next idea is a heavy-piece invasion of the eighth.
- **King moves** — leaves White an extra pawn deep in Black's camp with active pieces.
- **Ignore it** — White wins more material with {{Rxg7+}}.

## The takeaway

Always ask the same diagnostic question:

> *What single enemy piece keeps me from winning?*

Then pour your attention into removing it — by capture, by trade, by deflection, or by a tempo move that drives it away.

lessons.title: Deflection
lessons.summary: Force a piece to move where it shouldn't

steps.title: The Lure
steps.text:
**Deflection** is forcing an enemy piece *off* an important square or duty. Removing the defender takes the piece *off the board*; deflection just *bumps* it elsewhere — often with a capture or check it cannot refuse.

## The visual trigger

Look for a piece doing critical defensive work — guarding a back rank, blockading a pawn, defending a piece or a mating square. Now find a way to *force* it somewhere else.

## The geometry

Deflection lives at intersections:

- A piece is on a square that defends **square A**.
- You attack the piece on **square B** where it must move or be lost.
- Once it moves to B, A is unguarded.

The sacrifice or threat must be more urgent than the defensive duty — usually a check, a queen capture, or a fork.

## How to spot it

1. Find the enemy piece holding everything together.
2. Look for **forcing moves** that attack that piece: checks, big captures, mate threats.
3. After the forced response, evaluate: *is the abandoned square now winning for me?*

Here White's {{Ra8}} pressures the e8 rook along the eighth rank and threatens {{Rxe8+}} ideas. If Black trades with {{Rxa8}}, the e-file (and back rank) opens up.

> Pressure is the language of chess. The opponent's pieces answer when forced to.

steps.prompt: Apply pressure with **{{Ra8}}** — Black's rook is now begged to leave its post.
steps.hint: Aim a heavy piece at the back rank. The defender has to deal with it.

steps.title: Forced Exchange
steps.text:
From this position Black has only uncomfortable choices. The rook on e8 is overworked — defending the back rank *and* facing the white rook on a8.

## Black's tries

- **{{Rxa8}}** — trades but invites simplifications that favor the active side.
- **{{Rb8}}** — sidesteps but allows White to penetrate further.
- **King moves** — abandons the back rank entirely.

## The lesson

Deflection is rarely about the immediate material gain. It is about *who decides what happens next*. When the opponent has to react to your moves, you control the tempo of the position.

> Pressure forces decisions. Decisions under pressure usually go wrong.

lessons.title: Overloading
lessons.summary: A piece doing two jobs will fail at one

steps.title: Too Much Work
steps.text:
An **overloaded** piece is one that has more defensive duties than it can handle. Attack one of its jobs, and it fails at another.

## The classic shape

One enemy piece is doing two of these at once:

- Defending a square that, if invaded, would be mate.
- Defending another piece that is otherwise loose.
- Blocking a check while also guarding a key square.
- Holding a pin while also covering a knight fork square.

If a piece is doing **two** jobs, you only need to make it do **three** for it to fail.

## The geometry

There is no shape — overloading is bookkeeping. Map every defender's duties; find the piece with two; attack one of those duties.

## How to find it

1. List the enemy pieces that guard the most things.
2. For each, write down its duties — squares defended, pieces protected, lines covered.
3. Find an attack that forces the piece to drop one duty.
4. Profit from the abandoned square.

Here Black's queen on e7 is overloaded: she's the only piece between the rook on e2 and the king on e8. White plays {{Rxe7+}} — the queen falls because she cannot both stay home and shield the king.

> Loyal pieces still get fired when there is too much work.

steps.prompt: Snatch the overloaded queen with **{{Rxe7+}}** — she is shielding the king and cannot move.
steps.hint: The queen is doing two jobs at once. Attack one and the other fails.

steps.title: Spotting Overloads
steps.text:
Now the rook is on e7, two pawns up in material with a winning king-and-pawn endgame ahead. The overload did its work.

## Common overload patterns to memorize

- A pawn defending two pieces (knight + bishop).
- A knight that blockades a passed pawn *and* defends another minor piece.
- A queen that holds a back rank *and* defends a hanging knight.
- A rook that defends the back rank *and* opposes an enemy rook on a file.

## A useful question

Whenever you scan a position, ask: *which enemy piece defends more than one thing?* That piece is your weak spot. Find a move that forces it to choose, and you win.

> Strong moves do not just attack pieces. They attack *responsibilities*.

lessons.title: The In-Between Move
lessons.summary: Insert a stronger threat before the obvious recapture

steps.title: Don't Just React
steps.text:
**Zwischenzug** (German for *in-between move*) is a forcing move slipped into an expected exchange. The opponent expects you to recapture; instead, you play a check, a capture, or a bigger threat *first* — and *then* recapture, often with interest.

## The visual trigger

A zwischenzug usually appears when:

- A capture happens and a recapture is expected.
- The recapture would be "normal" but the position has another **forcing** resource — a check, a bigger capture, or a mate threat.
- The opponent's piece that just captured is *itself* loose, attackable, or pinned.

## The geometry

It is less about geometry and more about **tempo**. You spend one move on something more urgent before resuming the trade. The opponent must answer the check or threat; *then* you complete the trade with the position changed in your favor.

## How to spot it

1. When the opponent captures, slow down. Do not auto-recapture.
2. Look for **checks**, **captures**, and **major threats** that exist *before* the recapture.
3. Calculate: after your zwischenzug and the forced reply, can I still recapture or do better?
4. Compare the two lines side by side. If the inserted move gains material or position, play it.

> Strong players ask, *"What's most forcing?"* Weaker players ask, *"What's expected?"*

steps.title: A Practical Example
steps.text:
Imagine a typical exchange in the opening or middlegame: you have just been captured, and you'd like to recapture. Before doing so, run a quick zwischenzug check.

## The decision tree

1. **Is there a check?** A check forces the opponent's hand and is the highest-priority candidate.
2. **Is the capturer hanging?** The piece that just took yours might be undefended on its new square.
3. **Is there a bigger capture?** Maybe an enemy queen is loose two moves away.
4. **Is there a mating threat?** A quiet move that threatens mate is also a valid zwischenzug.

## A model line

In many openings you will see something like {{Bxc6}} bxc6, where Black recaptures because that is normal. But in some positions the strong reply is **not** bxc6 — instead Black plays a zwischenzug like {{Qd4}} or {{Bb4+}} hitting the white king first, *then* resolves the bishop trade with the position improved.

> Before recapturing, ask one more question. The masters always do.

lessons.title: X-Ray Attack
lessons.summary: Attack THROUGH a piece

steps.title: Seeing Through
steps.text:
An **X-ray attack** is when one of your long-range pieces threatens or defends *through* an intervening piece. The piece in front blocks the immediate attack, but if it ever moves — or is captured — the X-ray crashes through.

## The geometry

Four things on one line:

1. Your **rook**, **bishop**, or **queen** at one end.
2. Your **own piece** (or sometimes the enemy's) standing in the way.
3. The line continues *past* the blocker.
4. A target — usually a king, queen, or critical defender — sits at the far end.

Unlike a pin (which freezes a piece) or a skewer (which chases one off), the X-ray simply *sees past* whatever's in the middle.

## Two uses of the X-ray

- **Offensive X-ray** — your queen X-rays the enemy king through their own piece. Trade the blocker and the attack lands.
- **Defensive X-ray** — your rook X-rays one of your own pieces, defending it through another defender. After exchanges, the X-ray re-establishes guard.

## How to spot it

1. Trace every long-range piece you have, including beyond blockers.
2. Look for **king or queen** sitting on the far end of one of those lines.
3. Plan an exchange that removes the blocker.
4. After the smoke clears, the X-ray is suddenly an open attack.

In this position, White's rooks on d1 and d2 stack with the enemy king's rook on d8 down the d-file. After a series of trades, the *back* rook on d1 X-rays through and lands on the king.

> A pin freezes. A skewer chases. An X-ray *waits* — and wins anyway.

steps.title: Calculating Through Trades
steps.text:
X-rays often decide who comes out ahead in a chain of captures on the same square.

## The procedure

1. Identify the file, rank, or diagonal where pieces are stacked.
2. Count attackers and defenders.
3. Imagine the exchanges happening in order, *cheapest first*.
4. Whoever has the **last attacker** on the line wins the square.

## In this position

White has *two* rooks on the d-file. Black has one. After a sequence like {{Rxd8+}} {{Rxd8}} {{Rxd8+}}, White lands a rook on the eighth rank checking the king — the X-ray is the reason it works.

> X-ray vision is just patient counting along a single line.

lessons.title: Interference
lessons.summary: Block the enemy's defense line

steps.title: The Blocker
steps.text:
**Interference** (sometimes called *obstruction*) is the act of plopping a piece *between* an enemy attacker and what it is defending or attacking. The line is broken — and now the defended square or piece is suddenly exposed.

## The visual trigger

Look for an enemy piece — usually a rook, bishop, or queen — defending something important from a distance. Now ask: *can I plant a piece on the line between them?*

If yes, even sacrificing material may be worth it. The defense vanishes the moment the line is cut.

## The geometry

Interference needs:

1. An **enemy long-range piece** acting as a defender.
2. A **target square or piece** at the other end of its line.
3. A square *in between* where you can place a piece — usually with check or threat to make the move forcing.

## How to spot it

1. Find the enemy piece doing critical defensive work.
2. Trace its defensive line.
3. Look for an empty square along that line where one of your pieces can land **with a threat**.
4. After interference, exploit the unguarded target.

> A wall built in the right square is worth a piece.

steps.title: Novotny and Plachutta
steps.text:
Two beautiful interference patterns from the world of chess composition deserve a name.

## The Novotny

A piece is **sacrificed** on the intersection of two enemy defensive lines — typically a rook's line and a bishop's line crossing at one square.

- If the rook captures, it stops defending its line.
- If the bishop captures, it stops defending *its* line.
- Either way, one defender is gone.

## The Plachutta

The same idea, but the two defenders are *like-moving* pieces (e.g. two rooks on a rank and file, or two bishops on opposite diagonals). The sacrificed piece lands on the crossing point, and whichever rook or bishop captures **must abandon one of its lines**.

## Why these patterns matter

- They show that material is meaningless next to **lines of force**.
- They train your eye to see *intersections* — the square where two enemy lines meet is often the brick that holds the wall together.
- Even if you never compose endgames, the pattern of "sacrifice on the crossroad" wins games at every level.

> Beautiful tactics are rarely about pieces. They are about lines that *meet*.

lessons.title: Trapping Pieces
lessons.summary: Cut off an escape route

steps.title: Nowhere to Go
steps.text:
A piece deep in enemy territory is brave but vulnerable. **Trap it** — control every square it can flee to — and you win it without spending material.

## What makes a piece trappable

- It is **far from home**, with no friendly support.
- Its **mobility** is limited (a knight on the rim, a bishop blocked by pawns).
- It is the most valuable piece in its corner of the board (often a queen).
- The **attacker** has nearby pieces or pawns that can cover its retreats.

## The geometry

List every square the trapped piece can move to. If you can attack one of them or block another with each of your moves — without losing tempo — the piece dies one square at a time.

## How to spot it

1. Look for an enemy piece on **the wrong side of the board**.
2. Count the squares it can move to.
3. For each escape square, find a piece or pawn of yours that controls or blocks it.
4. Approach with a tempo move (often a check or a threat) so the trap is sealed before the piece can flee.

Here the black queen on d5 sits in front of her king with white rooks doubled on the e- and f-files. White can play moves that systematically take away every square the queen can reach.

> A queen far from home is just an expensive prisoner.

steps.title: Rim Knights and Trapped Rooks
steps.text:
Two of the most common trapping motifs you will see in real games:

## The rim knight

A knight on the **a-** or **h-file** controls only four squares instead of the usual eight. Push pawns at it. Block its retreats. Bring a piece next to it. Game over.

- **a4 + b5** vs. a Black knight on a6 → the knight has no good square.
- A bishop on c8 hemmed in by its own pawns, then attacked by a knight on a7.

> *"A knight on the rim is dim."* — Tarrasch

## The trapped rook

Rooks deep in enemy territory chasing a pawn (a2, h2) often get caught.

- The rook captures a pawn on a2.
- The opponent's king walks to b1.
- A piece (often a bishop or knight) covers the escape square.
- The rook is gone.

## How to find the trap

1. Identify the **far-from-home** enemy piece.
2. Count its escape squares.
3. Use **tempo moves** (checks, threats) to bring attackers in without giving the piece a chance to flee.

> Adventurous pieces need an adventurous owner — and an unobservant opponent.

lessons.title: Demolition of Defense
lessons.summary: Blast open the enemy position

steps.title: Sacrifices that Crack the Shell
steps.text:
Sometimes the only road to the enemy king runs through a brick wall — his pawn cover. **Demolition** sacrifices break that wall apart, exposing the king to your other pieces.

## The classic demolition patterns

- **Greek Gift** — {{Bxh7+}} on a kingside-castled king; bishop sacrifice followed by knight and queen.
- **Knight on f7** — {{Nxf7}} forks the queen and rook, or peels open the f-file.
- **Knight on h6 / f5** — pries open the king's pawn cover with check or major threats.
- **Exchange sacs on c3 / c6** — Sicilian-style: trading rook for knight to ruin the pawn structure.
- **Pawn storms** — pushing pawns *into* the enemy king to crack files and diagonals.

## The visual trigger

- The enemy king is **castled** behind intact pawns.
- You have a **pile of attackers** within two moves of the king (queen + 1-2 minor pieces).
- The defender lacks a useful **knight on f6** (or its mirror) to plug the holes.

## How to find a demolition

1. Count attackers near the enemy king.
2. Count *defenders* of his pawn shield.
3. If attackers >= defenders + 1, look for a sacrifice that opens a file or diagonal.
4. Calculate to mate or to a winning attack — at least 4-6 moves deep.

> Material can be replaced. A wide-open enemy king cannot be rebuilt.

In this Italian-style position {{Bxh7+}} is the textbook Greek Gift starter — read the next lessons to see how it unfolds.

steps.title: When to Demolish (and When Not To)
steps.text:
Demolition sacrifices are **calculated**, not played on instinct. Burn a piece in the wrong position and you simply lose.

## Three preconditions

1. **Attackers ready** — your queen and at least one minor piece can join the attack within two moves.
2. **Defender absent** — the key defender (almost always {{Nf6}} for Black, {{Nf3}} for White) is gone or pinned.
3. **No counterplay** — the opponent does not have a faster attack on your own king.

## A model decision

Before committing:

- Calculate the **forced** moves five-plus deep.
- At each branch, ask: *do I keep an attacking piece on the king?*
- Look for the **mate threat or perpetual** at the bottom of the tree.

## When to back off

- Your queen is far away and the rook lift is slow.
- The defender has a key piece you cannot remove.
- The opponent's counter-threat (like a passed pawn or a discovered attack) lands first.

> A demolition that does not finish the king finishes you instead.

lessons.title: The Quiet Move
lessons.summary: The move that kills without a check

steps.title: The Hardest Move to See
steps.text:
Beginners look at **checks**, **captures**, and **threats**. Masters look at all that *and* the **quiet moves** — moves that announce nothing but prepare an unstoppable threat next move.

## Why quiet moves are hard

- They do not capture or check, so they fail the brain's first scan.
- They often involve *retreats*, sidesteps, or tempo plays that look passive.
- The threat lives **on the next move**, not this one.

## The visual trigger

A quiet move is usually the answer to one of these questions:

- *I have a great attack but no immediate breakthrough — what move adds an attacker without releasing the pressure?*
- *My piece is one square short of the perfect post — can I get there without losing tempo?*
- *The opponent has only one defensive resource — can I take it away with a non-forcing move?*

## The geometry

Often it is a **mating-net** preparation:

- {{Kh1}} sidestepping a future discovered check.
- {{h3}} taking away the only escape square the king has.
- {{Re3}} preparing a rook lift to g3 or h3.
- {{Rd1}} centralizing before the storm.

## How to find them

1. Once you have a strong attack, list every **defender** the opponent has.
2. For each defender, ask: *can I prepare a move next that removes it?*
3. Look at *your* loose pieces — does a quiet move tuck them away or improve their post?
4. If the opponent has **no useful reply** to a quiet move, that is the move.

> A loud move forces an answer. A quiet move forces the opponent to find one — and there often isn't any.

steps.title: Train the Quiet-Move Reflex
steps.text:
Even when you are sure you have found the win, ask one more question: *Is there a quieter move that is even stronger?*

## A simple training exercise

1. Set up a complicated tactical position.
2. Find your best **forcing** move (capture, check, threat).
3. Now look at every **non-forcing** move that improves your position by even one square.
4. Compare. The quiet move is right when it leaves the opponent **without a useful reply**.

## Famous quiet-move types

- **Luft-takers** — moves like {{h3}} that close the door on the enemy king's escape.
- **Mating-net retreats** — pulling a bishop back to the long diagonal before launching the queen.
- **Doubling moves** — adding a second rook to a file before invading.
- **Critical-square covers** — placing a knight on a square that prevents the only enemy defensive resource.

## The mindset

Good tactical players see fireworks. Great tactical players see the **silence right before** the fireworks.

> The killer move is sometimes the one that whispers.

lessons.title: Pawn Breakthrough
lessons.summary: Sacrifice pawns to create a passer

steps.title: The Classic Motif
steps.text:
In a king-and-pawn endgame, **pawn breakthroughs** are the king of all motifs. Three pawns standing abreast against three opposing pawns can almost always force a passer with a small sacrifice.

## The textbook example

With White pawns on a5, b5, c5 versus Black pawns on a6, b7, c6, White plays {{b6}}:

- If `axb6`, then `c6` and the c-pawn runs.
- If `cxb6`, then `a6` and the a-pawn runs.
- Either way, one pawn becomes a queen.

## The visual trigger

Look for these features:

- **Three (or more) pawns abreast** facing the enemy.
- **No pieces** to interfere — pure pawn endgame.
- **Defending king too far** to stop the resulting passer.

## The geometry

A breakthrough trades pawns for **a clear running lane** for one of your pawns. Count the squares to the queening line and the squares the enemy king needs to reach the lane (the *square of the pawn*).

## How to find it

1. Identify the chain or formation that *would* produce a passer if the structure changed.
2. Look for the pawn sacrifice that opens the file or distracts a defender.
3. Count tempi to promotion.
4. Compare to the enemy king's path — if you arrive first, the breakthrough wins.

> Pawns are cheap. Queens are not.

steps.title: Beyond the Endgame
steps.text:
The breakthrough idea is not just for endgames. It appears all over the middlegame and attack.

## Common middlegame breakthroughs

- **{{f5}} or {{e5}} pawn breaks** that crack open the center against a king.
- **{{Nxf5}}** sacrifices that hand a knight for an open f-file and an attack on the king.
- **{{Rxa7}}** rook sacrifices to demolish queenside cover.
- **{{h5}}-{{hxg6}}** pawn waves against the kingside-castled king (especially with opposite castling).

## The shared principle

In every case, you give up material to **manufacture an unstoppable force**:

- An open file aimed at the king.
- A passed pawn that the defenders cannot stop.
- A diagonal that wrecks the king's pawn cover.

## How to evaluate the sacrifice

1. What **lines, files, or pawns** do I get in return?
2. Is the **target** (often the king or a queening square) close enough that the opponent cannot defend in time?
3. Are my **other pieces** ready to follow up?

> Material loses to motion. A breakthrough turns matter into momentum.

lessons.title: The Windmill
lessons.summary: Devastating discovered-check sequence

steps.title: The Windmill Pattern
steps.text:
The **windmill** is a relentless cycle of *discovered checks* that lets you snatch piece after piece while the enemy king has no time to breathe. It is one of the most beautiful — and most lethal — patterns in chess.

## The visual trigger

A windmill needs a very specific setup:

- A **rook or queen** giving check (or about to give check) on the seventh or eighth rank.
- A **bishop** (or sometimes a knight) sitting on a square where it both *delivers a discovered check* and *retreats safely*.
- An enemy king with **only one or two flight squares**, so it must keep returning to the same place.
- **Loose enemy pieces** along the rank or diagonal that the rook scoops up between checks.

## The geometry

The rook and bishop are the two grinding stones of the mill:

1. The bishop steps off the line — **discovered check** from the rook.
2. The king has no choice but to move to a single safe square.
3. The bishop **steps back**, capturing a piece on the way.
4. The rook *checks again* (or the bishop reveals a new check).
5. Repeat until the enemy army is gone.

## The most famous example

**Torre vs. Lasker, Moscow 1925** — the bishop on f6 and rook on g7 ground Lasker's pieces to dust over a dozen moves. Look it up after this lesson; it is unforgettable.

> A windmill turns the laws of chess into a meat grinder.

steps.title: How to Set One Up
steps.text:
Windmills do not happen by accident. They are *engineered*. Once you know the recipe, you start to see them long before they appear.

## The ingredients

- A **bishop** placed on a long diagonal aimed at the enemy king's pocket.
- Your **rook (or queen)** infiltrating to the seventh rank or back rank.
- The enemy king cornered with limited escape squares.
- Enemy pieces lined up along the rook's rank — easy targets between checks.

## The procedure

1. Place the **bishop** behind your rook so that moving the rook delivers a discovered check.
2. Drive the king to a square with no flight option except back where it started.
3. Move the rook *off* the discovered-check square (capturing material), check resolves.
4. Move the rook *back* with check again.
5. Continue until the position is winning.

## How to spot windmill *threats*

- Two of your long-range pieces share an attack on the king.
- The king has only one safe square between the two attackers.
- One of your pieces can capture and return without being captured.

> If you ever wondered why bishops on the long diagonal are scary, the windmill is the answer.

lessons.title: Activate Your King
lessons.summary: In the endgame, your king fights

steps.title: King Power
steps.text:
## The endgame king

In the **middlegame** the king is a fugitive — castled, hidden, defended by his pawns. In the **endgame**, with most pieces traded off, that timidity becomes a luxury you cannot afford. The king is now a **fighting piece**, roughly worth a strong minor piece, and every winning plan in a simple ending starts with him.

### What this position is

- White king on **e5**, already escorting his pawn from in front.
- Pawn on **e4**, two squares from the queening lane.
- Black king on **e8**, blocking the path.

This is the **K + P vs K** archetype — the most common winning structure in chess.

### The procedure to convert

1. **Lead with the king**, never the pawn. The pawn pushes only when the king has cleared the way.
2. **Outflank** the enemy king by stepping diagonally forward: {{Kd6}} or {{Kf6}}.
3. **Take the opposition** — when kings face each other one square apart and your opponent must move, you control the dance.
4. **Then push the pawn** to claim more space and force a queen.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing {{e5}} too early — the pawn arrives without escort and is blockaded.
- Stepping back with the king (e.g. Ke4) — you give up tempo and the opposition.
- Wandering the king sideways without any plan to outflank.

### A model line

{{Kd6}} ... Kd8 {{e5}} ... Ke8 {{Kc7}} — the king has cleared a corridor and the pawn is unstoppable.

> Activate the king before pushing the pawn.

steps.prompt: Step the king diagonally forward to **outflank** the defender. Apply the principle: *king first, pawn later*.
steps.hint: Don't touch the pawn yet — clear a lane for it with a diagonal step on the 6th rank.

lessons.title: King & Queen vs King
lessons.summary: The most important mate to learn

steps.title: Classic Mate
steps.text:
## K + Q vs K — the staple checkmate

This is the **first checkmate every player must own**. With king and queen against a lone king, the side with the queen always wins from any starting position — usually in **under ten moves**.

### What this endgame looks like

- One side has **king + queen**.
- The other has only the **king**.
- No pawns, no minor pieces, no rooks — pure technique.

### The key concept: the box and the wall

The queen builds an invisible **wall** that the lone king cannot cross, while your own king walks up to **support** the final blow. The only thing you must avoid is **stalemate** — that is the single hidden danger of this ending.

### Procedure to convert

1. Use the queen to **shrink the king's box**, staying a knight's-move away when possible.
2. **March your king up** to a square next to where you want to deliver mate.
3. Drive the enemy king to the **edge** of the board.
4. Deliver mate with the **queen on the edge**, defended (directly or remotely) by your king.

### Common mistakes

- Checking with the queen on every move — the king dances around forever.
- Trapping the lone king with **no legal squares** while the queen does *not* give check — this is **stalemate** and a draw.
- Forgetting to bring your own king up; the queen alone cannot mate.

### A model finish

From the position shown — Black king on **e8**, White king on **e6**, queen on **e5** — White plays {{Qb8#}} or {{Qh8#}}: the queen seals the 8th rank and the king on e6 covers d7, e7, and f7.

> The queen does the cutting, the king does the catching.

steps.prompt: Deliver **checkmate in one**. The enemy king is on the edge and your king is already supporting — finish the job.
steps.hint: Slide the queen along the **8th rank** so every escape square is covered or attacked.

lessons.title: Opposition
lessons.summary: The single most important endgame concept

steps.title: Face to Face
steps.text:
## What is the opposition?

**Opposition** is the situation where two kings stand on the same file, rank, or diagonal with **exactly one square between them**. The side **NOT** to move is said to *have* the opposition — the other king must give ground.

### Types you must know

- **Direct opposition** — kings one square apart on a file or rank (most common).
- **Diagonal opposition** — kings one square apart on a diagonal.
- **Distant opposition** — kings on the same line with **3 or 5** squares between them.

A simple test: if the count of squares between the kings is **even**, the side *to move* loses the opposition.

### Why it matters

In pure king-and-pawn endings, the opposition decides who can pass and who must retreat. Many drawn-looking positions are won — and many won-looking positions are drawn — purely on this single tempo.

### Common mistakes

- Stepping forward to the wrong square so the *opponent* gets the opposition.
- Confusing direct with diagonal opposition.
- Pushing a pawn while you have the opposition — you may give it back for free.

> The side that must move first, must move aside.

steps.title: With a Pawn
steps.text:
## Opposition with a pawn

Now White owns an extra **pawn on e4** and a king on **e6**. Black's king on **e8** stands in the way of the queening square. To win, White must combine **two ideas**:

1. Keep the king **in front of the pawn**, never behind it.
2. **Outflank** the enemy king by stepping diagonally to grab a key square.

### Key squares

For a pawn on the 5th rank or lower, the **key squares** are the three squares **two ranks ahead** of the pawn (here: d6, e6, f6). If your king reaches any one of them with the move, you win regardless of opposition.

### Procedure

1. Step the king diagonally forward: {{Kd6}} or {{Kf6}}.
2. The black king must give way; follow him along the file.
3. Push the pawn only when it can advance with the king's protection.
4. Promote and switch to the K+Q mate.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing {{e5}} first — Black plays Ke7 and you lose all progress.
- Going Ke6-e7?? — illegal? actually Ke7 walks into check from the king. Don't.
- Playing Ke4 / Kf4 — the king drifts away from his pawn.

### Model line

{{Kd6}} Kd8 {{e5}} Ke8 {{e6}} Kf8 {{Kd7}} and the pawn queens.

> King in front, pawn behind.

steps.prompt: Step **diagonally forward** to seize a key square. The principle: *the king leads, the pawn follows*.
steps.hint: Both flanks work — step to the **6th rank** and force Black to choose which side to retreat.

lessons.title: K + R vs K
lessons.summary: Drive the king to the edge and deliver mate

steps.title: The Technique
steps.text:
## K + R vs K — the textbook win

King and rook against a lone king is **always winning** for the stronger side. There is no opposition trick to learn, no zugzwang exception — just a clean technique you can repeat from any starting position in **roughly 16 moves**.

### What this endgame looks like

- **Rook + king** versus a bare king.
- The board is empty; everything is about coordination.

### The key concept: cut and shoulder

The rook **cuts** off a rank or file the enemy king cannot cross. Your king then **shoulders** him — taking the opposition — to push him toward that wall. Mate arrives when the lone king is pinned to the **edge** with no escape squares.

### Procedure to convert

1. Place the rook to **cut off** the enemy king on a rank or file, narrowing his prison.
2. **March your king** up to face the enemy king (direct opposition).
3. When the enemy king must move along the wall, **swing the rook** to the new cut-off line.
4. Repeat until he is on the **edge**, then deliver mate with {{Rg8#}}-style cut.

### Common mistakes

- **Stalemating** the lone king on the edge with the rook far away. Always check that he has at least one square *or* he is in check.
- Allowing the kings to be adjacent on the same file — the king attacks your rook.
- Wandering the king while the rook does all the work — you need both.

> Rook cuts, king shoulders, then mate on the edge.

steps.title: The Mating Net
steps.text:
## The final pattern

Look carefully at this position. Black's king sits on **h8**, his own pawn on **h7** blocking the only escape. The White king on **f7** controls **g7** and **g8** — every flight square. White's rook on **g1** has a clear lane to **g8**.

### Why this is a forced mate

- **g8** — covered by White king *and* the rook delivering mate.
- **g7** — covered by White king on f7.
- **h7** — occupied by Black's own pawn.

The enemy king has nowhere to run. The mating piece, the rook, slides into **g8** with check.

### The pattern to memorise

- Defending king on the **edge** (8th rank).
- Attacking king **two squares away**, controlling the escape diagonally.
- Rook delivers **mate on the edge file or rank**.

This exact picture — sometimes with a pawn cooperating, sometimes pure — is the **fingerprint** of K+R vs K mate. Burn it in.

> Once you see the cage, you can build it from anywhere.

steps.prompt: Deliver **checkmate** along the back rank. The principle: *the rook closes the cage your king has already built*.
steps.hint: The h7 pawn is doing your work — slide the rook to the **8th rank** with check.

lessons.title: Passed Pawns
lessons.summary: The engine of endgame victories

steps.title: What Is a Passed Pawn?
steps.text:
## What makes a pawn *passed*

A pawn is **passed** when:

- No enemy pawn stands on its **own file** ahead of it, **and**
- No enemy pawn stands on either **adjacent file** ahead of it.

Nothing but enemy pieces can stop it from reaching the 8th rank — and a piece eventually has to abandon it for other duties. That is why passed pawns are the **engine** of endgame victories.

### What this position is

A single White pawn on **e4**, two kings far apart, no defenders on the d- or f-files. The pawn is passed and four moves from queening. The only question is whether White's king can support it before Black's king blockades it.

### How to USE a passed pawn

1. Push the pawn when **escorted** or when the opponent cannot catch it (the *square rule*).
2. **Use it as a decoy** — the enemy king or pieces must abandon other targets to stop it.
3. **Trade pieces, not pawns** — simpler positions amplify the pawn's power.
4. On the wing furthest from the action, an *outside* passed pawn is even stronger because it pulls the enemy king away.

### Common mistakes

- **Pushing too soon** without escort — the pawn is rounded up by the enemy king.
- **Trading the wrong pawn** and leaving yourself with no passer.
- Forgetting the **square rule**: draw an imaginary square from the pawn to its queening file; if the enemy king cannot enter that square in time, the pawn queens unaided.

### Model line

{{e5}} Ke7 {{Kd2}} Kd6 {{Kd3}} — White's king is too slow; Black's king catches up and the pawn is lost. The lesson is sharp: **a passed pawn needs help**.

> A passed pawn must be pushed — but only when its king can keep up.

steps.prompt: Advance the passed pawn one square. The principle: *passers gain space the moment you push them*.
steps.hint: One square forward on the e-file — start the run.

steps.title: Support It!
steps.text:
## A pawn alone cannot win

After {{e5}}, it is Black to move. Notice the gap between the pawn on **e5** and its king on **e1** — four ranks apart. Black plays Ke7 and the pawn is **doomed** without help.

### What signs tell you to escort

- The enemy king is **closer** to the pawn than your own.
- No friendly piece can defend the queening square in one move.
- The opposing king already covers the **promotion square**.

### Procedure when your passer needs an escort

1. **Halt the push** and bring the king up: Kd2, Kd3, Ke4.
2. Use **opposition** so the enemy king cannot blockade.
3. Resume pushing only when the pawn has a king behind or beside it.
4. Use the pawn as a **shield** — it screens your king from sideways checks.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing every move on autopilot — *a passed pawn must be pushed* is a slogan, not a plan.
- Trading off your king's *active* path with random king moves.
- Defending the pawn with the king from **behind** instead of beside or in front.

### Model continuation

... Ke7 {{Kd2}} Kxe5? — but if instead {{Ke2}} Kf6 {{Kd3}} Kxe5 — the pawn falls. With the kings this far apart, only after the king is closer (e.g. on e3) can White safely push e6.

> Activate the king before pushing the pawn.

lessons.title: King and Pawn vs King
lessons.summary: The most common endgame — master it

steps.title: The Core Endgame
steps.text:
## K + P vs K — every player must know it

More games are decided by **king and pawn vs king** than by any other technical ending. It is the **gateway endgame** — every rook, queen, or minor-piece ending eventually simplifies into one of its patterns.

### What this endgame looks like

- One side has **king + a single pawn**.
- The other has only the **king**.
- A central pawn (b through g file) — rook pawns are a separate special case.

### The key concept: get in front with opposition

The entire result hinges on one question: **can the stronger side place his king IN FRONT of the pawn while holding the opposition?** If yes — the pawn promotes. If not — it is a draw by stalemate or by the defending king reaching the queening square.

### Procedure to convert

1. **Lead with the king**, never the pawn.
2. Reach a **key square** (see next page) with the king.
3. **Take the opposition**, then outflank diagonally.
4. Push the pawn only when the king has cleared the lane.
5. Promote and switch to the K+Q mate.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing the pawn first — it is captured or blockaded.
- Letting the enemy king reach the **queening square** — instant draw.
- Allowing **stalemate** with the pawn on the 7th rank and your king right behind it on the 6th in front of him.

> King in front, pawn behind.

steps.title: Key Squares
steps.text:
## Key squares win this ending

For a pawn on the **2nd–5th rank**, the **key squares** are the three squares **two ranks ahead** of the pawn. For our pawn on **e4**, the keys are **d6, e6, f6**.

For a pawn on the **6th rank**, the key squares are simply the three squares **directly in front** of it.

### The rule

If your king reaches **any key square**, you win — *regardless of opposition*. That is what makes them "key."

### Procedure with this position

White king is **already on e6** (a key square!). The win is now mechanical:

1. {{Kd6}} or {{Kf6}} — outflank to grab a second key square with tempo.
2. After Black retreats, push {{e5}}.
3. March the king ahead of the pawn until promotion.

### Common mistakes

- Stepping the king to **e7** — it leaves the pawn unprotected and walks into stalemate motifs.
- Pushing the pawn while the king is on a key square — you give the squares back.
- Treating rook-pawn (a/h) endings the same way — they are usually drawn even when the technique looks similar.

### Model line

{{Kd6}} Kf7 {{e5}} Ke8 {{Kc7}} and the pawn promotes.

> Reach a key square with the move and the pawn queens itself.

steps.prompt: Step to a **second key square** to outflank the defender. The principle: *king first, pawn later*.
steps.hint: Two key squares are one diagonal step away — pick either flank.

lessons.title: Philidor Position
lessons.summary: Defensive technique in rook endgames

steps.title: The Drawing Fortress
steps.text:
## Philidor — the saving technique

The **Philidor Position** (1777) is the gold-standard **defensive** method in **rook endgames**. If you remember nothing else from rook endings, remember this: when the attacker's king has **not yet crossed the 5th rank** and you can place your rook on the **6th rank** (from the defender's view), the position is a draw.

### What this endgame looks like

- The attacker has **king + rook + a single passed pawn**.
- The defender has **king + rook**.
- The defender's king sits **in front of the pawn**, on or near the queening square.

### The key concept: own the 3rd rank

The defender places his rook on the **third rank from the attacker** (his own 6th rank). This rank acts as a **wall**:

- The attacker's king cannot cross to the 6th without losing tempo to a check.
- When the attacker finally **pushes the pawn** to the 6th rank, the defender's rook drops to the **8th rank** (or 1st from the attacker's view) to **check from behind** — the king has no shelter.

### Procedure for the defender

1. Keep the **king on the queening square** of the pawn.
2. Place the **rook on the 3rd rank** from the attacker (your own 6th).
3. Wait. Make only rook moves *along that rank*.
4. The instant the pawn pushes to the 6th rank from the attacker, **swing the rook all the way back** to give endless side checks.

### Common mistakes

- Lifting the rook **off the 3rd rank** too early — the attacker's king walks in.
- Letting the **defending king leave** the queening square.
- Allowing the attacker's king to **reach the 6th rank** before you set up — at that point Lucena techniques win for the attacker.

### A model line (schematic)

... {{Ra6}} (defender's third rank) ... Kf6 ... {{Rb6+}} ... e6 {{Ra1}} (now check from behind) and the attacker's king cannot hide.

> The third rank is the wall — never leave it until the pawn does.

steps.title: The Third-Rank Defense
steps.text:
## Why the 3rd rank is everything

The **3rd-rank defense** is built on a small but inescapable logic: a king cannot advance into a square that another piece controls without first dealing with that piece.

### How the technique resolves

- While the **pawn is on its starting half**, the defender's rook holds the 3rd rank: the attacker's king has **no entry** beyond the 5th.
- The attacker has only one way to break the wall — **push the pawn** to the 6th rank himself.
- The instant the pawn arrives there, the rank is **closed off** by his own pawn — the attacker's king can no longer use it as shelter.
- The defender now drops the rook **all the way back to the 1st rank** and **checks from behind**: every check is delivered from a long distance and the attacker's king has nowhere to hide.

### What signs in your own games tell you to use it

- You are **a pawn down** in a rook ending.
- Your **king is in front of the enemy pawn**.
- The enemy **king has not yet reached the 6th rank**.
- You have a **rook with free play**.

If all four are true, set up Philidor. The half point is yours.

### Common mistakes

- Defending **passively** with the king alone — without rook coordination, the attacker's king strolls in.
- **Trading rooks** — you almost always lose the resulting K+P vs K.
- Forgetting to swing the rook back when the pawn arrives — the technique is two-stage, not one.

> Hold the third rank. Then check from behind.

lessons.title: Lucena Position
lessons.summary: The winning technique in rook endgames

steps.title: Building a Bridge
steps.text:
## Lucena — the winning technique

If **Philidor** saves a rook ending, **Lucena** (named after a 1497 manuscript by Luis Ramirez de Lucena) **wins** one. It is the companion you must own in tandem: half of all real rook endings convert to Philidor or Lucena.

### What this endgame looks like

- The attacker has **king + rook + a non-rook pawn on the 7th rank**.
- The attacker's king sits **on the queening square**, blocking his own pawn.
- The defender has **king + rook**, with the rook usually attacking the pawn from the side.

### The key concept: build a bridge

The attacker's king can step out from in front of the pawn, but only if it has **shelter from sideways checks**. Lucena's solution is to use the **rook itself as a shield**: place the rook **four ranks ahead of the pawn** (the *bridge rank*) and walk the king out through the checks, letting the rook step in to **block** when needed.

### Procedure to convert

1. **Lift the rook** to the 4th rank (one rank below the pawn-2 squares ahead): {{Rb4}} from the diagram.
2. **Step the king** off the queening square: e.g. {{Ke7}}.
3. When the enemy rook checks from the side, **interpose** with your rook one rank closer to the pawn ({{Rd4}}-style block).
4. Continue marching the king toward the rook; each side-check is blocked at a higher rank.
5. Once the king reaches the **6th rank**, push the pawn home and promote.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing the pawn to the 8th immediately — the queening square is **blocked by your own king** and you cannot escape the checks without the bridge.
- Placing the bridge rook on the **wrong rank** (3rd or 5th) — there must be exactly **one rank** between the rook and the pawn for the interposition to work.
- Allowing the **defender's king** to reach **the queening square's diagonal** before you build the bridge.

> Build the bridge first, then walk the king across.

steps.title: The Bridge
steps.text:
## Step-by-step bridge

From the diagram — White Kd8, pawn on d7, rook on b2; Black Kf7, rook on g1 — the winning sequence is a small symphony.

### The model line

1. {{Rb4}} — the rook climbs to the **bridge rank** (4th from White's view, 5th from the pawn's, exactly one rank behind the pawn-on-7).
2. ... Rg2 (or any waiting check). Black is helpless to stop the plan.
3. {{Ke7}} — the king starts the walk.
4. ... Re2+ — the first sideways check.
5. {{Kf6}} — king dodges forward.
6. ... Rf2+ {{Ke6}} Re2+ {{Kf5}} Rf2+ {{Rf4}} — the bridge **interposes**: the rook blocks the check, defended by its own king.
7. With the rook protecting, the king is now free to escort the pawn: pawn pushes, promotes.

### Procedure summary

1. Rook to the **4th rank** (or 4 squares ahead of the pawn's first move).
2. King steps **diagonally out** of the queening square.
3. Block side checks with the rook **on the bridge rank**.
4. Push the pawn when the rook is the shield.

### Common mistakes

- Skipping step 1 — without the bridge, the king is checked forever.
- Trying Lucena with a **rook pawn** (a/h) — it does not work; the bridge has nowhere to stand. Rook-pawn endings are usually drawn even a pawn up.
- Confusing Lucena (winning, attacker's king on the queening square already) with Philidor (drawing, attacker's king *not yet* on the 6th rank).

> Lucena wins, Philidor draws — together they cover most rook endings.

lessons.title: Bishop vs Knight Endings
lessons.summary: Which minor piece is better?

steps.title: Open vs Closed Position
steps.text:
## The eternal question

*Is a bishop better than a knight, or a knight better than a bishop?* The honest answer: **it depends on the position**. The two pieces are nominally equal in value (~3 pawns) but their strengths are almost opposite, and the **pawn structure** decides which wins out.

### When the bishop is better

- **Open positions** — long unobstructed diagonals.
- **Pawns on both wings** — the bishop reaches both sides in one move, the knight needs three or four.
- **Endings with passed pawns on opposite flanks** — the bishop is the perfect long-range stopper.
- The opponent has **weak squares of one colour** matching your bishop.

### When the knight is better

- **Closed positions** with locked pawn chains — the knight hops, the bishop bumps into pawns.
- **Strong outposts** in enemy territory (especially on the **5th** or **6th** rank).
- Pawns **all on one side** of the board — a knight is a quick local fighter.
- Defending a fortress — a knight near the king covers many squares.

### How to USE this in your games

1. **Identify your minor piece** before move 20 and ask: is the structure helping or hurting it?
2. **Trade or keep** with the structure in mind. If you have the bishop and pawns on one wing, look to break the wing open.
3. As the **knight side**, fight to keep pawns fixed and seek an outpost.
4. As the **bishop side**, fix enemy pawns on **your bishop's colour** so they become permanent targets.

### What signs tell you which piece is favoured

- Are there **3 or more locked pawn chains**? Knight likely better.
- Are there **passed pawns on both wings**? Bishop likely better.
- Is there an **uncontested outpost** on rank 5-6? Knight thrives there.
- Are pawns **all on the bishop's colour**? Bishop becomes "bad" — the knight takes over.

> The piece is only as good as the squares around it.

steps.title: Fischer's Dictum
steps.text:
## "The bishop is stronger"

Bobby Fischer famously declared **the bishop the superior minor piece** — but only after qualifying it: *in simplified, open positions*. He was a brilliant exploiter of the bishop's two strengths: **range** and **simultaneous coverage of two wings**.

### Two visual examples

- *Open position*: a bishop on **e3** simultaneously eyes **a7** and **h6** — eight squares of influence with a single tempo. A knight on the same square reaches at most eight squares but **none far away**.
- *Closed position*: with locked pawns on **d4/e5/f4 vs d5/e6/f5**, the bishop walks into its own wall while the knight skates over to **d6** or **f6** as if no pawns existed.

### How to USE the dictum

1. **Aim for the structure that favours your minor piece** before trading queens.
2. With the **bishop**, simplify into **open** endings; trade rooks if it opens lanes.
3. With the **knight**, **close** the position; trade your bishop for the opponent's knight if you keep a stronger knight.
4. Use **prophylaxis** to deny the opposite-piece structure — push pawns now to fix the colour complex you want.

### What signs tell you to apply this in your own games

- A trade is offered. **Don't accept reflexively** — first ask: *does the resulting structure favour my remaining piece?*
- A pawn break is available. *Will it open the position for my bishop or shut it for the enemy knight?*
- An outpost is being formed. *Whose piece can sit on it the longest?*

### Common mistakes

- Trading bishop for knight in an **open** position — Fischer would shake his head.
- Keeping your bishop alive in a **closed** position with no breaks — it sits behind its own pawns and rots.
- Treating the rule as absolute. **Position over piece**, always.

> The bishop is stronger — when the position lets it breathe.

lessons.title: Opposite-Colored Bishops
lessons.summary: Drawing tendencies and attacking potential

steps.title: The Drawing Endgame
steps.text:
## Opposite-coloured bishops in the endgame

When each side has a single bishop and they travel on **different colours**, the resulting endgame is famously **drawish**. The reason is geometric: the two bishops can never directly oppose each other, and the defender can build an unbreakable **fortress** on the colour his bishop controls.

### What this endgame looks like

- One bishop per side, **opposite colours** (one light, one dark).
- King and pawn count usually equal or close.
- Even with **two extra pawns**, the stronger side often cannot make progress.

### The key concept: the defender's colour

The defender:

- Places his **bishop and king on the colour** his bishop controls.
- **Blockades** every passed pawn on a square of his bishop's colour.
- Refuses to push pawns — pawn moves create new colour weaknesses.

The attacker has no way to remove the bishop, no way to breakthrough the colour wall.

### Procedure for the stronger side (when winning is possible)
