1. Look for **two passed pawns separated by 2+ files** — too far apart for one bishop to stop both.
2. Use the **king actively** as the third attacker.
3. Aim for **pawn breakthroughs on the attacker's bishop's colour**.
4. Avoid trading the **rook or queen** if you have one alongside — see the next page for why.

### Procedure for the defender

1. Place the king and bishop on the **right colour**.
2. **Blockade** the most advanced enemy pawn.
3. Move your bishop only along its diagonal — never trade pieces.
4. **Wait**. The half point usually arrives by itself.

### Common mistakes

- The stronger side **trading queens or rooks** into a pure opposite-bishop ending — many won positions become draws.
- The defender **pushing pawns** unnecessarily — every push opens a new weak square.
- Forgetting the **two-pawn rule**: even +2 is not enough if the pawns are connected and on the bishop's colour.

### Model line (schematic)

With **+2 pawns** on the same wing and connected, Black plays Be4-c2-d1 forever and White can never break the blockade.

> Opposite bishops in the endgame: half a point waiting to be claimed.

steps.title: Exception: With Queens
steps.text:
## The middlegame paradox

Here is one of chess's most beautiful inversions: in the **endgame**, opposite-coloured bishops favour the **defender**. In the **middlegame** — especially with **queens or rooks** still on the board — they favour the **attacker**.

### Why the inversion happens

If you launch an attack on the dark squares, the defender's **light-squared bishop** is *useless* for stopping it. He effectively defends with **one bishop fewer**. The attacker enjoys a permanent **piece-up feeling** in his attacking zone.

### Two visual examples in prose

- A White light-squared bishop on **b1** points at **h7**. Black has only a dark-squared bishop on g7. Black has **no defender** on the light squares around his king. White plays **Qd3** and the threat of mate on h7 is decisive.
- White's dark-squared bishop on **a3** rakes the long diagonal toward Black's king on g8 with pawns on **g7** and **h7**. Black's light bishop on g6 cannot oppose — the dark squares around the king are an invasion lane.

### How to USE the imbalance

1. **Identify which colour your bishop attacks** in the middlegame.
2. **Push pawns on the OPPOSITE colour** to fix targets your bishop can hit.
3. **Bring the queen** along your bishop's diagonal — they coordinate perfectly.
4. **Avoid trades** that would leave a pure opposite-bishop endgame — keep the heavy pieces.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- Your bishop and queen agree on a colour, the opponent's bishop disagrees.
- The enemy king's shelter has weaknesses on **your** colour.
- The position has **pieces still on the board** — opposite bishops only attack while there is firepower around them.

### Common mistakes

- **Trading queens** in an attack — the imbalance evaporates with the heavy pieces.
- Pushing pawns on **your bishop's colour** — they block your own diagonals.
- Believing "opposite bishops draw" applies in every phase. With queens, opposite bishops *win*.

> Same bishops draw, opposite bishops in the endgame draw — but opposite bishops with queens attack.

lessons.title: Rook and Pawn vs Rook
lessons.summary: The most common endgame at every level

steps.title: Half Wins, Half Draws
steps.text:
## R + P vs R — the most common endgame

No other endgame appears as often in serious play. Estimates from large game databases show that **R+P vs R arises in roughly half of all decisive endings** at club level and above. Roughly **50% of these are won and 50% are drawn** — and the result almost always hinges on whether the players know **Philidor** and **Lucena** by heart.

### What this endgame looks like

- **Rook + pawn** vs **rook**.
- A single passed pawn (any file).
- The result depends on the **king's position** and the **pawn's file**.

### The key concept: two named positions

- **Lucena** (winning) — the attacker's king has reached the **queening square**, his rook builds a *bridge* on the 4th rank.
- **Philidor** (drawing) — the defender's king sits on the queening square, his rook holds the **3rd rank** until the pawn is forced to advance, then checks from behind.

If you can identify which of these your position is closest to, you have a **road map**. If you cannot, you guess.

### Procedure for the attacker

1. **Cut off the defender's king** with your rook on a file the enemy king cannot cross.
2. **March your king** to the queening square — that is the goal.
3. Build the **Lucena bridge** with the rook on the 4th rank.
4. Step the king out under the bridge and queen the pawn.

### Procedure for the defender

1. **Race the king** to the queening square.
2. Place the **rook on the 3rd rank** (Philidor) until the pawn is pushed.
3. **Swing the rook back** and check from behind once the pawn is on the 6th.

### Common mistakes

- Putting the **defender's rook in front of the pawn**. It is **passive** and the king walks in.
- For the attacker, **pushing the pawn early** before the king has reached the queening square — Philidor draws.
- **Trading rooks** with a non-winning K+P vs K to follow.

> Half of every endgame study you ever do is preparing for R+P vs R.

steps.title: Key Rules of Thumb
steps.text:
## Three rules that win or save the half-point

If you forget the named positions in the heat of battle, three **rules of thumb** will get you most of the way home.

### Rule 1 — rook BEHIND the passed pawn

A rook that **defends or attacks from behind** a passed pawn (whether yours or your opponent's) is the **strongest possible placement**. The pawn pushes; the rook's scope grows. By contrast, a rook **in front** of a pawn shrinks as the pawn advances.

- *As the attacker*: place your rook **behind your own pawn** and walk it home.
- *As the defender*: place your rook **behind the enemy pawn** and tie down the attacker.

### Rule 2 — rook pawns (a/h) are usually drawn

The corner geometry is the defender's friend:

- The **defender's king** can often reach the corner and **stalemate motifs** appear.
- The attacker's **bridge has nowhere to stand** — the rank vanishes off the board.
- A defender even down a rook pawn frequently **holds** if his king reaches the corner.

### Rule 3 — the attacker must escort, not just push

The pawn is **escorted by the king**, not propelled by raw pushes. If your king lags behind, the defender's rook gives perpetual checks from the side or rear and you cannot make progress. **King first, pawn later** — same maxim, R+P vs R version.

### How to USE the rules in your games

1. The moment the position simplifies to R+P vs R, **assess king positions**.
2. Decide *which* named position you are heading for, **then play moves consistent with it**.
3. Always **double-check the file** — if it is an a- or h-pawn, recalculate from scratch.

### What signs tell you to apply each rule

- A passed pawn appears with rooks still on the board → ask *whose rook is behind it?*
- A rook pawn appears → assume **drawn** unless your calculation proves otherwise.
- A king is **far from the queening square** → switch to a *king-march* plan, not pushes.

> Rook behind, king in front, and the file matters.

lessons.title: Queen vs Advanced Pawn
lessons.summary: The famous race — usually the queen wins

steps.title: The Zig-Zag Technique
steps.text:
## Q vs P on the 7th — the famous race

A queen versus a pawn one step from promotion is the most cinematic endgame. The defender's king escorts a pawn that *will queen on the next move* unless the queen can wrestle a tempo. The technique that converts is the **zig-zag** — a sequence of checks and pins that forces the enemy king to **block its own pawn**, giving the queen time to bring her king closer.

### What this endgame looks like

- **King + queen** versus **king + pawn on the 7th rank**.
- The defender's king sits **next to or in front of** the pawn.
- The attacker's king is usually far away.

### The key concept: force the king onto the queening square

Each **check** forces the defending king to move. The trick is to alternate two ideas:

- A **diagonal check** along the queen's natural lines.
- A **pin or block** that costs the defender a tempo to deal with.

When the defender finally has only one legal move — **stepping onto the queening square** — the queen has *one full free move* to bring the king one square closer.

### Procedure to convert

1. **Check** the enemy king with the queen.
2. After the king moves, **pin the pawn** or **threaten promotion-square mate**.
3. The king is forced to **block the pawn**.
4. The attacker's **king takes a step** while the queen rests.
5. **Repeat** until the king arrives. Then mop up.

### Common mistakes

- **Stalemating** the lone king — always check that he has at least one square or is in check.
- Forgetting to **bring up your own king** between manoeuvres — the queen alone cannot win without escort.
- **Capturing the pawn** prematurely — sometimes correct, but sometimes leaves a drawn K vs K.

### A model line (schematic)

{{Qd5+}} Kc1 {{Qd2}} (pinning) Kb1 — and now White takes a tempo with {{Kc4}}, then resumes checks.

> The queen does not need to capture — she only needs tempi.

steps.title: The Exceptions
steps.text:
## Two pawns the queen cannot beat

The zig-zag wins **almost always**. The two famous exceptions are pawns whose queening square is too close to a corner for the defender to be forced onto it:

### 1. Bishop pawn (c/f) on the 7th

The defender uses a hidden **stalemate trick**: when the attacker's queen tries to force the king onto the queening square (c1 or f1), the defending king instead steps to the **corner** (a1 or h1). With the c-pawn or f-pawn frozen, this is **stalemate** — and a draw.

- *Picture it*: White Q somewhere, Black Kb1 with c2 pawn. White plays Qb2+? Black takes — wait, White must avoid stalemate motifs. With perfect defence, the queen cannot force the king off the corner without giving up the pawn.

### 2. Rook pawn (a/h) on the 7th

The **same stalemate trick** works on the corner files. The defending king parks in the corner; the queen can never deliver a pin without stalemating.

### Pawns the queen always beats

- **Knight pawn** (b/g) — no stalemate refuge.
- **Centre pawns** (d/e) — the king has too much room and gets caught.

### How to USE this in your games

1. Before trading down to a queen-vs-pawn race, **identify the file**. If it is a c/f or a/h pawn, **the race is drawn** — find another plan.
2. As the **defender**, push toward a **bishop or rook pawn** whenever you can; even down a queen, you may hold.
3. As the **attacker**, get your **king into the action** during the middlegame so the race is unnecessary.

### What signs tell you you are in this ending

- The position is heading toward queen versus a single passed pawn.
- The pawn is on the **6th or 7th rank** with a king right behind it.
- All other material is gone or about to be exchanged.

### Common mistakes

- Assuming **all pawns lose to a queen** — c, f, a, and h-pawns on the 7th draw with best play.
- Capturing the c- or a-pawn into a **drawn K vs K** without checking the king-distance rule.
- Allowing the defending king to reach the corner unchallenged.

> Queens beat pawns — except the corner four.

lessons.title: Good vs Bad Pieces
lessons.summary: Activity matters more than raw piece count

steps.title: Not All Bishops Are Equal
steps.text:
## What is a "good" piece?

A piece is judged not by its **name** but by what it **does**. Two bishops nominally worth 3 points each can play very differently: one rakes the long diagonal across the whole board; the other stares helplessly at its own pawn chain. The same is true of every piece — even queens.

### A precise definition

A piece is **good** when:

- It has **mobility** — squares it can step to or shoot at.
- It controls **important squares** — central, near the enemy king, or in the opponent's camp.
- It cooperates with **other pieces** — defended by friends, defending friends.
- It is **hard to remove** — no easy trade or attack.

A piece is **bad** when one or more of those properties fail.

### Two visual examples

- **Bad bishop** (the classic): Black has a c8-bishop with pawns frozen on **b7, c6, d5, e6**. Every diagonal is blocked by his own structure. The bishop is alive but **does nothing**.
- **Good knight on an outpost**: a White knight on **d5**, defended by a pawn on e4, with no enemy pawn able to dislodge it. From d5 it attacks **b6, c7, e7, f6**, central and aggressive.

### How to USE the concept

1. **Improve your worst piece every move** when nothing else is forced (Makagonov's rule).
2. **Trade your bad pieces** for the opponent's good ones — even a slightly losing trade may be worth it.
3. **Worsen the opponent's pieces** by fixing pawns that block them.
4. **Re-route** instead of recapturing — if a piece is bad after a trade, choose a different recapture.

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- One side has all pawns **on their bishop's colour** — the bishop is bad.
- A knight has only **passive squares** to retreat to — it is bad.
- A rook is **stuck on the back rank** with no open file — it is bad.

### Common mistakes

- Counting material and ignoring **piece quality**.
- **Trading** a slightly inferior piece for an equal one without checking which becomes more active.
- Leaving a bad bishop on the board for 30 moves while "saving it for later."

> The piece is only as strong as the squares around it.

steps.title: Improve Your Worst Piece
steps.text:
## Makagonov's principle

The Soviet trainer **Vladimir Makagonov** taught a single principle that compresses 80% of positional play into one sentence: *every move, improve your worst piece*. Tigran Petrosian used it to win a World Championship; Anatoly Karpov turned it into an art.

### The mental ritual

Before moving, scan your pieces and **rank them**:

1. *Where is my worst piece?* Check the rooks first — they are the slowest to develop. Then check minor pieces and the queen.
2. *Why is it bad?* Wrong square? Blocked by pawns? No targets?
3. *Can I move it now?* If yes, do it. If no, can I prepare it with a pawn move?

### Two visual examples

- A White rook stuck on **a1** while everything else is developed. Even with no "attack," {{Re1}} or **a4-a5-Ra3** — *the rook lift* — turns it into the most active piece in two moves.
- A bishop stranded on **c1** behind its own pawn on d2. The slow regroup **b3-Bb2** makes it the strongest diagonal piece on the board.

### How to USE it in your games

1. After every opponent's move, **don't look for tactics first**. Look for *which of your pieces is sleeping*.
2. Spend a tempo improving it. Most opponents do not punish quiet improvements.
3. When **all your pieces are well placed**, *that* is the moment to attack.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- The position is **balanced** with no obvious threats.
- You have a piece on its **starting square** past move 15.
- The opponent has a clear plan and you have none — improving a worst piece is always a useful waiting move.

### Common mistakes

- **Forcing play** while one of your pieces is still asleep.
- Confusing *active* with *attacking*. A piece that **defends a key square** can be the worst piece if it is overworked.
- Ignoring your **king** in the endgame — it is a piece too, often the worst one.

> When you don't know what to play, improve your worst piece.

lessons.title: Outposts
lessons.summary: Squares no enemy pawn can touch

steps.title: The Dream Square
steps.text:
## Outposts — defined precisely

An **outpost** is a square that satisfies three conditions:

1. It is in the **opponent's half** of the board (ranks 4-6 from your view).
2. **No enemy pawn** can ever attack it (the pawns on adjacent files have already passed it or been traded).
3. It is **defended by one of your pawns** (or otherwise impossible to challenge).

A piece on an outpost is essentially **immune** — it cannot be kicked. For a knight, this is paradise.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Classical outpost*: White pawn on **e4**, no Black pawn on **d-** or **f-files** anymore. **Nd5** sits forever, attacking **b6, c7, e7, f6**. Black's only ways to remove it are to **trade a piece** for it (often costly) or **allow an inferior knight back**.
- *Half-open file outpost*: Black has played ...c5 and exchanged into a structure where **d4** is no longer reachable by a Black pawn. White lifts **Nf3-d2-c4-d4** — the knight arrives, plants itself, and dominates the centre.

### How to USE outposts in your games

1. **Spot the squares early** — by move 15 you should know which 5th or 6th-rank squares are outposts for either side.
2. **Reroute the right piece**. A knight is the king of outposts; a bishop is good if its diagonal is open; a rook on a half-open file with an outpost in front is devastating.
3. **Defend your outpost** with a pawn. If it isn't pawn-defended, the opponent will challenge it with a minor piece and trade.
4. **Create new outposts** by inducing pawn weaknesses with threats and tactics.

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- The opponent has **pushed a flank pawn** that left a hole on a 5th or 6th rank square.
- You have a **knight without a future** — look for a re-routing path to an outpost.
- A **half-open file** runs from your rook to a hole — pile pieces on it.

### Common mistakes

- Calling any **central square** an outpost. If a pawn can still kick the piece, it isn't an outpost.
- Failing to **defend** the outpost — even an unkickable square is no good if a piece can be traded off cheaply.
- Settling on a knight outpost on a **2nd-rank square**. Outposts must be in enemy territory to matter.

> A knight on the 6th is a piece up; a knight on a 5th-rank outpost is the price of admission to a winning game.

steps.title: How to Create Them
steps.text:
## Creating outposts on demand

Outposts do not always appear by accident. Strong players **engineer** them by **provoking pawn weaknesses** and **fixing structures** so that a square becomes permanently weak.

### Three reliable methods

1. **Provoke a flank pawn push**. If you can force ...g6 or ...h6, the **f6** square may become an outpost for a White knight on e4-d5.
2. **Trade pieces that defend the hole**. If only a knight on f6 covers d5, trade it; the d5 outpost becomes permanent.
3. **Fix the enemy pawn chain**. Lock pawns on a colour so that the squares of the opposite colour become weak — entire colour complexes are then yours.

### Two visual examples in prose

- After {{Bb5}} {{a6}} Ba4 {{b5}} the move ...b5 commits Black to a structure with a hole on **c5**. White will later play **Nf3-d2-b3-c5** or **Bb3-c2** to dominate that square.
- In a **King's Indian** structure, Black plays ...Nh5 and exchanges his bishop on g7. The dark squares around Black's king (especially **f6** and **h6**) become eternal outposts for White.

### How to USE this in your own games

1. **Never trade a piece your opponent wants traded** without asking *why*. If their bad bishop is offered, trading often hands them an outpost.
2. **Push pawns that fix targets**, not pawns that ease the opponent.
3. **Plan three or four moves of re-routing** to bring a knight to its outpost — outposts are worth tempi.

### What signs tell you a hole is forming

- The opponent's pawns on **two adjacent files** can no longer cover one square between them.
- The opponent has just made a **pawn break** that leaves a **backward pawn** behind.
- A **fianchetto bishop** has been traded — the squares around the king are loose.

### Common mistakes

- **Rushing** to occupy an outpost before the squares are truly fixed — the pawn that supposedly cannot kick may still kick.
- **Trading the outpost piece** for a poor reason. Once it's gone, you may not get another.
- Treating every weakness as exploitable. Some holes are **too deep** to reach without overextending.

> Outposts are not found — they are built.

lessons.title: Pawn Structure
lessons.summary: Pawns are the soul of chess

steps.title: Philidor Was Right
steps.text:
## Pawns — the soul of chess

In 1749, **François-André Philidor** wrote *L'Analyse du jeu des Échecs* and stunned readers with one sentence: *les pions sont l'âme du jeu* — **pawns are the soul of chess**. He was right because pawns shape **everything else**.

### Why pawns matter so much

- They are the **only piece that cannot retreat**. Every pawn move is **permanent**.
- They **define which squares are weak** and which are strong.
- They **lock or open** the position, deciding which pieces thrive.
- They **point** to where the action belongs — you attack on the side your pawns lead.

### Two visual examples in prose

- A **King's Indian** structure with White pawns on c4-d5-e4 and Black on c7-d6-e5 sends an unmistakable signal: White attacks on the **queenside** (where his pawns can advance), Black attacks on the **kingside** (where his pawns chain points).
- A **Caro-Kann** structure with Black pawns on c6-d5 against White's c2/d4 produces a symmetrical-looking centre that actually leaves Black to play on the **queenside** with c-pawn breaks while White seeks central or kingside play.

### How to USE pawn structure in your games

1. **Identify the structure** by move 10. Common families: Carlsbad, IQP, Hanging Pawns, Maroczy Bind, Stonewall, Hedgehog.
2. **Memorise typical plans** for each. Each structure carries its own playbook.
3. **Treat pawn moves as decisions**, not reflexes. Ask: *am I improving my structure or my opponent's?*
4. **Trade into your favourite structure** during the middlegame.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- The position has **simplified** but pieces remain — structure now dominates.
- A **pawn break** is available — pause and ask if it improves your skeleton.
- The opponent is offering a **trade** that would change the structure — recompute.

### Common mistakes

- **Pushing a pawn for tactical reasons** without considering the long-term skeleton.
- **Trading pawns automatically** when the resulting structure favours the opponent.
- Treating **doubled pawns** as always bad — sometimes they grant a half-open file worth more than the structural blemish.

> Read the pawns first. The pieces follow.

steps.title: Pawn Weaknesses
steps.text:
## The four classical pawn weaknesses

Learn these names — they are the vocabulary of every middlegame post-mortem.

### Isolated pawn (isolani)

A pawn with **no friendly pawn on either adjacent file**. It cannot be defended by another pawn and so must be defended by **pieces** — tying them down. The square in front of it is also a **permanent outpost** for the enemy.

- *Example*: White pawn on **d4** with no c- or e-pawn. The d5 square is Black's outpost forever.

### Doubled pawns

Two pawns of the same colour on the same file. They cannot defend each other, slow each other's advance, and one of them is usually **backward**.

- *Compensation*: doubled pawns often grant a **half-open file** for the rook — it is not always a weakness.

### Backward pawn

A pawn that:

- **Cannot be defended** by a friendly pawn (the neighbours have moved past it).
- **Cannot advance safely** (the square in front is controlled).

The square in front is a **permanent outpost** for the opponent.

### Passed pawn

The one structural feature that is almost always a **strength** — covered in the endgame lesson. Mentioned here because some passed pawns are also **isolated** or **doubled**, which complicates their evaluation.

### How to USE this in your games

1. **Spot weaknesses for both sides** during the post-mortem of every game.
2. **Provoke them in the opponent's camp** with timely pawn breaks.
3. **Avoid creating them in your own camp** unless you get clear compensation (open files, attacking lines).
4. **Target weaknesses with pieces, not pawns**. Pawns slow down; pieces capture.

### What signs tell you a weakness is fixable

- A **piece exchange** is on offer that would make the weakness exploitable.
- A **pawn break** is one tempo away.
- The opponent's **king is committed** to the side where the weakness lies.

### Common mistakes

- Counting weaknesses **statically**. Some weaknesses are dynamic and disappear with one move.
- **Trading away** the right piece to attack a weakness.
- Ignoring **your own weaknesses** while attacking the opponent's. The race is to keep yours covered.

> A weakness is only a weakness if it can be attacked.

steps.title: Structure Shapes the Plan
steps.text:
## Pawn structure tells you where to play

Every opening produces a **typical pawn skeleton**, and each skeleton carries its own **plan map**. Once you know the structure, you have most of the plan.

### Five common skeletons and their plans

1. **Carlsbad** (White pawns c3-d4 vs Black c6-d5): the famous **minority attack** on the queenside (b4-b5 to break c6).
2. **IQP** (isolated d-pawn): the side **with** the IQP attacks; the side **against** it blockades on **d5** and trades pieces.
3. **King's Indian / Benoni** (locked centre with d5 vs d6): White plays on the **queenside** with c5; Black on the **kingside** with f5-f4.
4. **Maroczy Bind** (White pawns on **c4** and **e4**): White restricts Black's d-pawn; Black seeks ...b5 or ...f5 breaks.
5. **Hedgehog** (Black pawns on a6, b6, d6, e6): Black waits, then explodes with ...b5 or ...d5.

### How to USE structure-driven plans

1. **Recognise the structure** by move 10-12. The names matter because the plans are catalogued.
2. **Pick a side of the board to attack** based on which way your pawns lead.
3. **Play prophylactic moves** against the opponent's typical break.
4. **Avoid passive piece placement** if your structure demands aggressive piece play (IQP) or vice versa (Hedgehog).

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- The opening has played out and the **centre is fixed**.
- Both sides have completed development and are choosing where to attack.
- A **pawn break** is on the horizon — the structure tells you whose break is more dangerous.

### Common mistakes

- Playing the **wrong wing**. King's Indian players who try to attack on the queenside lose; Carlsbad players who try the kingside lose.
- Playing a structure-typical break **too early** before piece coordination is ready.
- Ignoring the structure entirely and "making moves." Strong players are recognisable by *which structure they aim for*.

> Read the pawns. They are telling you the plan.

lessons.title: King Safety
lessons.summary: A safe king wins games

steps.title: Tuck Him Away
steps.text:
## King safety — defined

**King safety** is the measure of how well your king is shielded from **direct attack**. It is not just "having a wall of pawns" — it is the combination of **shelter**, **defenders**, and the **absence of open lines** pointing at the king.

### What this position is

The Italian Opening: pieces developed, knights on c3 and f3, bishops on c4 and c5, central pawns locked. Both kings sit on **e1** and **e8** — exposed in the centre, with **two open files (the d-file and any half-open file)** ready to host enemy rooks. **Castling now** is the priority before pieces start landing on weak squares.

### Three pillars of safety

1. **Pawn shelter** — three pawns in front of the king (f2-g2-h2 or a7-b7-c7).
2. **Defenders nearby** — at least the knight on **f3** (or f6) covering critical squares like h2/h7.
3. **Closed lines** — no open files pointing at the king, no diagonals leading to him.

### How to USE the concept

1. **Castle by move 10** in 90% of games. Sometimes earlier, rarely later.
2. **Don't push pawns near the king** unless there's a concrete tactical reason.
3. **Watch the diagonals** to your king — a long bishop or queen pointing in is a future sacrifice.
4. **Trade attackers**, not defenders. Every piece you trade off the board reduces the attacker's power and yours.

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- The opponent has retained **both bishops and queen** with development complete — an attack is brewing.
- A **pawn lever** like h4-h5 or g4 is being prepared — clamp down before it lands.
- Your king is **still on e1 / e8** past move 10 — castle this move.

### Common mistakes

- Delaying castling to **grab a pawn** in the centre — the resulting open files swallow the king.
- **Pushing g3 or h3** automatically — every pawn move near the king creates a hook for an opponent's pawn break.
- Trading off a **defender** (often the f6 / f3 knight) without an equally strong replacement.

> Castle early, castle short, then keep the wall up.

steps.prompt: Castle your king into safety. The principle: *get out of the centre before the position opens*.
steps.hint: Short castling — kingside, the most common and quickest shelter.

steps.title: After Castling
steps.text:
## You castled — now what?

Castling alone is not safety; it is the **opening move** of safety. The work begins after the king lands.

### Maintaining the fortress

1. **Keep the pawns home**: f2-g2-h2 (or a7-b7-c7 for queenside). The shape is the wall.
2. **Keep a defender on f3 / f6**: the knight covers **h2 / h7** and the **g5 / g4** invasion squares. Trading it without replacement is dangerous.
3. **Keep a back-rank escape**: Kh1 / Kh8 may be required if a back-rank check is threatened — *luft* with h3 / h6 only when needed.
4. **Trade attackers**, not defenders.

### Two visual examples in prose

- After **O-O**, Black plays ...Bg4 pinning the f3-knight. White's wall is **f2-g2-h2** but the **f3 defender is paralysed**. White must dissolve the pin (h3, then if Bxf3 recapture with the queen) before launching anything else.
- A White king on g1 with pawns f2/g2/h2 is **structurally safe**, but if the queen leaves d1 to attack, the **back rank** becomes a worry. A timely **h3** creates *luft* and saves the king from future Re1 threats.

### How to USE it in your games

1. **Audit your castled position every five moves**. Are the pawns still there? Is the f-knight still there?
2. When the **opponent retains attackers**, retain defenders.
3. **Open the centre** only when your king is *safer* than your opponent's.

### What signs tell you the wall is failing

- A **pawn move near your king** (g3, h3, f3) — every one is a potential weakness.
- A **defender has been traded** — recompute safety from scratch.
- An **open file or long diagonal** leads to your king.

### Common mistakes

- Pushing **h3 or g3** prophylactically when nothing was attacking — you weakened yourself for free.
- **Trading queens** when you were the attacker — king safety questions vanish but so does your initiative.
- Forgetting **back-rank mate** patterns. Many games are lost on move 30 by an undefended first rank.

> Castling is not the end of king safety — it is the beginning.

lessons.title: Space Advantage
lessons.summary: More squares, more options

steps.title: What Is Space?
steps.text:
## Space — defined precisely

**Space** is the **count of squares** behind your pawn line that your pieces can use freely. The deeper your pawns advance into enemy territory, the more space you control. Your **own pieces** then have more room to manoeuvre and **the enemy's pieces** have less.

### A simple test

Draw a line at the **middle of the board**. The side whose pawns sit **further forward** controls more space. In the position shown, White has pushed both **d4** and **e4**; Black's pawn sits on e5 only. White has the larger zone to play in.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Maroczy Bind*: White pawns on **c4** and **e4** clamp Black's d-pawn forever. Black's minor pieces have only the squares **behind his own pawns**, while White rotates pieces between the wings at will.
- *King's Indian*: Black plays ...e5 and locks the centre with d6/e5. White's c4-d5 chain pushes Black backward, giving White a queenside space advantage. Black accepts cramped pieces in exchange for the kingside attack he plans later.

### How to USE space in your games

1. **Push pawns** to the 4th and 5th rank when they are **safely supported**.
2. **Keep pieces on the board** — your space cramps the opponent's pieces; if he trades, his pieces breathe again.
3. **Manoeuvre** in your space. Knights especially love big, open quadrants.
4. **Combine** space with weak squares — the squares the opponent gave up by retreating become outposts.

### What signs tell you you have space

- Your pawns sit on the **4th rank or beyond** while his are on the 3rd.
- Your pieces have **multiple good squares** to choose from; his have one or two.
- The opponent's pieces are **doubly placed** behind their own pawns.

### Common mistakes

- **Overextending** — too much space without piece support invites breaks (...c5, ...f5) that destroy the centre.
- **Trading carelessly** when you have space — every trade gives the cramped side relief.
- **Hesitating to push** when the opponent cannot react — space is *won by pushes*, not by hopes.

> Space is the by-product of pushing pawns when your pieces are ready.

steps.title: Exploiting Space
steps.text:
## Converting space into something concrete

A space advantage is **not a goal in itself** — it is a **resource**. The plan is always to convert space into a **second advantage**: weak squares, pawn breaks, an attack, an outpost, or a winning endgame.

### Capablanca's two rules

1. **The cramped side should trade pieces**. Less material, more room per piece.
2. **The side with space should AVOID trades**. Keep his pieces stuffed onto few squares.

These rules are not optional. Almost every space-vs-cramped game is decided by whether each side respects them.

### How to USE the space

1. **Press slowly**. Build threats on multiple files; the cramped side cannot defend them all.
2. **Re-route pieces** between wings. The cramped opponent re-routes more slowly than you do.
3. **Plan a pawn break** that turns space into an attack: f4-f5, h4-h5, c4-c5 are typical.
4. **Double on a file** the opponent cannot contest because his rooks are stuck behind cramped pieces.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *King's Indian, White side*: White has space on the queenside. He plays **a3, Rb1, b4, c5** — the slow build-up the cramped side cannot match. By the time Black has organised, the queenside is collapsing.
- *French Advance*: White owns the **e5/d4** wedge. His plan: build the queenside (Be3, Qd2, Rb1, b4-b5) while Black struggles to find squares for his bishop and knights.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- Your pawns are on the **4th-5th rank**, his on the **2nd-3rd**.
- He has a **bad bishop** stuck behind his own pawns.
- His pieces step on each other — knights blocking bishops, rooks blocking queens.

### Common mistakes

- **Trading queens** when you have space — the attacking potential of space evaporates.
- **Closing the position** further with your own pawns — your pieces cannot attack walls.
- Forgetting that **space is bought with risk** — extended pawns can become weak in an endgame.

> Squeeze the position with patience; the cramped side suffocates.

lessons.title: Weak Squares and Colors
lessons.summary: Squares your opponent can't defend

steps.title: The Holes
steps.text:
## Weak squares — defined

A **weak square** is a square that **cannot be defended by a friendly pawn**, *now or ever*. Once weak, it stays weak — pawns do not retreat. The most dangerous weak squares lie in your **own half** of the board, especially within range of the enemy.

### What this position is

A classic Italian-style middlegame. Both sides have castled, both have all minor pieces in play. Look closely at **d5** and **d4**: each of these squares is a **3rd-rank** central hole that one side has not yet secured. Whoever plants a piece there first dominates.

### How holes form

1. A **flank pawn push** (...g6, ...h6, ...b6) leaves the unmarched square behind it weak.
2. A **pawn break** advances one pawn but leaves another **backward**, with a weak square in front of it.
3. A **fianchetto bishop** is traded — the squares around it are forever weak.
4. **Doubled pawns** along a file leave the squares **between** the doubled pawns vulnerable.

### How to USE weak squares

1. **Spot them** — every time the opponent moves a pawn, ask *what square did he just abandon forever?*
2. **Bring a piece** — knights are the kings of holes; bishops thrive on holes that connect to a long diagonal; rooks claim files that lead through holes.
3. **Defend** the piece on the hole with a pawn so it cannot be cheaply traded.
4. **Combine** with the opponent's bad piece — if his bishop cannot reach the hole, your knight reigns.

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- The opponent has played a **flank pawn move** without preparation.
- A **half-open file** runs from your rook into a possible hole.
- The opponent has a **bad bishop** that cannot defend the hole's colour.

### Common mistakes

- **Misjudging** a square as weak when a pawn can still reach it.
- Failing to **occupy** the hole — a hole no one fills is just a square.
- **Trading the piece** on the hole for a less valuable one.

### A model line (schematic)

... {{Nd5}} — a knight on the hole, defended by a pawn, attacking everything around — this is the picture of a weak-square strategy at work.

> A weak square is a permanent address — make sure your piece moves in.

steps.title: Color Complexes
steps.text:
## Beyond squares — complexes

Deeper than any single weak square is a **colour complex**: a **set of squares of one colour** that are systematically weak. When the opponent's pawns are all on **one colour**, every square of the **opposite colour** is potentially weak.

### How a complex forms

- The opponent's pawns chain along a **single colour** (often the colour of his bishop).
- His **bishop on the same colour** can defend pawns but **never** the squares between them.
- He has **traded** the bishop of the *opposite* colour, leaving him with no diagonal defender.

### Two visual examples in prose

- **Dark-square weakness**: Black plays ...e5 and ...g6 with bishops traded. Pawns sit on c7, d6, e5, f7, g6, h7 — almost all on **light squares**. The **dark squares** (d4, e3, f4, g5, h6) are an open boulevard for White's pieces.
- **Light-square weakness around a king**: Black has played ...g6 and traded his light-square bishop. The squares **f5, h5, e6, g4** are all weak. White lifts a knight to **e6** or pushes **h4-h5** and the king is doomed.

### How to USE colour complexes

1. **Trade** the opponent's bishop **of the weak colour** if you can — without it, he has no diagonal defender.
2. **Place pieces and pawns** on the **strong colour** (yours) and target the squares of the weak colour.
3. **Push pawns** that fix the opponent's structure on one colour — sacrifices to lock the chain are often correct.
4. **Use a queen-bishop battery** along the weak diagonal — devastating with a colour-weak king.

### What signs tell you a complex is forming

- The opponent has **only one bishop** and his pawns are on the **same colour**.
- A **fianchettoed bishop** has just been traded — the squares around the king (one colour) are weak.
- An **endgame is heading** for opposite-coloured bishops with pawns fixed on one colour.

### Common mistakes

- **Trading your own bishop** of the weak colour — you handed away the antidote.
- **Pushing pawns onto your own bishop's colour** — your bishop is now bad and your colour is now weak.
- Treating a single weak square as a *complex*. A complex is **systemic**.

> Squares are tactical. Colours are strategic.

lessons.title: Open Files
lessons.summary: Lanes of invasion for your rooks

steps.title: Why Rooks Love Open Files
steps.text:
## Open and half-open files — defined

- **Open file** — a file with **no pawns of either colour**. Both rooks have an unobstructed lane.
- **Half-open file** — a file with **no pawn of your colour** but at least one **enemy pawn**. Your rook has a target; the opponent's rook is blocked.
- **Closed file** — a file with **friendly pawns** in the way. Your rook on it is asleep.

### What this position is

The pawns have melted away — only c, f, g, h-pawns remain on each side, with d- and e-files **fully open**. Both kings are still in the centre. Whoever **claims** the open files first will have the freer hand.

### Why files matter so much

A rook is a **slow piece** until you give it an open file. On a closed file it does almost nothing. On an open file it threatens **invasion** — penetration to the **7th rank** is one of the most decisive ideas in chess.

### How to USE open files

1. **Identify the open and half-open files** at every stage.
2. **Bring rooks to those files** as soon as development allows.
3. **Contest** the file — if both rooks land on it, **trade** rooks only when you keep a follow-up rook ready (doubling).
4. **Penetrate** to the 7th rank (or 2nd from your perspective) — the *pigs on the 7th* idea.
5. On a **half-open file**, attack the enemy pawn with rook + queen.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- A pawn break has just **opened a file** — race to claim it.
- The opponent has a **backward pawn on a half-open file** — pile pieces on it.
- The enemy king is **on the same file** as your rook with no pawn cover.

### Common mistakes

- Putting **only one rook** on the open file when the opponent contests it — you lose the trade.
- Leaving the **a- and h-files** unclaimed; rim files matter when they lead to the king.
- **Trading rooks** on the open file when your remaining rook is worse than the enemy's.

> A rook on an open file is a piece. A rook on a closed file is a target.

steps.title: Doubling & The 7th Rank
steps.text:
## Doubling rooks — and the 7th rank

The most powerful claim on an open file is **two rooks stacked** on it. Doubling rooks does three things:

1. **Wins** the file in any rook trade — the second rook recaptures and dominates.
2. **Triples** the threat to invade the 7th rank.
3. **Coordinates** with a queen for a heavy-piece battery (a queen between or in front of the rooks creates *Alekhine's gun*).

### Pigs on the 7th

A rook on the **7th rank** (or 2nd from the defender's perspective) is so strong it earned its own nickname — the *pig*. Two rooks doubled on the 7th are *blind pigs* (they trample everything).

Why:

- They attack **pawns on the 7th**, all undefended by other pawns.
- They cut off the **enemy king** to the back rank.
- They threaten **mate** on the 8th rank if the king cannot escape.

### How to USE this in your games

1. **Plan the doubling** — first rook to the file, second rook prepared to follow (often via a rook lift).
2. **Trade off defenders** of the 7th rank before invading.
3. **Co-ordinate with the queen** — the queen + rook on the 7th is a typical mating attack.
4. **Combine with weak pawns** — if all enemy pawns sit on the 7th rank, doubled rooks gobble them.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Capablanca's classic technique*: rooks on c1/c2 contesting the c-file; opponent disputes; rook trade favours White; second rook follows; **Rc7** then **Rxc7** — the file becomes a winning highway.
- *Alekhine's gun*: queen on c1 in front of both rooks on c2 and c3 (or any vertical stack). The opponent cannot contest the file; one penetration ends the game.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- An open file points **toward the enemy king** or **a weak pawn**.
- The opponent has **only one rook ready** to contest the file — your doubling will win it.
- The 7th rank has **multiple targets**.

### Common mistakes

- **Doubling on the wrong file** — the file with no targets is wasted heavy-piece firepower.
- **Penetrating to the 7th** before the rook is supported — a single rook on the 7th can be trapped.
- **Trading queens** when the queen was the partner — the rooks alone cannot mate without an open king.

> Two rooks doubled on the 7th rank do not win — they finish.

lessons.title: The Bishop Pair
lessons.summary: Two bishops are worth more than you think

steps.title: Why Two Bishops?
steps.text:
## The bishop pair — defined

The **bishop pair** is one of the most stable long-term advantages in chess. Two bishops together are worth approximately **+0.5** of a pawn more than two knights or a knight+bishop combination — Larry Kaufman's statistical study confirmed this nominal value across millions of games.

### Why the pair is more than the sum of two bishops

- Each bishop covers **only its own colour**. **Two bishops together** cover **all 64 squares**.
- They **complement** each other: the dark bishop guards what the light bishop cannot, and vice versa.
- They cooperate over **long distances** — far better than two knights can in open positions.
- They **convert advantages** more reliably in endgames where space and tempo matter.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Open ending*: White has bishop pair, all queenside pawns vs all kingside pawns. The light-squared bishop blockades on one wing while the dark-squared bishop walks the long diagonal toward the kingside. The opponent's two knights cannot keep up.
- *Quiet middlegame*: with central tension resolved and pawns symmetric, White's bishops on **b2** and **c4** rake long diagonals at Black's king on g8. Two bishops + queen attack motifs (the *fianchetto + Italian* battery) are devastating.

### How to USE the pair

1. **Open the position** — the pair shines in open games. Trade pawns, not pieces.
2. **Avoid trading** either bishop unless you trade up (e.g. for a strong knight).
3. **Place the bishops** on long, contested diagonals — never on short ones.
4. **Press in the endgame** — the pair's value compounds as material drops.

### What signs tell you the pair is decisive

- The position is **simple and open**.
- The opponent has a **knight without an outpost**.
- **Pawns on both wings** — the bishops reach both, the knights do not.

### Common mistakes

- **Holding the pair passively** in a closed position — closed positions favour the knight.
- **Trading one bishop** for a knight to win a pawn — often the wrong material balance.
- Forgetting that **opposite-coloured bishops** in the endgame cancel the pair's value (only one bishop's colour matters there).

> Two bishops, one strategy: open the board and let them sing.

steps.title: When to Trade
steps.text:
## Trading rules with the bishop pair

The most useful question to ask in any bishop-pair middlegame: **"Which trade benefits me?"** The answer follows two simple rules.

### Rule 1 — if you HAVE the pair

1. **Open the position**: trade pawns to clear lines.
2. **Refuse minor-piece trades** that involve a bishop. If the opponent offers Bxc6, decline if possible.
3. **Trade pieces other than your bishops** if a trade is unavoidable — even queens, sometimes.
4. **Avoid creating a knight outpost** for the opponent. Closed positions help knights, hurt bishops.

### Rule 2 — if you GAVE UP the pair

1. **Close the position**: keep pawns interlocked, refuse pawn trades that open lines.
2. **Aim for a knight outpost**, ideally on the 5th or 6th rank.
3. **Trade off the opponent's good bishop** — leave him with the bad one.
4. **Push pawns onto the colour** of the opponent's remaining bishop to make it bad.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Ruy Lopez Exchange*: White plays {{Bxc6}} voluntarily. Black gets the bishop pair but **doubled c-pawns**. White's plan is to **simplify into an endgame** where the doubled pawns matter more than the pair.
- *Nimzo-Indian Sämisch*: White plays {{f3}} and {{e4}} with the bishop pair, but with a closed centre and weak doubled pawns on c. Black aims for ...c5, blockades, and rides the structural compensation despite missing the pair.

### How to USE these rules

1. **Decide before move 15** which side wants the pair and which side wants the closed centre.
2. Make every **pawn move** consistent with that decision.
3. **Trade or refuse trades** in line with the rules — even a small inaccuracy here can flip a winning game.

### What signs tell you to apply the rule

- You have **two bishops** vs **bishop + knight** or **two knights**.
- The opponent has just played a move that **trades into a knight outpost** — refuse it.
- The position is **about to open** with a pawn break — embrace it if you have the pair, prevent it if you do not.

### Common mistakes

- **Trading the pair too early** for a small concrete gain.
- **Closing your own position** to *protect* the pair — you smothered them.
- **Ignoring the structural cost** of giving up the pair — even one tempo of compensation can be too little.

> The pair is bought once, sold once. Choose carefully.

lessons.title: Prophylaxis
lessons.summary: Prevent before you attack

steps.title: Nimzowitsch's Idea
steps.text:
## Prophylaxis — defined

**Prophylaxis** is the act of making a move that **prevents** a plan your opponent intended. Coined by **Aron Nimzowitsch** in *My System*, refined by **Tigran Petrosian**, and turned into a winning style by **Anatoly Karpov**, prophylaxis is the heart of mature positional play.

### A precise definition

A **prophylactic move** has at least one of these properties:

- It **stops a pawn break** the opponent was preparing.
- It **denies a square** the opponent's piece wanted.
- It **defends in advance** a target the opponent was planning to attack.
- It **trades** a piece the opponent needed for their plan.

It does **not** add to your own attack — that is the point. The opponent's plan dies before it lives.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Karpov's classic Kh1*: in countless games, Karpov played a quiet **Kh1** before any kingside action. The king-move took three squares (g1-h1) but cleared the back rank for a future rook lift, escaped a possible diagonal pin, and removed any tactic on the g1-a7 diagonal — three potential opponent ideas, eliminated in one move.
- *Petrosian's a4*: faced with a brewing ...b5 break, Petrosian would play **a4** *one move before* the opponent ever considered b5. The break never happens; the opponent's plan stalls; the game continues on Petrosian's terms.

### How to USE prophylaxis in your games

1. **Before every move**, mentally pass — pretend it is your opponent's turn. *What is his best move?*
2. **Identify his plan**, not just his next move. A prophylactic response usually disables a 3-move plan.
3. **Choose between** continuing your own plan and stopping his. The right answer depends on which is faster.
4. **Quiet moves** are often prophylactic — Kh1, h3, a3, Re1 — moves that *do nothing* but deny something.

### What signs tell you to apply it

- The opponent is preparing a **pawn break** (...c5, ...f5, ...b5).
- A piece of yours is **almost overworked** — preempt the trade.
- Your own attack is **two tempi away** — spend one tempo on defence first.

### Common mistakes

- Believing prophylaxis means **passive defence**. It is *active prevention*.
- **Over-prophylaxis** — defending against threats that are not real, while the opponent quietly improves elsewhere.
- **Missing** the opponent's plan because you only looked at his last move.

> Stop your opponent first. Win second.

steps.title: How to Spot It
steps.text:
## A practical drill

Prophylaxis is a **habit**, not a calculation. The drill that builds the habit takes about ten seconds per move.

### The three-question prophylactic checklist

Before every move, ask:

1. **"If it were my opponent's turn, what would he play?"** — try to find his best move.
2. **"Why does he want that move?"** — what plan is it part of?
3. **"Can I prevent it without ruining my position?"** — if yes, do it. If no, ignore and continue.

In the position shown — Italian middlegame, both castled, fully developed — Black wants ...d5 to challenge the centre. White's prophylactic answer is **{{a3}}** (preventing ...Bb4 ideas after a possible ...Nd4) or even **Re1** (preparing a possible Bf1-e3 redeployment).

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Stopping ...d5*: White recognises the central break and plays **{{Re1}}** + **{{h3}}**. Each is a tiny move, but together they make ...d5 unattractive: the e-file pin is gone, the f3-knight has luft, and Black has no easy follow-up.
- *Stopping a sacrifice*: a Black knight is on f6 eyeing ...Nxe4 sacrifices. White plays **{{Re1}}** in advance — the rook now defends e4 indirectly, and the entire ...Nxe4 idea is removed from the board.

### How to USE the drill

1. **Slow down** by ten seconds per move. The cost is trivial; the benefit is enormous.
2. **Train with master games**: cover the next move and predict the master's prophylactic choice.
3. **Notice the moves you cannot predict** — those are the prophylactic ones a human attacker would have missed.

### What signs tell you the position is ripe for prophylaxis

- The position is **balanced** with no immediate tactics.
- Both sides have completed development; the game is about plans, not pieces.
- Your opponent has a **clear plan** and you do not — disrupt his.

### Common mistakes

- Skipping the drill in **time pressure** — that is exactly when prophylaxis matters most.
- **Reacting** to the opponent's last move instead of anticipating his next plan.
- **Confusing prophylaxis with passivity**. A good prophylactic move *also* prepares your own ideas; the best ones are *both*.

> Karpov did not play moves. He prevented them.

lessons.title: Maneuvering
lessons.summary: Slow regrouping for a winning setup

steps.title: The Art of Doing Nothing
steps.text:
## Manoeuvring — defined

**Manoeuvring** is the art of **slowly regrouping** your pieces to ideal squares while the opponent has no immediate threats. The position usually calls for it when the centre is **closed** or stable: with no tactical fireworks possible, the only way to make progress is to **improve piece placement** by a fraction every move.

### What it looks like

In a closed Italian or Ruy Lopez middlegame, neither side has obvious breaks. White might play:

1. **Nf3-e1-d3** — the knight re-routes to a square where it eyes both the queenside (b4, c5) and the kingside (f4).
2. **Bc1-d2-e3** or even **Bc1-e3-c5** — the bishop walks to a long diagonal.
3. **Qd1-e2-c2** — the queen finds a square supporting either wing's break.
4. **Rf1-e1-e3-g3** — the famous **rook lift**, slow but devastating.

Nothing happens for fifteen moves. Then suddenly, a pawn break lands and every piece is **already pointed at the breakthrough**.

### The key concept: every move improves something

A proper manoeuvring move:

- Brings a piece to a **better square** than the previous one.
- Does **not weaken** any of your own pawns or squares.
- **Maintains** or improves coordination.
- Often improves **two pieces at once** — a single move that defends, attacks, or unblocks multiple lines.

### How to USE manoeuvring in your games

1. **Identify your best piece configuration** — the *dream setup* — and work backwards.
2. **Pick a knight tour** that ends on a strong outpost (e.g. Nb1-d2-f1-g3-f5).
3. **Move waiting** when the opponent has no improvement — *zugzwang* in slow motion.
4. **Exchange your worst piece** if you cannot improve it.

### What signs in the position tell you to apply it

- The **centre is locked** with chained pawns.
- No **tactical motif** is available for either side.
- Your **worst piece** has a clear path to a better square.

### Common mistakes

- **Forcing** the issue with a premature pawn break — the manoeuvring side wins by patience.
- **Repeating moves** without improvement — repetition draws, and the cramped opponent thanks you.
- **Trading down** when you have the better setup — keep pieces on the board to exploit your superior coordination.

> When nothing is forced, improve a piece.

steps.title: Karpov's Way
steps.text:
## The model practitioner — Karpov

**Anatoly Karpov** is the historical master of manoeuvring. His games against Ulf Andersson, Boris Spassky, and Viktor Korchnoi are textbook studies in **patience plus precision**. He would shift one piece at a time, denying the opponent every active idea, until the position was so suffocated that **one tactical blow** ended the game.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Karpov–Unzicker, 1974*: a Ruy Lopez where Karpov played the famous knight tour **Nb1-d2-f1-g3** while doubling rooks on the a-file. By move 30 every Black piece was pinned in place; Karpov then opened the queenside and Unzicker collapsed in three moves.
- *Karpov–Kasparov, 1985*: a Sicilian where Karpov spent 15 moves manoeuvring his light-squared bishop from c1 to a3 to b2 to e5. Each step looked harmless; together they built an unstoppable kingside attack.

### How to USE Karpov-style manoeuvring

1. **Identify the squares your opponent fears most** — usually the squares his pawns can no longer cover.
2. **Re-route every piece** to that quadrant of the board, one move at a time.
3. **Wait** for the opponent to commit a small concession (a pawn move, a piece trade) — then strike.
4. **Trust the position**. Manoeuvring requires faith that the squares you accumulate will pay off.

### What signs tell you Karpov-style is right

- You have **better pieces** but no immediate way to convert.
- The opponent's plan **requires a break** he cannot yet make.
- The position is **closed enough** that pieces, not pawns, decide.

### Common mistakes

- **Impatience** — a single hasty move can ruin twenty patient ones.
- **Mistaking manoeuvring for aimlessness**. Every move must have a clear target.
- **Ignoring tactical opportunities** that arise during the manoeuvre. Karpov never missed them when they appeared — manoeuvring is the *default*, not the *only* mode.

> Patience is the move you have not yet calculated.

lessons.title: The Exchange Sacrifice
lessons.summary: Give up a rook for a minor piece

steps.title: Giving Up the Rook
steps.text:
## The exchange sacrifice — defined

Giving up a **rook for a minor piece** (bishop or knight) is called *sacrificing the exchange*. The numerical cost is roughly **2 points** (rook ~5, minor ~3). The strategic prize: a **permanent positional advantage** that compounds for the rest of the game.

### Why give up the rook?

A rook is **slow until you give it an open file**. If your rook has no file and your opponent's minor piece is **strong** (outpost, attacker on the king, occupier of a key square), trading rook-for-minor often **buys** a long-term advantage:

- A **dominant minor piece** for the rest of the game.
- A **structural advantage** — broken pawns, weak king, or weak colour complex on the opponent's side.
- An **attack** that cannot be parried any other way.
- Removal of a key **defender** without which the opponent's position collapses.

### The historical master: Petrosian

**Tigran Petrosian** turned the exchange sacrifice into a personal weapon. His trademark **{{Rxc3}}** in the Sicilian — giving up rook for knight to wreck White's pawn structure — became known by his name. He saw the sacrifice not as a tactic but as a **trade of resources** he understood better than anyone.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *Petrosian–Reshevsky, 1953*: Black plays **Rxc3 bxc3** and Black's bishop pair, plus White's wrecked queenside pawns, gave a permanent and decisive advantage. White had material; Black had everything else.
- *Modern Sicilian*: Black plays ...Rxe3 to remove a White knight pinning Black's pieces. The resulting open e-file is unusable for White (no rook to use it) while Black's central pawns stream forward.

### How to USE the exchange sacrifice

1. **Identify the rook with no file** — that is the candidate to sacrifice.
2. **Identify the dominant minor piece** — your rook gladly trades for that.
3. **Calculate** that the resulting structure is permanent — exchange sacrifices are *not* speculative.
4. **Follow up** with active play: bring the second rook into the game, push pawns, attack.

### What signs tell you to consider it

- Your rook is **passive** with no realistic future.
- The opponent has a **strong outpost minor** that is otherwise unremovable.
- The opponent's **king or pawn structure** can be permanently damaged by the trade.

### Common mistakes

- **Sacrificing speculatively** — exchange sacrifices need clear long-term compensation.
- Giving up the **wrong rook** — keep the active one, sacrifice the passive one.
- **Trading more material** afterwards — your remaining pieces must coordinate, not simplify.

> Sometimes the rook is the bad piece. Trade it.

steps.title: When It Works
steps.text:
## The three conditions for a sound exchange sacrifice

Not every rook-for-minor trade is a *sacrifice* — many are simply blunders. Genuine exchange sacrifices satisfy at least **two of these three** conditions.

### Condition 1 — the resulting structure favours you long-term

After the smoke clears, your **pawn structure is intact** while the opponent's is **damaged**. Doubled pawns, isolated pawns, weak colour complexes — all permanent and worth a roughly two-point material concession.

### Condition 2 — your minor piece is exceptional

The minor piece that **survives** must be:

- An **outpost piece** that cannot be removed.
- A piece of a **bishop pair** that now dominates open lines.
- A **defender of the enemy king's weak colour** — irreplaceable.

### Condition 3 — the opponent's remaining rook has no future

The opponent keeps a rook, but if it has **no open file**, **no penetration squares**, and **no targets**, that rook is no better than a knight in the resulting middlegame. A rook with no file is little more than a heavy piece on the back rank.

### Two visual examples in prose

- *The classic Sicilian Rxc3*: Black plays {{Rxc3}} bxc3 — White is up the exchange, but his queenside is wrecked, his bishop on c1 is bad, and Black's bishop pair plus pawn play guarantees long-term pressure. All three conditions are met.
- *Stopping a kingside attack*: White plays {{Rxf6}} gxf6 — material lost, but Black's kingside is shredded, the dark squares around the king are weak, and White's queen + bishop now have a permanent attacking field. Conditions one and two satisfied.

### How to USE the conditions

1. **Score the position** against the three conditions before sacrificing.
2. If at least **two are clearly met**, the sacrifice is sound.
3. If **only one** is met, look harder — usually it is a blunder.
4. Always **calculate the next 4-5 moves** to confirm the long-term picture survives forced exchanges.

### What signs tell you the sacrifice is right

- The opponent's **bishop or knight is irremovable** without giving up the exchange.
- The opponent's **king or pawn shield** has a structural weakness you can exploit.
- Your **other pieces are more active** than your opponent's even after the sacrifice.

### Common mistakes

- **Sacrificing the active rook** instead of the passive one.
- **Failing to follow up** — the sacrifice is the *first* move of a plan, not the plan itself.
- **Misjudging the structure**. Permanence is everything; if the damage can be repaired in three moves, the sacrifice was unsound.

> Exchange sacrifices are not gambles — they are accountancy.

lessons.title: Attacking the Uncastled King
lessons.summary: A king in the center is a target

steps.title: Why Centralized Kings Die
steps.text:
A king stuck in the center is exposed to attacks from both wings, with open files often pointed straight at his face. When your opponent delays castling, the priority is simple: **keep the king there and pry the position open.**

## When this idea appears

- The opponent has spent two or three moves on something other than development (premature pawn grabs, queen sorties, repeated knight moves).
- A pawn break is available that opens the **e-file** or **d-file**.
- You have a development lead of one or two pieces, often with a queen and bishop already eyeing the center.

## How to prepare

1. **Develop with threats** — every move should add an attacker or take away an enemy tempo.
2. **Open lines** — push pawns or trade pawns to open the e- or d-file.
3. **Centralize the queen** — but only when she cannot be chased.
4. **Sacrifice if needed** — a pawn or even a piece is cheap when the king has no roof.

## A model line (Italian-style)

In the position above, after a typical Italian setup, White's pieces are coordinated and Black still has to find time to castle. Plans like {{Ng5}} or breaks with {{d4}} aim to keep the king pinned in the center.

## How to spot it

1. Look at the enemy king — is he still in the center after move 8 or 10?
2. Count your developed pieces vs. the opponent's.
3. Find the pawn break that opens a line on the king.
4. Calculate forcing sequences before quiet ones.

> Morphy did not win because he was a magician. He won because he opened lines and his opponents had not castled.

Speed is everything: every tempo you spend on a non-attacking move is a tempo your opponent uses to escape.

steps.title: The Recipe
steps.text:
Attacking the uncastled king follows a remarkably consistent script. Memorize the steps and you will recognize the pattern from across the room.

## The five-step recipe

1. **Develop everybody.** Knights and bishops first, queen last. A piece on its starting square is worth nothing.
2. **Open the center.** Pawn breaks like {{d4}}, {{e5}}, or {{c4}} expose the central files.
3. **Aim heavy pieces** at the e-file (or d-file).
4. **Sacrifice for tempo** if the opponent is one move away from safety. A pawn or a piece is cheap when the alternative is letting him castle.
5. **Calculate to mate** or to a winning material gain — not just "a strong attack".

## What to give up

- A pawn for an open file is almost always good.
- A piece for two pawns + open lines + a king on the run is often winning.
- A queen for a forced mate is an obvious yes.

## What to *not* do

- Move the same piece twice without forcing reason.
- Trade attackers for defenders.
- Push pawns that weaken your **own** king if it is also exposed.

## Pattern checklist for tactical alarms

- **e-file open** + enemy king on e8 → look for rook or queen sacrifices on e6.
- **Pinned f-pawn** → {{Nxf7}} or {{Bxf7+}} ideas.
- **Queen on d8 or e7** → check whether a knight can fork her with the king.

> Material counts when both kings are safe. When one king is naked, only **time** counts.

lessons.title: Opposite-Side Castling Attacks
lessons.summary: Race to the enemy king with pawns

steps.title: The Pawn Storm
steps.text:
When you castle on **one side** and your opponent castles on the **other**, the rules of attack change. Your pawns become *attackers*, because pushing them does not weaken your own king's cover.

## When this idea appears

- Both sides have committed kings on opposite wings (one short, the other long).
- The center is **closed or stable** so neither side can blast through it.
- Each side has an extra pawn or two near the enemy king.

## The standard plan

With White castled kingside and Black castled queenside, White attacks with **queenside pawns** ({{a4}}, {{b4}}, {{a5}}). With opposite castling roles reversed, you push *kingside* pawns ({{h4}}, {{g4}}, {{h5}}, {{g5}}).

## How to prepare

1. **Identify the target king's pawn cover.** The pawns directly in front of his castled position are the wall to break.
2. **Push the pawn that meets a defender first** — the one that can be exchanged for an enemy piece.
3. **Keep your pieces ready** to invade the moment a file or diagonal opens.
4. **Avoid premature exchanges** of attackers — every minor piece you give up is a brick missing from your battering ram.

## A model attack idea

Against a short-castled king with pawns on f7-g7-h7, the typical kingside attacker plays:

- {{h4}} preparing the storm.
- {{g4}} adding a second pawn to the wave.
- {{h5}} fixing the target pawn or threatening to trade.
- {{hxg6}} or {{g5}} to crack open the file.
- A rook or queen swings to {{h1}}-{{h3}} or directly down the open file.

> *"Opposite castling means mate in 20 moves — to somebody."*

steps.title: Speed Counts
steps.text:
Opposite-side castling is a **footrace**. Both sides are pushing pawns at the enemy king. Whoever opens lines first usually wins — sometimes by mere tempi.

## How to count tempi

1. Count how many moves you need to **break open** the enemy king's pawn cover.
2. Count how many moves your *opponent* needs to break **yours**.
3. If you are even, the side **to move** wins.
4. If you are one tempo behind, you need a **sacrifice** to make up the difference.

## Practical priorities

- **Do not move your king pawns** — those are your shield.
- **Do not waste moves** retreating pieces unless they are about to be lost.
- **Trade off the opponent's defenders** — especially the knight that guards his castled position.
- **Bring all heavy pieces** to the attack file or diagonal.

## Avoid these mistakes

- Pushing pawns in front of *your own* king to "create space" — you just opened lines for the opponent.
- Slowing down to grab a pawn far from the action.
- Over-protecting your king with a passive piece that should be attacking.

## How to spot the right moment

- The enemy's defensive knight has been traded.
- Your h-pawn (or a-pawn) is one move from {{h5}} or {{a5}} and the file will open.
- Your queen or rook is already on or near the attacking file.

When all those line up, **strike now** — even a piece sacrifice can be correct.

> In opposite-castling races, the second-fastest attacker is the one who gets mated.

lessons.title: The Greek Gift (Bxh7+)
lessons.summary: Classic bishop sacrifice against the castled king

steps.title: The Pattern
steps.text:
The **Greek Gift** is the most famous sacrifice in chess: a bishop is dropped on h7 (or h2 for Black), the king takes — and walks straight into a mating attack with knight and queen.

## The standard sequence

A model line looks like this:

1. {{Bxh7+}} — bishop sacrifice.
2. **Kxh7** — king must take (or the bishop comes home with a piece won).
3. {{Ng5+}} — knight check.
4. **Kg8** (or **Kg6** in some variants) — the king flees.
5. {{Qh5}} — queen joins, threatening **Qh7#**.
6. The defender's only resources are *forced*, and most of them lose.

## When this attack appears

- Black has castled **short** with pawns on f7-g7-h7.
- The bishop on **d3** (or c2-b1 battery) eyes the h7 pawn.
- A **white knight** can leap to **g5** with check and tempo.
- The white queen has a clear path to **h5**.
- The defending knight on **f6** (the natural shield of h7) is **gone**, **pinned**, or **distracted**.

## Why it is named that

The Greeks supposedly left the wooden horse outside Troy as a "gift" — and the Trojans dragged it inside to their doom. A bishop on h7 looks like a careless gift, but it carries a whole attack inside it.

> The piece you accept may not be the gift you wanted.

steps.title: Checklist Before Sacrificing
steps.text:
The Greek Gift either wins or *loses* — there is no middle ground. Before you give the bishop, run through this list.

## The yes/no checklist

1. **No defender on f6.** Can Black's knight reach f6 to plug the hole? If yes, *abort*.
2. **Knight ready for g5.** Is a white knight one move from {{Ng5}} after the king takes?
3. **Queen route to h5.** Is the path from d1 to h5 (or h3 to h5) free of obstructions?
4. **No flight to g6.** If the king runs to **g6**, do you have moves like **Qh5+** or **f4-f5** that follow up?
5. **No interference from Black's queen or bishop** that lands a counter-check.
6. **No counter-attack** that is faster on your own king.

If every answer is *yes*, the sacrifice is almost always sound.

## A model continuation

After {{Bxh7+}} **Kxh7** {{Ng5+}}:

- **Kg8**: {{Qh5}} threatens {{Qh7#}}. Most defenses fail.
- **Kg6**: White often plays {{Qg4}} or {{h4}} bringing more attackers.
- **Kh6**: rare but dangerous — calculate {{Nxf7+}} and {{Qd2+}}.

## When *not* to do it

- The defending knight is solidly on **f6** with no way to remove it.
- Your queen is far away (e.g. on a1) and cannot reach **h5** in time.
- The opponent has a piece (usually a bishop on g4 or e6) that can interpose with check.
- You have no follow-up after **Kg8**.

> The Greek Gift rewards calculation. It punishes hope.

lessons.title: The Rook Lift
lessons.summary: Bring a rook to attack via the 3rd rank

steps.title: Lift and Swing
steps.text:
The **rook lift** is one of the most aggressive piece maneuvers in chess: the rook leaves its first rank, climbs to the **third rank**, and *swings* across to join the kingside (or queenside) attack.

## When this idea appears

- The position is **half-closed** or has a fixed pawn structure — the rook cannot use a file directly.
- Your **king** is castled and safe.
- The enemy king is castled and you have **other attackers** already nearby (queen, knight, bishop).
- A pawn on the third rank (e.g. {{d3}}, {{e3}}) makes room for the rook to enter.

## The standard maneuver

The textbook version on the kingside looks like this:

1. {{Re1}}-{{Re3}} — the rook lifts to the third rank.
2. {{Rg3}} or {{Rh3}} — the rook swings to a kingside attacking square.
3. With queen on h5 or knight on f5, the attack often becomes decisive.

## How to prepare

- Make sure the third rank is **clear** (no friendly pawns blocking the path).
- Have a kingside **pawn pivot** (h-pawn push, g-pawn ready) so the lifted rook can find a target.
- Coordinate with the queen — she is the partner that finishes most rook-lift attacks.

## How to spot it

1. Is there a way to reach the enemy king *that does not require an open file*?
2. Is your back-rank rook idle, with no open file to claim?
3. Are your other attacking pieces nearby?

If all three answers are yes, the lift is the move.

> A rook on the 3rd rank is no longer a defender. It is a missile.

steps.title: When to Use It
steps.text:
Rook lifts are a *positional weapon* with **tactical** consequences. They appear in many great attacking games once both sides have castled and the center is stable.

## The ideal conditions

- **Closed or half-closed center** — the d- and e-files are not usable.
- **Castled enemy king** — kingside or queenside, the lifted rook can reach either.
- **Friendly pieces nearby** — the rook is one piece in a coordinated attack, not a lone hero.
- **Pawn structure** with a **third-rank highway** — typically achieved by a {{d3}} or {{e3}} pawn.

## Combinations to remember

- **Lift + h-pawn push** — {{Re3}}, then {{h4}}-{{h5}} to crack the kingside.
- **Lift + queen swing** — {{Re3}}, {{Qh5}}, mate threats on h7.
- **Lift + knight maneuver** — {{Re3}}, {{Nf5}}, doubling attackers on key squares.
- **Lift + sacrifice** — once enough attackers are stationed near the king, a knight or bishop sacrifice often delivers mate.

## A model line

In many Italian Game and Ruy Lopez middlegames, White plays {{Re1}}-{{Re3}}-{{Rg3}} or {{Re3}}-{{Rh3}}, joining the queen at h5 in a textbook attack on the castled king. The same idea appears on the queenside when Black has castled long.

## Common mistakes

- Lifting too early — before the center is stable, the rook is exposed to {{e5}} or {{d5}} pawn breaks.
- Lifting *into* a pin — be aware of enemy bishops on the long diagonal.
- Lifting with **no follow-up** — the rook needs partners. A solo lift is just a slow rook.

> A lifted rook with friends is mate. A lifted rook alone is wood.
